source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A chronic autoimmune and digestive disorder in which eating gluten triggers an immune response that damages the small intestine; requires lifelong avoidance of gluten, as there is no cure.
symptoms: Some people have no symptoms at all
clinical_signs: Iron-deficiency anemia on blood testing
Villous atrophy of the small intestine on biopsy
Growth delay in children
Skin rash (dermatitis herpetiformis) in some patients
warning_signs: Severe, persistent diarrhea with signs of dehydration
Significant unintended weight loss
Signs of severe malnutrition or vitamin deficiency
risk_factors: Other autoimmune conditions (type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease)
Certain chromosomal disorders (Down syndrome, Turner syndrome)
causes: Not an infectious disease; occurs when the immune system in a genetically predisposed person reacts abnormally to gluten, a protein in wheat, barley, and rye, damaging the small intestine lining; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent celiac disease itself
Strict lifelong avoidance of gluten is the only way to prevent symptoms and intestinal damage once diagnosed
diagnosis: Diagnosed with blood tests for specific antibodies, followed by a small intestine biopsy to confirm villous damage; genetic testing can help rule out celiac disease in uncertain cases.
treatment: The only effective treatment is a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet, which allows the small intestine to heal and relieves symptoms; working with a registered dietitian can help ensure a balanced diet while avoiding gluten.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent digestive symptoms, unexplained anemia, or unexplained weight loss or growth delay in a child, especially with a family history of celiac disease.
related_conditions: Type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease (associated autoimmune conditions)

description: A chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks myelin, the protective covering of nerves in the brain and spinal cord, disrupting communication between the brain and body; the most common disabling neurological disease of young adults.
symptoms: Vision problems (blurred or double vision, pain with eye movement)
Numbness or tingling in the limbs
clinical_signs: Nystagmus or other abnormal eye movements
Spasticity or abnormal reflexes on neurological exam
Lesions (plaques) visible on brain or spinal cord MRI
Cognitive changes (memory, processing speed)
warning_signs: Sudden, significant vision loss in one eye
Rapidly worsening weakness or loss of bladder/bowel control
Severe new neurological symptoms suggesting an acute relapse needing urgent evaluation
risk_factors: Low vitamin D or reduced sun exposure
causes: Not an infectious disease and not transmitted between people; results from an autoimmune attack on myelin in the central nervous system, likely triggered in genetically susceptible individuals by one or more environmental factors; the precise cause remains unknown.
prevention: No proven way to prevent MS
Not smoking may reduce risk and disease severity
Maintaining adequate vitamin D levels is an area of ongoing research for risk reduction
diagnosis: Diagnosed using a combination of clinical history, neurological examination, MRI of the brain and spinal cord to detect characteristic lesions, and sometimes cerebrospinal fluid analysis; there is no single definitive test.
treatment: There is no cure, but disease-modifying therapies can reduce the frequency and severity of relapses and slow disease progression; corticosteroids are used to treat acute relapses, and symptom-specific treatments and rehabilitation help manage individual symptoms such as spasticity, fatigue, or bladder problems.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for new or worsening neurological symptoms such as vision changes, numbness, weakness, or balance problems, especially if episodic or unexplained.

source: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A progressive, immune-mediated inflammatory condition affecting the joints and the sites where tendons and ligaments attach to bone, occurring in 10-20% of people with psoriasis.
symptoms: Joint stiffness, pain, and swelling in one or more joints
Scaly, inflamed skin patches typical of psoriasis
Nail pitting, thickening, or separation from the nail bed
clinical_signs: Tenderness at sites where tendons attach to bone (enthesitis)
Asymmetric or symmetric joint swelling
Back pain and stiffness (spondylitis) in some patients
Reduced range of motion in affected joints
warning_signs: Sudden, severe joint swelling and pain (rule out infection)
Rapidly progressing joint damage and deformity (arthritis mutilans, a rare severe form)
Eye pain, redness, or vision changes (possible uveitis)
risk_factors: Having psoriasis, the strongest risk factor
causes: Not an infectious disease; caused by an overactive immune system that creates inflammation in the joints and entheses, with genetic and environmental factors contributing; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent psoriatic arthritis
Early treatment of psoriasis and prompt evaluation of new joint symptoms may help reduce joint damage
diagnosis: Diagnosed through a physical exam of skin and joints, patient and family history, and imaging (X-ray, ultrasound, or MRI) to assess joint damage; no single blood test can confirm the diagnosis, though tests help rule out other conditions.
treatment: Treatment includes medications that target both skin and joint symptoms, such as disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and biologic therapies; NSAIDs and corticosteroid injections may help with pain and inflammation, and treatment is often adjusted to reach low or no disease activity.
when_to_seek_care: See a doctor soon if joint pain, stiffness, or swelling develops, especially with a personal or family history of psoriasis, since early treatment is linked to better outcomes and less joint damage.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) / National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), NIH
description: A chronic autoimmune and inflammatory disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy joint tissue, mainly affecting the hands, wrists, and knees, and potentially causing long-lasting pain, instability, and deformity.
symptoms: Joint pain and swelling, usually in multiple joints
Joint stiffness, especially in the morning
clinical_signs: Symmetric joint swelling and warmth
Rheumatoid nodules under the skin
Reduced joint range of motion
Positive rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies on blood testing
warning_signs: Rapid, severe joint swelling and loss of function
Signs of lung involvement (shortness of breath)
Signs of vasculitis (skin ulcers, numbness)
Chest pain (increased cardiovascular risk with RA)
risk_factors: Older age (though it can occur at any age)
Family history and certain genetic factors
causes: Not an infectious disease; caused by the immune system mistakenly attacking the lining of the joints (synovium), leading to chronic inflammation; the exact trigger is unknown, though genetic and environmental factors (such as smoking) increase risk. Not transmitted between people.
prevention: Avoiding tobacco use, which is a known modifiable risk factor
Maintaining a healthy body weight
No guaranteed way to prevent RA, as the exact cause is not fully understood
diagnosis: Diagnosed through clinical examination for joint swelling and tenderness, blood tests (rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibodies, inflammatory markers), and imaging; early diagnosis within six months of symptom onset is recommended to guide timely treatment.
treatment: Managed with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), including biologic therapies, to slow joint damage and control inflammation; supportive care includes physical therapy and pain management.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent joint pain, swelling, or morning stiffness lasting more than a few weeks, especially if it affects multiple joints symmetrically.

source: National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A chronic autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks the glands that produce moisture, most often causing dryness of the eyes and mouth, and predominantly affecting women.
symptoms: Dry eyes (burning, itching, or gritty sensation)
Dry mouth (difficulty chewing, swallowing, or speaking)
Dry cough that doesn't go away
clinical_signs: Reduced tear production on testing (Schirmer's test)
Dental decay and mouth infections such as thrush from lack of saliva
Swollen salivary or lacrimal glands
Skin rashes and vaginal dryness in some patients
warning_signs: Persistent glandular swelling
Unexplained weight loss or persistent fevers
New neurological symptoms or vision disturbances
Signs of lymphoma (persistent swollen lymph nodes), given the increased risk in this condition
risk_factors: Age over 40 at typical onset (though it can occur at any age)
Having another autoimmune condition, such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus
causes: Not an infectious disease; occurs when the immune system attacks the body's own moisture-producing glands, likely from a combination of genetic and environmental factors, possibly triggered by a prior viral or bacterial infection; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent Sjögren's disease
Ongoing dental and eye care can help prevent complications from dryness
Regular monitoring can help detect associated conditions such as lymphoma early
diagnosis: Diagnosed using a combination of symptom evaluation, blood tests for specific antibodies (anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB), eye tests measuring tear production, and sometimes a lip biopsy to examine salivary glands.
treatment: There is no cure, but symptoms are managed with artificial tears and saliva substitutes, medications to stimulate tear and saliva production, and, for systemic or more severe disease, immunosuppressive or biologic medications.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for persistent dry eyes or dry mouth lasting more than a few months, and seek prompt evaluation for glandular swelling, unexplained weight loss, fevers, or new neurological symptoms.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues, potentially causing widespread inflammation and damage to the skin, joints, kidneys, heart, lungs, blood cells, and brain.
symptoms: Skin rash, including a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the cheeks and nose
clinical_signs: Photosensitive skin rash
Oral or nasal ulcers
Proteinuria (sign of kidney involvement)
Low blood cell counts on laboratory testing
warning_signs: Signs of kidney involvement (lupus nephritis): swelling, changes in urination
Neuropsychiatric symptoms: seizures, severe confusion, stroke-like symptoms
Severe chest pain or shortness of breath
High fever with severe illness
risk_factors: Being female (more commonly diagnosed in women)
Family history of lupus or other autoimmune disease
Race/ethnicity (higher prevalence and severity in some populations, including African American women)
causes: Not an infectious disease; the exact cause of lupus is unknown but likely involves a combination of genetic, hormonal, and environmental factors that lead the immune system to attack healthy tissue. Not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent lupus, as the cause is not fully understood
Managing known triggers (e.g., sun protection) can help reduce flares in people already diagnosed
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on a combination of clinical features and laboratory tests, including antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing and other autoantibody panels, along with assessment of organ involvement.
treatment: Main treatment involves medications that suppress the immune system, including hydroxychloroquine, corticosteroids, and biologic therapies such as belimumab or rituximab; treatment is tailored to individual symptoms and organ involvement, with regular monitoring for flares.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent unexplained fatigue, joint pain, or rash, especially a facial rash worsened by sun exposure; seek urgent care for signs of kidney or neurological involvement.

source: World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa / PAHO-WHO
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: An acute diarrheal infection caused by toxigenic Vibrio cholerae that can cause severe dehydration and death within hours if untreated.
clinical_signs: Sunken eyes and skin tenting (dehydration)
Low blood pressure and rapid pulse
Reduced urine output
warning_signs: Severe dehydration
Hypovolemic shock (weak pulse, cold extremities)
In children: fever, extreme drowsiness, convulsions, or coma
risk_factors: Living with HIV or otherwise low immunity
Lack of access to safe water and sanitation
Living in or traveling to endemic or outbreak areas
causes: Caused by toxigenic strains of Vibrio cholerae serogroups O1 and O139; transmitted mainly through ingestion of food or water contaminated with the bacterium; person-to-person transmission is uncommon.
prevention: Access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation
Good food and hand hygiene
Oral cholera vaccines as an additional control measure
Community surveillance and rapid outbreak response
diagnosis: Clinical suspicion in patients with severe acute watery diarrhea, confirmed by laboratory identification of Vibrio cholerae, often as part of outbreak surveillance.
treatment: Prompt oral rehydration solution (ORS) for most cases; severe cases require rapid intravenous fluids and antibiotics.
when_to_seek_care: Seek immediate medical care for severe watery diarrhea and vomiting, especially with signs of dehydration, since cholera can be fatal within hours without treatment.
related_conditions: Other acute infectious gastroenteritis (Shigella, E. coli, rotavirus)

also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A contagious, vaccine-preventable disease caused by toxin-producing Corynebacterium diphtheriae, mainly affecting the upper respiratory tract and sometimes the skin.
clinical_signs: Thick grey membrane covering the throat or tonsils
Enlarged, tender cervical lymph nodes ("bull neck")
Hoarseness or stridor in laryngeal disease
warning_signs: Airway obstruction from the pharyngeal membrane
Signs of myocarditis (irregular heartbeat, chest pain, breathlessness)
Signs of nerve involvement (difficulty swallowing, limb weakness)
risk_factors: Close contact with an infected person or carrier
Travel to areas with ongoing transmission
causes: Caused by toxin-producing strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae; spread through close physical and respiratory contact with an infected person, or contact with infected skin lesions in cutaneous diphtheria.
prevention: Vaccination (multiple primary doses plus booster doses)
Antibiotic prophylaxis for close contacts
Isolation of confirmed cases
diagnosis: Clinical presentation combined with laboratory isolation of toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae by culture (with toxigenicity testing) or PCR.
treatment: Diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) to neutralize circulating toxin, plus antibiotics to eliminate the bacteria and stop toxin production; supportive care including airway management for severe cases.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt medical attention for sore throat with fever, swollen neck glands, or difficulty breathing, particularly if vaccination status is incomplete or unknown.

description: A chronic neglected tropical disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae that primarily affects the skin, peripheral nerves, upper respiratory tract, and eyes; curable with multidrug therapy.
symptoms: Skin patches lighter or reddish compared to surrounding skin
Loss of sensation in affected skin patches
Numbness or tingling in hands or feet
clinical_signs: Palpably thickened peripheral nerves
Loss of eyebrows (in advanced disease)
Skin nodules or plaques in multibacillary disease
warning_signs: Muscle weakness or paralysis, especially of hands and feet
Sudden loss of eyesight
Signs of nerve damage progressing rapidly (reaction states)
risk_factors: Prolonged close contact with an untreated person with leprosy
Living in poverty or crowded conditions
causes: Caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae; thought to spread via inhalation of nasal and oral droplets during prolonged, close contact with an untreated case, not through casual contact.
prevention: Early detection and prompt multidrug therapy to stop transmission
Contact tracing and monitoring of close contacts
Preventive antibiotic treatment for some contacts of cases
diagnosis: Clinical assessment of skin lesions and nerve involvement, classified using the WHO paucibacillary/multibacillary system to guide treatment.
treatment: Multidrug therapy (MDT) combining dapsone, rifampicin, and clofazimine, provided free of charge through WHO; treatment duration is typically 6-12 months or longer depending on disease type.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for unexplained, long-lasting skin patches with numbness, or any loss of sensation or weakness in the hands or feet.

specialty: Infectious Disease, Emergency Medicine, Neurology, Critical Care
description: A severe bacterial infection of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord, caused by Neisseria meningitidis, which can also cause bloodstream infection and be fatal within hours.
clinical_signs: Nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness on examination)
Positive Kernig's or Brudzinski's sign
Petechial or purpuric rash
warning_signs: Hemorrhagic (purple/red) skin rash that does not fade under pressure
Rapid circulatory collapse (septicemia)
Seizures
Loss of consciousness
risk_factors: Living in or traveling to the African meningitis belt or outbreak areas
Close contact with a case or carrier
Young age (infants and young children) or young adulthood
causes: Caused by the bacterium Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus); spread person to person via respiratory droplets or throat secretions from infected individuals or asymptomatic carriers.
prevention: Vaccination against relevant meningococcal serogroups
Antibiotic prophylaxis for close contacts
Avoiding crowded, high-risk settings during outbreaks
diagnosis: Clinical suspicion based on signs and symptoms, confirmed with cerebrospinal fluid analysis and culture or PCR testing.
treatment: Requires urgent hospitalization and treatment with appropriate antibiotics as soon as possible, along with supportive medical care.
when_to_seek_care: Seek emergency medical care immediately for sudden fever with stiff neck, severe headache, confusion, or a rapidly spreading rash, as this is a medical emergency.

description: A highly contagious respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis that is most dangerous for infants and causes prolonged, severe coughing fits.
symptoms: Mild cough progressing to severe coughing fits
"Whooping" sound when gasping for breath after a coughing fit
clinical_signs: Paroxysmal coughing episodes
Post-tussive vomiting
Facial redness or petechiae during coughing spells
warning_signs: Apnea (pauses in breathing) in infants
Cyanosis (turning blue) during coughing fits
Signs of exhaustion or poor feeding in infants
risk_factors: Infants under 1 year, especially unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated
Waning vaccine-induced immunity in adolescents and adults
Close contact with an infected person
causes: Caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis; spread via airborne droplets from coughing or sneezing of an infected person.
prevention: Childhood vaccination (DTaP series)
Adolescent and adult booster vaccination (Tdap)
Vaccination during pregnancy to protect newborns
Good respiratory hygiene
diagnosis: Clinical evaluation of symptoms; laboratory testing of nasal or throat swabs (e.g., PCR) can confirm infection.
treatment: Antibiotics (such as azithromycin, erythromycin, or clarithromycin) can reduce severity and contagiousness if started early; infants and severe cases may require hospitalization.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for a prolonged or severe cough, especially with a "whooping" sound, breathing difficulty, or in infants with any breathing pauses or color changes.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
specialty: Infectious Disease, Emergency Medicine, Critical Care
description: A serious, non-contagious infection caused by a nerve toxin from environmental bacteria entering the body through wounds, leading to muscle stiffness and spasms.
symptoms: Painful muscle stiffness throughout the body
clinical_signs: Risus sardonicus (fixed facial grimace)
Board-like abdominal rigidity
Opisthotonus (arched back from spasms) in severe cases
warning_signs: Generalized muscle spasms triggered by light, sound, or touch
Spasms of the vocal cords or breathing muscles
Elevated blood pressure and rapid heart rate (autonomic instability)
risk_factors: Never vaccinated or not up to date with tetanus boosters
Unhygienic umbilical cord care in newborns (neonatal tetanus)
causes: Caused by the toxin tetanospasmin, produced by Clostridium tetani spores that enter the body through breaks in the skin; not spread from person to person.
prevention: Up-to-date tetanus vaccination throughout life (part of DTaP/Tdap series)
Proper wound cleaning and care
Tetanus prophylaxis after high-risk wounds
Clean birth practices to prevent neonatal tetanus
diagnosis: Based on clinical signs and a history of a wound or injury; there is no laboratory test that can confirm or rule out tetanus.
treatment: Requires immediate hospitalization; treatment includes tetanus immune globulin (TIG), wound care, medications to control muscle spasms, and supportive care which may include mechanical ventilation.
when_to_seek_care: Seek immediate medical care for a contaminated or deep wound, especially if vaccination status is not up to date, or for any jaw stiffness or muscle spasms after an injury.

specialty: Infectious Disease, Pulmonology (Neurology or Orthopedics if extrapulmonary)
description: A chronic infectious disease, most often affecting the lungs, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis; preventable and curable with antibiotics, but a leading infectious cause of death worldwide.
symptoms: Prolonged cough (2+ weeks), sometimes with blood
clinical_signs: Crackles or reduced breath sounds on chest auscultation
Cachexia in advanced disease
Lymphadenopathy in extrapulmonary TB
Abnormal chest X-ray findings (cavitation, infiltrates)
warning_signs: Coughing up blood (hemoptysis)
Severe difficulty breathing
Signs of meningitis (in TB meningitis: headache, neck stiffness, confusion)
Rapid, unexplained weight loss with high fever
risk_factors: Close contact with someone who has active TB
Living or working in crowded/high-burden settings
causes: Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis; spread through the air when a person with active pulmonary TB coughs, sneezes, or spits, releasing infectious droplets that others inhale.
prevention: BCG vaccination for infants/children in high-burden settings
Early diagnosis and prompt treatment of active cases
TB preventive treatment for high-risk contacts
Good ventilation and respiratory hygiene
Screening of close contacts and high-risk groups
diagnosis: WHO-recommended rapid molecular tests or biomarker-based point-of-care tests as the initial test; sputum smear microscopy and culture; tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) to detect infection; chest imaging.
treatment: Standard treatment uses a combination of antibiotics (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 4-6 months. Drug-resistant TB requires alternative regimens, including shorter all-oral regimens (e.g., BPaLM/BPaL) for eligible patients per WHO guidance.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for a cough lasting more than 2-3 weeks, unexplained weight loss, fever, or night sweats, especially with known TB exposure or HIV infection.

description: A life-threatening infection caused by Salmonella Typhi that spreads through contaminated food and water, remaining a public health problem where sanitation is inadequate.
clinical_signs: Relative bradycardia (slow pulse relative to fever height)
Rose-colored spots on the trunk (uncommon)
Abdominal tenderness
Hepatosplenomegaly
warning_signs: Confusion or delirium
Severe abdominal pain suggesting intestinal perforation
Gastrointestinal bleeding
Signs of shock
risk_factors: Lack of access to safe water and sanitation
Consuming food from street vendors in endemic areas
Close contact with a chronic carrier
causes: Caused by the bacterium Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi; spread through the fecal-oral route via contaminated food or water, or direct person-to-person spread.
prevention: Typhoid conjugate vaccine
Safe drinking water and adequate sanitation
Hand hygiene, especially before food handling and after toilet use
Avoiding unwashed raw produce and unpasteurized dairy
diagnosis: Confirmed through blood culture; the bacteria may also be identified in stool or other body fluids.
treatment: Antibiotic treatment; choice of antibiotic depends on local resistance patterns given increasing antimicrobial resistance, including multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant strains.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for prolonged fever with headache, fatigue, and abdominal symptoms, particularly after travel to an endemic area or known exposure.

source: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A rare but serious blood disorder in which the bone marrow fails to make enough new blood cells, most often because the immune system mistakenly attacks blood-forming stem cells; can develop suddenly or gradually and range from mild to life-threatening.
clinical_signs: Unexplained or easy bruising
Nosebleeds and bleeding gums
Pale skin
Low counts of red cells, white cells, and platelets on blood testing (pancytopenia)
warning_signs: Signs of serious infection (high fever, chills) due to very low white blood cell counts
Significant, spontaneous bleeding, including blood in urine or stool
Severe shortness of breath or chest pain from severe anemia
Signs of intracranial bleeding (severe headache, confusion)
risk_factors: Some inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (in a minority of cases)
causes: Not an infectious disease; most often caused by an autoimmune process in which the immune system attacks and destroys hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow; some cases are inherited, but most are acquired and not transmitted between people.
prevention: Avoiding known toxic chemical exposures when possible
No proven way to prevent most cases, since the cause is often unclear
diagnosis: Diagnosed through blood tests showing low counts of all blood cell types (pancytopenia), confirmed with a bone marrow biopsy showing reduced blood-forming cells.
treatment: Treatment may include immunosuppressive therapy to stop the immune attack on the bone marrow, blood and platelet transfusions to manage symptoms, medications that stimulate blood cell production, or a stem cell (bone marrow) transplant, which can be curative in eligible patients.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt medical evaluation for persistent unexplained fatigue, frequent infections, or easy bruising and bleeding, and seek emergency care for high fever, significant bleeding, or severe shortness of breath.
related_conditions: Myelodysplastic syndrome (a related bone marrow disorder)
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (an associated condition in some patients)
Leukemia (differential and a rare later complication)
Fanconi anemia (an inherited cause in some cases)

source: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
specialty: Hematology, Internal Medicine, Gastroenterology (when bleeding is suspected)
description: The most common type of anemia, occurring when the body lacks enough iron to make sufficient hemoglobin for red blood cells to carry oxygen effectively; a leading global indicator of poor nutrition and health.
clinical_signs: Pallor of the skin and mucous membranes
Low hemoglobin and low ferritin on blood testing
Small, pale red blood cells on blood smear (microcytic, hypochromic)
Brittle nails or hair thinning in longstanding deficiency
warning_signs: Chest pain or rapid heartbeat
Severe shortness of breath at rest
Fainting or severe dizziness
Signs of significant gastrointestinal bleeding (black stool, vomiting blood)
risk_factors: Gastrointestinal conditions affecting absorption (celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease)
Chronic blood loss (e.g., from ulcers or gastrointestinal cancers)
Infancy and young childhood during rapid growth
causes: Not an infectious disease; caused by inadequate iron intake, impaired absorption, or chronic blood loss, all of which reduce the iron available to make hemoglobin; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Eating iron-rich foods (meat, beans, leafy greens) or fortified foods
Iron supplementation during pregnancy or for other high-risk groups as advised by a healthcare provider
Identifying and treating sources of chronic blood loss
diagnosis: Diagnosed with blood tests showing low hemoglobin and low ferritin (iron stores); further testing may be needed to identify an underlying cause, such as gastrointestinal bleeding.
treatment: Treated with oral iron supplements in most cases, or intravenous iron for those who cannot tolerate or absorb oral iron; addressing the underlying cause of iron loss or poor absorption is essential for lasting treatment.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare professional for persistent fatigue, shortness of breath, or pale skin rather than self-diagnosing or self-treating with iron supplements, since excess iron can be harmful and the underlying cause needs evaluation.
related_conditions: Gastrointestinal bleeding sources (peptic ulcer, colorectal cancer)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A common and painful type of inflammatory arthritis caused by the buildup of uric acid crystals in and around joints, most classically affecting the big toe, occurring in episodic flares.
symptoms: Sudden, intense joint pain, often starting at night
Swelling, redness, and warmth in the affected joint
Tenderness so severe that even light touch is painful
Lingering joint discomfort after the worst pain subsides
clinical_signs: Visible joint swelling and redness, most classically at the base of the big toe
Uric acid crystals identified in joint fluid under a microscope
Tophi (chalky nodules of uric acid crystals) in longstanding, uncontrolled disease
warning_signs: High fever with a hot, swollen joint (possible joint infection requiring urgent evaluation)
Rapidly increasing joint swelling with systemic symptoms (fever, chills)
Draining or ulcerated tophi
risk_factors: Diet high in purine-rich foods (red meat, organ meats, shellfish) and sugary drinks/foods
causes: Not an infectious disease; caused by elevated uric acid levels in the blood leading to the formation of needle-like urate crystals in joints, which trigger intense inflammation; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Limiting alcohol, especially beer and hard liquor
Reducing intake of purine-rich foods and sugary foods/drinks
Maintaining a healthy weight
Staying physically active
Taking prescribed uric acid-lowering medication as directed if previously diagnosed
diagnosis: Diagnosed most definitively by identifying uric acid crystals in fluid drawn from the affected joint, typically during a flare; blood uric acid levels and clinical presentation also support diagnosis.
treatment: Flares are treated with anti-inflammatory and pain-relieving medications (such as NSAIDs); prescription medications that lower uric acid levels can prevent future flares and the formation of tophi in people with recurrent gout.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for sudden, severe joint pain and swelling to confirm the diagnosis and start treatment, and seek urgent care if a hot, swollen joint is accompanied by fever, which could indicate infection rather than a gout flare.
related_conditions: Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, a differential)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
specialty: Rheumatology, Orthopedics, Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
description: The most common type of arthritis, in which the cartilage and other tissues of a joint break down over time, most often affecting the hands, hips, back, and knees, causing pain and reduced function; not considered a normal part of aging.
symptoms: Joint pain during or after use
Joint stiffness, especially in the morning or after rest
clinical_signs: Crepitus (a grating sensation or sound with joint movement)
Bony enlargement around affected joints
Tenderness on joint examination
Joint space narrowing visible on X-ray
warning_signs: Sudden, severe joint swelling with warmth and fever (possible joint infection, requiring urgent evaluation)
Rapidly worsening joint deformity or inability to bear weight
Signs of a blood clot (calf swelling and pain) after joint surgery
risk_factors: Repetitive joint stress from certain occupations or sports
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from the breakdown of cartilage and other joint tissues over time due to mechanical stress, prior injury, and biological factors; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Maintaining a healthy weight to reduce joint stress
Regular low-impact physical activity
Protecting joints from injury during sports and physical activity
Managing joint injuries promptly to reduce long-term risk
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on a clinical history and physical examination of joint symptoms, supported by X-rays showing joint space narrowing and other characteristic changes.
treatment: There is no cure, but symptoms can be managed with physical activity, weight management, physical therapy, over-the-counter or prescription pain relievers, and supportive devices; joint replacement surgery may be considered for severe, advanced disease.
when_to_seek_care: Talk with a healthcare provider about persistent joint pain, stiffness, or swelling that affects daily activities, and seek urgent care for sudden severe joint swelling with fever, which could indicate infection.
related_conditions: Bursitis and tendinitis (differential for localized joint pain)
Osteoporosis (a distinct but related bone condition)

source: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A disease in which bones become weak and brittle due to loss of bone mass and deterioration of bone tissue, greatly increasing the risk of fractures; there are typically no symptoms until a bone breaks.
symptoms: Usually none until a fracture occurs
Back pain from a collapsed or fractured vertebra
clinical_signs: Low bone mineral density on DEXA (bone density) scan
Curved upper back (kyphosis) from vertebral compression fractures
Fractures occurring from relatively minor falls or stress
warning_signs: Sudden, severe back pain (possible vertebral fracture)
A fracture from a minor fall or bump, especially of the hip, spine, or wrist
Sudden loss of height or new stooped posture
risk_factors: Family history of osteoporosis or fractures
Low calcium and vitamin D intake
Long-term use of certain medications (e.g., glucocorticoids)
causes: Not an infectious disease; occurs when the creation of new bone does not keep up with the removal of old bone, most often related to hormonal changes (such as reduced estrogen after menopause), aging, and lifestyle or medication factors; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake throughout life
Regular weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercise
Avoiding smoking and limiting alcohol intake
Fall-prevention measures for older adults
Bone density screening for those at higher risk
diagnosis: Diagnosed primarily using a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) bone density scan, which measures bone mineral density and fracture risk.
treatment: Managed with adequate calcium and vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, fall prevention, and medications such as bisphosphonates that slow bone loss or, in some cases, medicines that help build new bone.
when_to_seek_care: Speak with a healthcare provider about bone density screening, especially after menopause or with risk factors, and seek prompt care for a fracture from a minor fall, sudden back pain, or new loss of height.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: The most common type of skin cancer, arising from basal cells in the outer layer of skin; grows slowly and rarely spreads elsewhere, but can cause significant local damage if not treated.
symptoms: A new, expanding, or changing growth, spot, or bump on the skin
A sore that bleeds and doesn't heal after several weeks
A shiny, pearly bump, often pink, red, or skin-colored
A rough or scaly red patch
clinical_signs: Small, visible blood vessels on the surface of the lesion
A central indentation or ulcer with raised, pearly edges
Slow growth over months or years
Most common on sun-exposed areas (face, ears, neck, scalp)
warning_signs: A sore that bleeds repeatedly or won't heal
Rapid growth or change in a skin lesion
A lesion that becomes painful or itchy
Large or deeply invasive lesions near the eyes, nose, or ears
risk_factors: Cumulative sun exposure over a lifetime
Fair skin, light eyes, or light hair
History of sunburns, especially in childhood
Family or personal history of skin cancer
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from DNA damage to basal cells caused mainly by ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun or tanning devices; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Seeking shade and avoiding peak sun hours
Wearing protective clothing and broad-spectrum sunscreen
Avoiding tanning beds
Regular skin self-exams and professional skin checks
diagnosis: Diagnosed through visual examination of the skin, confirmed with a skin biopsy to examine the tissue under a microscope.
treatment: Highly treatable, most often with surgical removal (including Mohs surgery for sensitive areas); other options include topical medications, cryotherapy, or radiation therapy depending on the size and location.
when_to_seek_care: See a dermatologist for any new, changing, or non-healing skin growth or sore, particularly on sun-exposed skin.
related_conditions: Squamous cell carcinoma (another common skin cancer)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A cancer that begins in the cells lining the bladder, most often diagnosed in older adults; blood in the urine is the most common warning sign.
symptoms: Blood in the urine (hematuria), often without pain
Feeling the need to urinate without being able to
Lower back pain on one side
clinical_signs: Visible or microscopic blood detected on urinalysis
A pelvic mass in more advanced cases
Urinary frequency or urgency without a clear infection
warning_signs: Heavy or persistent blood in the urine
Inability to urinate
Unexplained weight loss with urinary symptoms
Bone pain or persistent fatigue (possible signs of spread)
risk_factors: Smoking, the most important risk factor
Exposure to certain workplace chemicals (used in dye, rubber, leather, and paint industries)
causes: Not an infectious disease; usually results from acquired DNA changes in bladder cells over a person's lifetime, often related to exposure to tobacco smoke or certain chemicals; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Not smoking, which prevents about half of all cases
Limiting exposure to certain workplace chemicals
Drinking plenty of fluids
Prompt evaluation and treatment of blood in the urine
diagnosis: Diagnosed with urine tests, imaging of the urinary tract, and cystoscopy (direct visual examination of the bladder) with biopsy to confirm the diagnosis.
treatment: Treatment depends on how deeply the cancer has invaded the bladder wall and may include transurethral resection, intravesical therapy (medication placed directly in the bladder, including BCG immunotherapy), chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or removal of the bladder (cystectomy) for more advanced disease.
when_to_seek_care: Talk to a doctor about any blood in the urine or unusual, persistent changes in urination, since these symptoms can also come from other conditions but should always be evaluated.
related_conditions: Prostate conditions (differential for urinary symptoms in men)
Schistosomiasis (a risk factor in endemic areas)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A cancer that forms in breast tissue, most commonly in the ducts or lobules; the most common cancer in women in most countries worldwide, though roughly half of cases occur in women with no specific risk factors other than sex and age.
symptoms: A new lump or mass in the breast or underarm
Change in the size or shape of the breast
Skin dimpling or changes on the breast
clinical_signs: Palpable, often painless breast lump
Skin retraction or dimpling ('peau d'orange')
Nipple retraction or discharge
Axillary lymphadenopathy
warning_signs: Bone pain (possible sign of metastasis)
Unexplained shortness of breath
Unexplained weight loss
Yellowing of the skin (advanced/metastatic disease)
risk_factors: Being female and older age (the two primary risk factors)
Family history of breast or ovarian cancer, including inherited BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations
Early menstruation or late menopause (longer hormone exposure)
Not having children, or having them later in life
Obesity, alcohol use, and physical inactivity
causes: Not an infectious disease; arises from genetic mutations in breast cells, most of which develop during a person's lifetime rather than being inherited; a smaller proportion of cases are linked to inherited mutations (e.g., BRCA1/BRCA2). Not transmitted between people.
prevention: Maintaining a healthy body weight
Regular physical activity
Limiting alcohol consumption
Breastfeeding, which may lower risk
Regular screening (mammography) for early detection
Risk-reducing options for those with high-risk genetic mutations, guided by a specialist
diagnosis: Diagnosed through clinical breast examination, imaging (mammography, ultrasound, or MRI), and confirmed with a tissue biopsy; genetic testing may be offered for those with strong family history.
treatment: Treatment depends on cancer type and stage and may include surgery (lumpectomy or mastectomy), radiation therapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, and targeted therapies, often used in combination.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt medical evaluation for any new breast lump, change in breast shape or skin, or nipple changes or discharge; follow recommended screening schedules even without symptoms, as early detection improves outcomes.
related_conditions: Ovarian cancer (shared genetic risk with BRCA mutations)

description: A cancer of the cervix, almost always caused by persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV); a highly preventable and, if caught early, curable cancer through vaccination and screening.
symptoms: Often no symptoms in early or precancerous stages
Vaginal bleeding, including after intercourse or between periods
clinical_signs: Abnormal cervical cells detected on screening (Pap test or HPV test)
Visible cervical lesion on examination in more advanced disease
Pain during sexual intercourse
warning_signs: Heavy or persistent vaginal bleeding
Severe pelvic or back pain
Unexplained weight loss (advanced disease)
Swelling of the legs (advanced disease affecting lymphatics)
risk_factors: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types (especially HPV 16 and 18)
Multiple sexual partners or early sexual activity
Lack of access to cervical cancer screening
causes: Almost all cases (95-100%) are caused by long-term infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), a common sexually transmitted infection; most HPV infections clear on their own, but persistent infection can lead to precancerous changes and, over years, cervical cancer.
prevention: HPV vaccination, most effective when given to girls aged 9-14 before HPV exposure
Regular cervical cancer screening starting at age 30 (or age 25 for women living with HIV)
Prompt treatment of precancerous lesions detected on screening
Avoiding tobacco use
diagnosis: Screening uses HPV testing or Pap (cytology) testing to detect precancerous changes; diagnosis of cancer is confirmed with colposcopy and biopsy of abnormal cervical tissue.
treatment: Precancerous lesions can be treated with simple outpatient procedures; invasive cervical cancer treatment depends on stage and may include surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, often in combination.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for abnormal vaginal bleeding, unusual discharge, or pelvic pain, and follow recommended cervical cancer screening schedules even without symptoms, since precancerous changes rarely cause symptoms.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
also_known_as: Colon cancer, bowel cancer, rectal cancer
description: A cancer that develops when cells in the colon or rectum grow out of control, often starting as a polyp; one of the most preventable and, when caught early, most curable cancers through regular screening.
symptoms: Blood in or on the stool
Diarrhea, constipation, or a feeling that the bowel doesn't empty completely
Abdominal pain, aches, or cramps that don't go away
clinical_signs: Low red blood cell count (anemia) found on blood testing
Abnormal mass detected on rectal or abdominal examination
Narrowing of stool caliber
warning_signs: Significant rectal bleeding
Signs of bowel obstruction (severe abdominal pain, inability to pass stool or gas, vomiting)
Jaundice or an enlarged liver felt on exam (possible spread to the liver)
Unexplained, persistent weight loss
risk_factors: Family history of colorectal cancer or polyps
Diet high in processed and red meat, low in fruits/vegetables/whole grains
causes: Not an infectious disease; most cases arise from precancerous polyps that develop genetic changes over time, influenced by lifestyle factors and, in some cases, inherited genetic syndromes; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Routine colorectal cancer screening (colonoscopy or other tests) starting at age 45
Removal of precancerous polyps found during screening
Maintaining a healthy weight and regular physical activity
Limiting red and processed meat, alcohol, and tobacco use
diagnosis: Diagnosed through colonoscopy with biopsy of suspicious tissue; imaging (CT scan) and blood tests help determine the extent of disease.
treatment: Treatment depends on stage and location and typically includes surgery to remove the tumor, often combined with chemotherapy and, for rectal cancer, radiation therapy.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for blood in the stool, a persistent change in bowel habits, unexplained abdominal pain, or unintended weight loss; follow recommended screening schedules starting at age 45 even without symptoms.

icd11: 2C90 (Malignant neoplasms of kidney, except renal pelvis)
source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A cancer that forms in the tissues of the kidney, most commonly renal cell carcinoma; often found incidentally on imaging done for other reasons, since early-stage disease frequently causes no symptoms.
symptoms: Pain or a lump in the side or lower back
Loss of appetite and unexplained weight loss
clinical_signs: A palpable abdominal or flank mass on examination
Persistently elevated blood pressure
Low red blood cell count (anemia) on blood testing
Elevated calcium levels in some cases
warning_signs: Heavy or persistent blood in the urine
Rapid, unexplained weight loss
New, persistent bone pain (possible sign of spread)
Sudden severe flank pain
risk_factors: Certain inherited conditions (e.g., von Hippel-Lindau disease)
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from genetic changes in kidney cells that accumulate over time, influenced by lifestyle factors and, in some cases, inherited genetic syndromes; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Not smoking
Maintaining a healthy weight
Managing blood pressure
Limiting exposure to certain industrial chemicals when possible
diagnosis: Diagnosed through imaging (CT or MRI scan), often after blood is found in the urine or a mass is discovered incidentally; biopsy may be used to confirm the diagnosis in some cases.
treatment: Surgery to remove part or all of the affected kidney is the primary treatment for localized disease; targeted therapy and immunotherapy are used for more advanced or metastatic kidney cancer.
when_to_seek_care: See a doctor for blood in the urine, persistent flank or back pain, or an unexplained lump in the abdomen or side.
related_conditions: Bladder cancer (differential for blood in urine)

source: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A group of cancers of the blood-forming tissues, including bone marrow, characterized by abnormal growth of white blood cells that crowd out normal blood cells; classified as acute or chronic and by the type of blood cell involved (myeloid or lymphocytic).
clinical_signs: Pallor from anemia
Petechiae (tiny red spots) from low platelets
Enlarged liver or spleen on examination
Abnormal white blood cell counts on complete blood count
warning_signs: Uncontrolled bleeding or extensive bruising
High fever with signs of severe infection
Severe bone pain
Signs of significantly enlarged spleen (early fullness, left-sided abdominal pain) with risk of rupture
risk_factors: Older age for most types (though some types occur mainly in children)
Exposure to benzene and certain other chemicals
causes: Not an infectious disease and not transmitted between people; results from genetic mutations in developing blood cells in the bone marrow that cause abnormal, uncontrolled growth of white blood cells; in most cases the specific trigger for these mutations is unknown.
prevention: No proven way to prevent most leukemias
Avoiding tobacco use and limiting exposure to known chemical carcinogens such as benzene when possible
Limiting unnecessary radiation exposure
diagnosis: Diagnosed through blood tests showing abnormal blood cell counts, followed by bone marrow aspiration and biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and identify the specific type of leukemia.
treatment: Treatment depends on the type and can include chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, radiation therapy, and stem cell transplantation; some slow-growing chronic leukemias may only require monitoring initially rather than immediate treatment.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent unexplained fatigue, fever, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, or swollen lymph nodes, so that blood testing can be done to investigate the cause.

description: The leading cause of cancer death worldwide, arising from malignant cells in the lung tissue; strongly linked to tobacco smoking, though it also occurs in people who have never smoked.
symptoms: Coughing up blood or bloody/rust-colored sputum
Unexplained weight loss and loss of appetite
clinical_signs: Hoarse voice
New wheezing
Recurrent pneumonia or bronchitis
Abnormal findings on chest imaging
warning_signs: Significant hemoptysis (coughing up blood)
Severe or worsening shortness of breath
Facial or arm swelling (possible superior vena cava obstruction)
Signs of spread such as bone pain, neurological symptoms, or jaundice
risk_factors: Tobacco smoking (responsible for about 80% of lung cancer deaths)
Occupational exposure to asbestos, arsenic, and other carcinogens
Previous radiation therapy to the chest
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from accumulated genetic damage to lung cells, most commonly from inhaled tobacco smoke or other carcinogens; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Avoiding or quitting tobacco use
Avoiding secondhand smoke exposure
Testing homes for radon and mitigating high levels
Minimizing occupational exposure to known lung carcinogens
Screening with low-dose CT for eligible high-risk individuals
diagnosis: Diagnosed through imaging (chest X-ray or CT scan) followed by tissue biopsy to confirm cancer type; further staging tests assess the extent of spread.
treatment: Treatment depends on cancer type and stage and may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted molecular therapies, and immune checkpoint inhibitors, often used in combination.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for a persistent cough, coughing up blood, unexplained weight loss, or chest pain, especially in people with significant smoking history or other risk factors.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: The most serious type of skin cancer, arising from pigment-producing skin cells; less common than other skin cancers but more likely to spread if not caught and treated early.
symptoms: A new mole or growth on the skin
A change in the size, shape, or color of an existing mole
A small scaly patch or rash
clinical_signs: Asymmetry (one half of the mole doesn't match the other)
Irregular or blurred border
Multiple colors or shades within one spot
Diameter larger than a pencil eraser (about 6mm)
Evolving size, shape, or color over time (the "ABCDE" signs)
warning_signs: A mole that bleeds, itches, or becomes painful
Rapid growth or change in an existing mole
A new dark spot that stands out from the person's other moles ("ugly duckling" sign)
A sore that does not heal within several weeks
risk_factors: Skin that burns, freckles, or reddens easily in the sun
History of sunburns, especially in childhood, or tanning bed use
Family or personal history of skin cancer
Blue or green eyes, blond or red hair
causes: Not an infectious disease; most cases are caused by DNA damage to skin cells from ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure from the sun or tanning devices; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Seeking shade, especially between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. when UV rays are strongest
Wearing protective clothing, hats, and sunglasses
Using broad-spectrum sunscreen
Avoiding tanning beds
Regular skin self-exams and professional skin checks, especially for those at higher risk
diagnosis: Diagnosed through visual examination using the ABCDE criteria, followed by a skin biopsy of any suspicious lesion to confirm the diagnosis and determine how deep it has grown.
treatment: Treatment typically involves surgical removal of the tumor; more advanced or spreading melanoma may also be treated with immunotherapy, targeted therapy, radiation therapy, or chemotherapy.
when_to_seek_care: See a doctor for any new or changing mole, a sore that doesn't heal, or any skin spot showing the ABCDE warning signs, since early detection greatly improves treatment success.
related_conditions: Basal cell carcinoma (a more common, less aggressive skin cancer)
Squamous cell carcinoma (another common skin cancer)
Atypical (dysplastic) moles (a risk marker and differential)

icd11: 2B60-2B6Y (Malignant neoplasms of lip, oral cavity or pharynx)
source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
specialty: Otolaryngology (ENT), Oncology, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery
description: Cancers that develop in the tissues of the mouth (oral cavity) or the middle part of the throat (oropharynx); strongly linked to tobacco and alcohol use, with a growing share of oropharyngeal cases caused by HPV.
symptoms: A sore on the lip or in the mouth that doesn't heal
A lump or thickening in the cheek or neck
Difficulty chewing, swallowing, or moving the jaw or tongue
clinical_signs: A white or red patch on the gums, tongue, or lining of the mouth
Unexplained bleeding in the mouth
Numbness in the mouth, lip, or face
Persistent sore throat, earache, or hoarseness (more typical of oropharyngeal cancer)
warning_signs: A mouth or throat sore or lump lasting more than a few weeks
Unexplained, significant weight loss
A lump in the neck (possible spread to lymph nodes)
New difficulty breathing or swallowing
risk_factors: Tobacco use, including smokeless tobacco and betel nut
Heavy alcohol use, especially combined with tobacco use
causes: Not an infectious disease itself, though HPV infection (a risk factor for many oropharyngeal cancers) is sexually transmitted; results from genetic changes in cells of the mouth or throat, most often driven by tobacco, alcohol, or HPV exposure.
prevention: Avoiding all forms of tobacco
Limiting alcohol use
HPV vaccination to reduce the risk of HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer
Regular dental checkups, which often include an oral cancer screening
diagnosis: Diagnosed through visual and physical examination of the mouth and throat, followed by biopsy of any suspicious area; imaging tests help determine the extent of disease.
treatment: Treatment depends on the location and stage and may include surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, often used in combination; HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers generally respond well to treatment.
when_to_seek_care: See a dentist or doctor for any mouth sore, lump, or patch that doesn't heal within a few weeks, or for persistent throat pain, difficulty swallowing, or unexplained weight loss.
related_conditions: Genital HPV infection (shared risk factor for oropharyngeal cases)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A group of cancers originating in the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or peritoneum; often causes few or vague symptoms early on, making it harder to detect at an early, more treatable stage.
symptoms: Difficulty eating or feeling full quickly
clinical_signs: Abdominal distension from fluid buildup (ascites)
Palpable pelvic mass on examination
Constipation or changes in bowel habits
warning_signs: Persistent, new, or worsening bloating, pelvic pain, or feeling full quickly that occurs almost daily for more than a
few weeks
Significant unexplained abdominal swelling
Rapid, unexplained weight change with abdominal symptoms
risk_factors: Inherited gene mutations (BRCA1, BRCA2, Lynch syndrome)
Family history of ovarian or breast cancer
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from genetic changes in ovarian, fallopian tube, or peritoneal cells that accumulate over time, with some cases linked to inherited gene mutations; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Use of oral contraceptives, which lowers risk with longer use
Pregnancy and breastfeeding are associated with lower risk
Genetic counseling and risk-reducing surgery for those with high-risk inherited mutations
There is no recommended general population screening test
diagnosis: Diagnosed through pelvic examination, imaging (transvaginal ultrasound), blood tests such as CA-125, and confirmed with tissue biopsy, usually obtained during surgery.
treatment: Treatment typically involves surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible, combined with chemotherapy; targeted therapies may be used depending on tumor characteristics, such as BRCA mutation status.
when_to_seek_care: See a doctor if new or worsening bloating, pelvic pain, or early fullness occurs almost daily for more than a few weeks, since these symptoms may have other causes but should always be evaluated.
related_conditions: Breast cancer (shared genetic risk with BRCA mutations)
Irritable bowel syndrome (common misdiagnosis due to overlapping symptoms)

source: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A cancer that forms in the tissues of the pancreas, often producing few or non-specific symptoms until the disease is advanced, making it one of the more difficult cancers to detect and treat early.
symptoms: Pain in the upper abdomen or back
clinical_signs: Jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes) from bile duct obstruction
Dark urine and light-colored stools
Palpable abdominal mass or fluid buildup (ascites) in advanced disease
warning_signs: New-onset jaundice, especially painless
Rapid, significant unintended weight loss
Sudden new diabetes diagnosis in an older adult without typical risk factors (can be an early sign)
Persistent abdominal pain radiating to the back
risk_factors: Certain inherited genetic syndromes (including BRCA2 mutations)
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from genetic changes in pancreatic cells that accumulate over time, influenced by lifestyle and, in some cases, inherited genetic mutations; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Not smoking
Maintaining a healthy weight
Limiting alcohol use, which can contribute to chronic pancreatitis
Genetic counseling for those with strong family history
diagnosis: Diagnosed using imaging (CT or MRI scan), blood tests including the CA 19-9 tumor marker, and confirmed with a tissue biopsy.
treatment: Treatment depends on whether the tumor can be surgically removed and may include surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy; because the disease is often diagnosed at an advanced stage, treatment frequently focuses on controlling growth and managing symptoms.
when_to_seek_care: See a doctor for persistent abdominal or back pain, unexplained weight loss, or jaundice, especially if these symptoms persist beyond a couple of weeks.
related_conditions: Chronic pancreatitis (a risk factor and differential)
Diabetes (can be an early sign or a risk factor)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) / U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A cancer that forms in the prostate gland of the male reproductive system; the most common cancer among men (aside from skin cancer) in many countries, and often slow-growing.
clinical_signs: Elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) on blood testing
Abnormal findings on digital rectal exam
Urinary hesitancy or urgency
warning_signs: Chronic pain in the back, hips, or pelvis (possible bone metastasis)
Unintended weight loss
Leg weakness or numbness, or loss of bladder/bowel control (possible spinal cord compression from metastatic
disease)
risk_factors: Older age (average age at diagnosis is 70)
Family history of prostate cancer, especially a first-degree relative diagnosed young
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from genetic changes in prostate cells accumulating over time, with age, race, and family history as the main known risk contributors; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No proven way to prevent prostate cancer, since major risk factors (age, race, family history) can't be controlled
Maintaining a healthy weight and regular physical activity may help lower risk
A diet with plenty of fruits and vegetables and limited red/processed meat may help lower risk
diagnosis: Screening uses a PSA blood test, sometimes with digital rectal examination; diagnosis is confirmed with a prostate tissue biopsy, usually guided by imaging.
treatment: Options include active surveillance for low-risk, slow-growing cancers, as well as surgery (prostatectomy), radiation therapy, hormone therapy, and chemotherapy for more advanced disease, chosen based on cancer risk and patient factors.
when_to_seek_care: Speak with a healthcare professional about screening starting around age 55 (earlier if higher risk), and seek evaluation for urinary symptoms, blood in urine or semen, or unexplained pelvic or back pain.

source: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A cancer that develops in the tissues of the thyroid gland; most cases are found early because they cause a noticeable lump or nodule in the neck, and most types have a very favorable prognosis when treated.
symptoms: Often no symptoms early on; frequently found as a lump felt during a routine exam
A lump or swelling in the neck
A feeling of fullness or a lump sensation in the throat
clinical_signs: A firm, painless thyroid nodule on physical examination
Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck
Abnormal findings on thyroid ultrasound
warning_signs: A rapidly growing neck mass
New or worsening difficulty breathing or swallowing
Persistent hoarseness lasting more than a few weeks
A hard, fixed neck lump
risk_factors: Radiation exposure to the head or neck, especially in childhood
Family history of thyroid cancer or certain genetic syndromes (such as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2)
History of goiter or other thyroid disease
Most solitary thyroid nodules found in people under 30 or over 60
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from genetic changes in thyroid cells, with radiation exposure being one of the few well-established environmental risk factors; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Avoiding unnecessary radiation exposure to the head and neck, especially in children
Genetic counseling and testing for families with hereditary thyroid cancer syndromes
Prompt evaluation of any new thyroid nodule or neck lump
diagnosis: Diagnosed through physical examination, thyroid ultrasound to characterize any nodules, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy to determine whether a nodule is cancerous.
treatment: Treatment usually involves surgery to remove part or all of the thyroid gland, often followed by radioactive iodine therapy to destroy remaining thyroid tissue; lifelong thyroid hormone replacement is typically needed after surgery, and targeted therapies are available for advanced or recurrent disease.
when_to_seek_care: See a doctor for any new lump or swelling in the neck, persistent hoarseness, or difficulty swallowing, even though most thyroid nodules turn out to be benign.
related_conditions: Benign thyroid nodules (much more common differential)
Hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism (can coexist or follow treatment)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (associated genetic syndrome)

source: National Institutes of Health (NIH), NIH News in Health
description: A condition in which a blood clot forms in a deep vein, most often in the leg; can be serious because part of the clot can break off and travel to the lungs, causing a pulmonary embolism.
symptoms: Swelling in the affected leg, ankle, or foot, usually on one side
Cramping pain, often starting in the calf
Skin that appears red, pale, or bluish over the clot
clinical_signs: Unilateral leg swelling on examination
Tenderness along the affected vein
Approximately 30-40% of cases have no noticeable symptoms
warning_signs: Sudden shortness of breath or rapid breathing (possible pulmonary embolism, a medical emergency)
Chest pain that worsens with coughing or deep breathing
Coughing up blood
Dizziness or fainting
risk_factors: Prolonged immobility (long flights, bed rest, surgery)
Combined oral contraceptive or hormone therapy use
Personal or family history of DVT or pulmonary embolism
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from a combination of factors that promote blood clotting, including slowed blood flow, blood vessel damage, and increased clotting tendency; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Moving legs regularly during long periods of sitting or immobility
Walking as soon as possible after surgery or illness
Staying well hydrated during travel
Using preventive blood thinners or compression devices when recommended after surgery or hospitalization
diagnosis: Diagnosed through a physical exam combined with imaging, most commonly a compression ultrasound of the affected leg; blood tests such as D-dimer can help support or rule out the diagnosis.
treatment: Treated with anticoagulant (blood-thinning) medications to prevent the clot from growing and to reduce the risk it will break off and travel to the lungs; in some cases, procedures to remove or dissolve the clot may be used.
when_to_seek_care: See a doctor immediately for leg swelling, pain, warmth, or redness, and seek emergency care immediately for sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing up blood.
related_conditions: Cellulitis (differential for leg swelling and redness)
Antiphospholipid syndrome and other clotting disorders (associated risk factors)

description: A condition of persistently elevated blood pressure that is a leading cause of premature death worldwide; often called the "silent killer" because it usually causes no symptoms until it leads to serious complications.
clinical_signs: Elevated blood pressure reading on repeated measurement
Irregular heartbeat
Signs of end-organ damage on examination in longstanding disease (e.g., retinal changes)
warning_signs: Severe headache with confusion
Chest pain
Vision problems
Shortness of breath
Nausea and vomiting with very high blood pressure readings (hypertensive emergency)
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from a combination of genetic and modifiable lifestyle factors that raise the pressure of blood against artery walls; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Reducing salt intake
Eating a balanced diet rich in fruits and vegetables
Regular physical activity
Avoiding tobacco and limiting alcohol use
Maintaining a healthy body weight
Regular blood pressure monitoring
diagnosis: Diagnosed through regular blood pressure measurement by a health professional, as hypertension is usually asymptomatic; confirmed with repeated elevated readings over time.
treatment: Managed with lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, reduced salt and alcohol, smoking cessation) and antihypertensive medications when needed to reduce blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.
when_to_seek_care: Seek regular blood pressure checks even without symptoms, and seek immediate care for symptoms such as severe headache, chest pain, vision changes, or confusion with a very high blood pressure reading.

also_known_as: Coronary heart disease, coronary artery disease, heart attack (acute presentation)
description: A group of conditions involving narrowing or blockage of the coronary arteries due to atherosclerosis, which can cause angina (chest pain) or a heart attack (myocardial infarction) when blood flow to the heart muscle is severely reduced or blocked.
symptoms: Pain or discomfort in the arms, neck, jaw, shoulder, or back
clinical_signs: ECG changes (ST-segment changes, new bundle branch block)
Elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin) during a heart attack
Irregular heart rhythm
warning_signs: Chest pain or pressure lasting more than a few minutes or that goes away and comes back
Pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck, or back
Sudden shortness of breath
Nausea, vomiting, lightheadedness, or cold sweat with chest discomfort (heart attack symptoms)
causes: Not an infectious disease; caused by atherosclerosis — a build-up of fatty plaque that thickens and hardens artery walls, narrowing or blocking blood flow to the heart; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Managing blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood glucose
Tobacco cessation
Healthy diet low in salt, sugar, and unhealthy fats
Regular physical activity
Limiting harmful alcohol use
diagnosis: Diagnosed using electrocardiogram (ECG), blood tests for cardiac biomarkers (such as troponin), stress testing, and coronary angiography or imaging to visualize blockages.
treatment: Treatment for high cardiovascular risk includes medicines to control blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes; acute heart attacks require urgent restoration of blood flow (medicines and/or procedures such as angioplasty); ongoing management often includes aspirin, beta blockers, and other cardiac medications.
when_to_seek_care: Seek emergency medical care immediately for chest pain or pressure lasting more than a few minutes, especially with spread to the arm/jaw/back, shortness of breath, or cold sweat, as this may be a heart attack.

source: National Institutes of Health (NIH), National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
specialty: Pulmonology, Hematology, Emergency Medicine, Critical Care
description: A life-threatening condition in which a blood clot, most often originating in a deep leg vein, travels to and blocks an artery in the lungs; a major complication of deep vein thrombosis requiring emergency treatment.
symptoms: Chest pain that worsens with coughing or deep breathing
clinical_signs: Rapid breathing on examination
Low blood oxygen levels
Signs of DVT (leg swelling) in the originating limb, when present
Low blood pressure in severe cases
warning_signs: Severe, sudden shortness of breath
Fainting or severe dizziness (possible large PE causing circulatory collapse)
Chest pain with a rapid heart rate
Coughing up blood
risk_factors: Recent surgery, hospitalization, or prolonged immobility
Deep vein thrombosis (the most common source)
Personal or family history of blood clots
causes: Not an infectious disease; occurs when part or all of a blood clot, usually from a deep leg vein, breaks free and travels through the bloodstream to lodge in a pulmonary artery, blocking blood flow to part of the lung; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Preventing and promptly treating deep vein thrombosis
Moving regularly during long periods of immobility or travel
Using preventive blood thinners or compression devices after surgery or during hospitalization when
recommended
Staying well hydrated during long trips
diagnosis: Diagnosed using imaging such as CT pulmonary angiography, sometimes supported by blood tests (D-dimer) and assessment of oxygen levels; a ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan may be used in certain situations.
treatment: Treated urgently with anticoagulant medications to prevent further clotting; more severe cases may require clot-dissolving medication (thrombolytics) or procedures to remove the clot; hospitalization is typically required.
when_to_seek_care: Seek emergency medical care immediately for sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, rapid heart rate, or coughing up blood, as pulmonary embolism can be fatal without prompt treatment.
related_conditions: Deep vein thrombosis (the most common underlying source)
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (a long-term complication)
Pneumonia (differential for chest pain and shortness of breath)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A medical emergency that occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked (ischemic stroke) or a blood vessel in the brain bursts (hemorrhagic stroke), causing brain cells to begin dying within minutes.
symptoms: Sudden numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg, especially on one side of the body
Sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes
Sudden trouble walking, dizziness, or loss of balance
Sudden severe headache with no known cause
clinical_signs: Facial drooping on one side
Arm drift or weakness when raised
Slurred or abnormal speech
Asymmetric neurological exam findings
warning_signs: Any FAST sign (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty) — Time to call emergency services
Sudden loss of balance or coordination
Sudden vision loss
Sudden severe headache unlike any before
risk_factors: Atrial fibrillation and other heart rhythm conditions
causes: Not an infectious disease; caused by an interruption of blood supply to the brain, either from a blockage (ischemic stroke, the most common type) or bleeding from a ruptured blood vessel (hemorrhagic stroke); not transmitted between people.
prevention: Controlling blood pressure, diabetes, and cholesterol
Not smoking
Regular physical activity and a healthy diet
Managing atrial fibrillation and other heart conditions
Limiting alcohol use
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on sudden onset of focal neurological symptoms, confirmed with brain imaging (CT or MRI) to distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke and guide emergency treatment.
treatment: Ischemic stroke may be treated with clot-dissolving medication (tPA) or mechanical clot removal if given within a narrow time window after symptom onset; hemorrhagic stroke management focuses on controlling bleeding and pressure; all stroke care requires urgent hospitalization.
when_to_seek_care: Call emergency services immediately for any sudden FAST symptoms (face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty) or other sudden neurological symptoms — every minute of delay increases the risk of permanent brain damage.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A highly contagious disease caused by the varicella-zoster virus, producing an itchy, blister-like rash; after recovery the virus remains dormant in the body and can reactivate later in life as shingles.
symptoms: Itchy, fluid-filled blister rash spreading over the body
clinical_signs: Rash progressing from macules to papules to vesicles before crusting
Lesions present in multiple stages simultaneously
Rash often first appearing on the chest, back, and face
warning_signs: Signs of bacterial skin infection (increasing redness, warmth, pus)
Signs of pneumonia (difficulty breathing, chest pain), more common in adults
High fever lasting more than 4 days
Signs of dehydration or difficulty staying awake
risk_factors: Being unvaccinated and not previously infected
Close contact with someone who has chickenpox
Pregnancy (risk of severe disease and fetal complications)
causes: Caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), a member of the herpesvirus family; spreads mainly through close contact with an infected person, including respiratory droplets and contact with fluid from blisters; highly contagious, with up to 90% of non-immune close contacts becoming infected.
prevention: Two doses of varicella vaccine for children, adolescents, and adults without evidence of immunity
Avoiding close contact with infected individuals until all lesions have crusted
Isolation of infected people during the contagious period
diagnosis: Usually diagnosed clinically based on the characteristic rash; laboratory testing can confirm the diagnosis when the presentation is atypical, such as in vaccinated individuals with breakthrough infection.
treatment: Supportive care to relieve itching and fever is typical for healthy children; antiviral medication (such as acyclovir) may be used for people at higher risk of severe disease, including adults, pregnant women, and those with weakened immune systems.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for signs of bacterial skin infection, breathing difficulty, high or persistent fever, or if the infected person is an infant, pregnant, or has a weakened immune system.

icd11: LA80-LA9Z (Structural developmental anomalies of the circulatory system)
source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: Structural problems with the heart present at birth, ranging from small holes that may close on their own to complex, life-threatening malformations requiring surgery in infancy; the most common type of birth defect.
symptoms: Often no symptoms in mild defects
Poor feeding or poor weight gain in infants
clinical_signs: Bluish tint to the skin, lips, or nails (cyanosis)
A heart murmur detected on examination
Swelling in the legs, abdomen, or around the eyes
Low oxygen saturation detected on newborn pulse oximetry screening
warning_signs: Severe difficulty breathing or persistent cyanosis in a newborn
