Extreme fatigue or lethargy with feeding
Failure to gain weight adequately
Sudden collapse or loss of consciousness
risk_factors: Certain maternal conditions during pregnancy (diabetes, obesity, lupus)
Genetic conditions such as Down syndrome
Family history of congenital heart defects
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from abnormal heart development during early pregnancy; causes are unknown in most cases, though genetic and certain maternal or environmental factors can contribute; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Managing chronic maternal health conditions before and during pregnancy
Rubella vaccination before pregnancy
Avoiding known harmful exposures (certain medications, alcohol) during pregnancy
Folic acid supplementation before and during early pregnancy
diagnosis: Can be diagnosed before birth via fetal ultrasound, or after birth through physical examination, pulse oximetry screening, echocardiogram, or other cardiac imaging.
treatment: Treatment depends on the type and severity and ranges from watchful monitoring for mild defects to catheter-based procedures or open-heart surgery for critical defects, often performed in infancy; many people with treated CHD live into adulthood with ongoing cardiac care.
when_to_seek_care: Newborns should receive routine pulse oximetry screening before hospital discharge; seek prompt medical care for a baby with bluish skin, rapid breathing, poor feeding, or poor weight gain.

source: National Institutes of Health (NIH), National Library of Medicine (NCBI Bookshelf)
description: A common condition in newborns causing yellowing of the skin and eyes due to elevated bilirubin; usually mild and resolves on its own, but severe or untreated cases can cause permanent neurological damage.
symptoms: Yellowing of the skin, starting on the face and spreading downward
Yellowing of the whites of the eyes
clinical_signs: Jaundice typically appearing 2-4 days after birth
Elevated bilirubin level on blood or transcutaneous testing
Jaundice usually resolving within 1-2 weeks without treatment in mild cases
warning_signs: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life
Jaundice spreading to the arms and legs, or very high bilirubin levels
High-pitched crying, arching of the back, or extreme lethargy (possible signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy)
Jaundice persisting beyond 2-3 weeks
risk_factors: Exclusive breastfeeding with inadequate intake in the first days of life
Blood type incompatibility between mother and baby
Family history of significant neonatal jaundice
causes: Not an infectious disease; occurs because newborns naturally break down red blood cells quickly while the liver is still immature and less able to process bilirubin; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Ensuring adequate feeding in the first days of life to support bilirubin excretion
Routine bilirubin screening before hospital discharge
Close follow-up for infants with known risk factors
diagnosis: Diagnosed through visual assessment combined with measurement of bilirubin levels, using a transcutaneous device or a blood test, plotted against standardized risk charts based on the infant's age in hours.
treatment: Mild jaundice often resolves with more frequent feeding; moderate to severe jaundice is treated with phototherapy (special light therapy) to help break down bilirubin, and severe cases may require an exchange transfusion.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt medical evaluation for jaundice appearing in the first 24 hours of life, jaundice spreading to the arms and legs, poor feeding, extreme sleepiness, or jaundice lasting more than 2-3 weeks.
related_conditions: Kernicterus (a rare, serious complication from untreated severe jaundice)
Hemolytic disease of the newborn (a cause in blood type incompatibility)
Biliary atresia (a serious differential for prolonged jaundice)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: An infection of the middle ear, most common in young children, that occurs when fluid builds up behind the eardrum, often following a cold or upper respiratory infection.
symptoms: Tugging or pulling at the ear (in infants and toddlers)
clinical_signs: Fluid or bulging visible behind the eardrum on examination
Fluid draining from the ear (otorrhea)
Reduced hearing or muffled response to sound
Loss of appetite
warning_signs: High fever that doesn't improve
Severe ear pain with swelling or redness behind the ear (possible mastoiditis)
Stiff neck, severe headache, or confusion (possible spread of infection)
Persistent fluid drainage or hearing loss after treatment
risk_factors: Young age (most common between 6 and 24 months)
Recent cold or upper respiratory infection
causes: Caused by bacteria (most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae and nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae) or viruses that lead to fluid buildup and infection in the middle ear, often following a cold; not directly contagious, though the preceding respiratory infection can spread between people.
prevention: Routine childhood vaccinations, including pneumococcal and influenza vaccines
Avoiding exposure to secondhand smoke
Breastfeeding when possible
Avoiding bottle-feeding infants while lying flat
Good hand hygiene to reduce respiratory infections
diagnosis: Diagnosed through examination of the eardrum with an otoscope to look for fluid, redness, or bulging; additional tests such as tympanometry may be used to confirm fluid in the middle ear.
treatment: Many ear infections resolve on their own; treatment may start with pain relief and a period of watchful waiting, with antibiotics prescribed if symptoms persist beyond 48-72 hours or in more severe cases.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for ear pain with fever or symptoms lasting more than a day or two, and seek prompt care for severe pain, swelling behind the ear, stiff neck, or fluid drainage.
related_conditions: Otitis media with effusion (fluid without active infection)
Swimmer's ear (otitis externa, a different condition affecting the outer ear canal)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A highly contagious viral infection of the stomach and intestines and the most common cause of severe diarrhea and dehydration in infants and young children worldwide.
clinical_signs: Signs of dehydration (decreased urination, dry mouth and throat)
Sunken eyes or sunken soft spot on an infant's head
Lethargy or unusual fussiness
warning_signs: Few or no wet diapers (significant dehydration)
Dizziness when standing (in older children/adults)
Extreme lethargy or difficulty waking
No tears when crying
risk_factors: Infancy and early childhood (ages 3 months to 5 years at highest risk)
Attending childcare centers or settings with many young children
Close contact with an infected person
causes: Caused by rotavirus, a highly contagious virus that damages the lining of the small intestine; spreads through the fecal-oral route, including contact with contaminated hands, surfaces, or objects, and can spread even before symptoms appear.
prevention: Rotavirus vaccination (oral vaccine given in infancy)
Frequent handwashing, especially after diaper changes and before eating
Cleaning and disinfecting contaminated surfaces
diagnosis: Usually diagnosed clinically based on symptoms; laboratory testing of a stool sample can confirm rotavirus infection when needed.
treatment: There is no specific antiviral medicine for rotavirus; treatment focuses on preventing and managing dehydration with oral rehydration solution, and severe cases may require intravenous fluids and hospitalization.
when_to_seek_care: Contact a healthcare provider promptly for signs of dehydration in a child, such as decreased urination, dry mouth, no tears when crying, or unusual sleepiness or fussiness.

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: Inflammation of the appendix and the most common cause of acute abdominal pain requiring emergency surgery; untreated, it can lead to serious complications such as a burst appendix, abscess, or peritonitis.
symptoms: Abdominal pain that often starts near the navel and moves to the lower-right abdomen
clinical_signs: Tenderness in the lower-right abdomen on physical exam
Pain that worsens with movement, coughing, or walking
Elevated white blood cell count on blood testing
Constipation or diarrhea in some cases
warning_signs: Sudden worsening of abdominal pain followed by a brief improvement, then more severe pain and fever (possible
rupture)
Rigid, board-like abdomen
High fever with a rapidly worsening, distended abdomen (possible peritonitis, a medical emergency)
risk_factors: Most common between ages 10 and 30, though it can occur at any age
Blockage of the appendix by stool, a foreign body, or, rarely, a tumor
causes: Not contagious; occurs when the appendix becomes blocked or infected, most often by feces moving through the large intestine, leading to inflammation and swelling; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent appendicitis
Prompt medical attention for progressively worsening abdominal pain reduces the risk of complications from a
burst appendix
diagnosis: Diagnosed through review of symptoms and medical history, a physical exam checking for lower-right abdominal pain, blood and urine tests, and imaging tests such as ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI.
treatment: Most cases are treated with surgical removal of the appendix (appendectomy), performed via laparoscopy or open surgery; doctors typically also prescribe antibiotics, and some mild, uncomplicated cases may be treated with antibiotics alone.
when_to_seek_care: See a doctor or go to the emergency room right away for progressively worsening abdominal pain, especially if it moves to the lower-right abdomen and is accompanied by fever, nausea, or vomiting.
related_conditions: Ovarian cyst or ectopic pregnancy (differential in women)
Urinary tract infection or kidney stone (differential)

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: Hard deposits of cholesterol or bilirubin that form in the gallbladder; very common, affecting 10-15% of the population, though most gallstones cause no symptoms.
symptoms: Sudden, rapidly intensifying pain in the upper right abdomen (biliary colic)
Pain that may spread to the upper back or between the shoulder blades
clinical_signs: Tenderness in the upper right abdomen on examination
Pain that often occurs after eating a fatty meal
Gallstones visible on abdominal ultrasound
warning_signs: Fever and chills with abdominal pain (possible infection)
Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)
Dark urine and pale, clay-colored stool
Pain lasting several hours without relief
risk_factors: Being female, especially with extra estrogen from pregnancy, hormone therapy, or birth control pills
Rapid weight loss or very low-calorie diets
causes: Not an infectious disease; forms when bile contains too much cholesterol or bilirubin, or when the gallbladder does not empty properly; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Maintaining a healthy weight through gradual, steady weight loss rather than rapid weight loss
Regular meals rather than prolonged fasting
A balanced diet, though no diet has been proven to reliably prevent gallstones
Discussing gallstone risk with a doctor before major weight-loss treatment
diagnosis: Diagnosed primarily with abdominal ultrasound, which can detect gallstones in the gallbladder; blood tests may help assess for complications such as infection or bile duct blockage.
treatment: Gallstones without symptoms usually don't need treatment; symptomatic gallstones are most often treated with surgical removal of the gallbladder (cholecystectomy), typically performed laparoscopically; nonsurgical treatments are rarely used.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for sudden, severe upper abdominal pain, and seek immediate care for pain with fever, jaundice, or pain lasting several hours, which may indicate a serious complication.
related_conditions: Pancreatitis (a complication when a stone blocks the pancreatic duct)
Cholangitis (bile duct infection, a serious complication)

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A more severe and long-lasting form of gastroesophageal reflux (GER), in which stomach contents repeatedly flow back into the esophagus, causing bothersome symptoms or complications over time.
symptoms: Heartburn (burning feeling in the chest behind the breastbone)
Regurgitation of food or sour liquid
clinical_signs: Esophagitis (inflammation of the esophagus) seen on endoscopy
Dental erosion from stomach acid
In infants: arching of the back, irritability, and poor weight gain
warning_signs: Chest pain with shortness of breath, or pain spreading to the jaw or arm (seek emergency care to rule out a heart
problem)
Difficulty or pain swallowing (dysphagia/odynophagia)
Unintended weight loss
Vomiting blood or black, tarry stools
risk_factors: Certain foods and drinks (fatty or fried foods, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, spicy foods)
Eating large meals or lying down soon after eating
causes: Not an infectious disease; occurs when the lower esophageal sphincter, the muscle that normally prevents stomach contents from moving back into the esophagus, becomes weak or relaxes abnormally; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Maintaining a healthy weight
Eating meals 2-3 hours before lying down
Avoiding foods and drinks that trigger symptoms
Elevating the head during sleep
Avoiding smoking
diagnosis: Often diagnosed based on symptoms and medical history alone; when needed, doctors may use upper GI endoscopy, an upper GI series (X-rays), esophageal pH monitoring, or esophageal manometry to confirm the diagnosis or assess complications.
treatment: Lifestyle changes (weight loss, dietary changes, elevating the head of the bed) are often recommended first; medications include antacids, H2 blockers, and proton pump inhibitors; a small number of cases may need endoscopic procedures or surgery if symptoms don't improve.
when_to_seek_care: See a provider if symptoms don't improve with over-the-counter medicines or diet changes, and get emergency help right away for chest pain with shortness of breath or pain in the jaw or arm.
related_conditions: Barrett's esophagus (a possible complication of chronic GERD)

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: Swollen and inflamed veins around the anus or in the lower rectum; a very common condition caused by increased pressure in this area, classified as external (under the skin around the anus) or internal (in the lining of the anus and lower rectum).
symptoms: Anal itching (more common with external hemorrhoids)
Rectal bleeding, often noticed as bright red blood (more common with internal hemorrhoids)
Pain or discomfort around the anus
clinical_signs: Visible swollen tissue around the anus (external hemorrhoids)
Prolapse of internal hemorrhoids through the anus in more advanced cases
Bright red blood on toilet paper or in the toilet bowl
warning_signs: Heavy or persistent rectal bleeding
Severe pain, especially with a hard, tender lump (possible thrombosed hemorrhoid)
Rectal bleeding with unexplained weight loss or change in bowel habits (needs evaluation to rule out other causes
such as colorectal cancer)
risk_factors: Prolonged sitting, especially on the toilet
causes: Not an infectious disease; caused by increased pressure on the veins around the anus and lower rectum from straining, constipation, or other factors; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Eating high-fiber foods to soften stools and ease passage
Drinking plenty of water and other liquids
Avoiding straining during bowel movements
Not sitting for prolonged periods, especially on the toilet
diagnosis: Often diagnosed based on medical history and a physical examination; internal hemorrhoids may require an anoscopy or similar procedure to visualize the anal canal and lower rectum directly.
treatment: Mild cases often improve with increased fiber and fluid intake, over-the-counter creams, and warm sitz baths; more severe or persistent hemorrhoids may require in-office procedures (such as rubber band ligation) or surgery.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for persistent rectal bleeding, significant pain, or a lump near the anus, since these symptoms can also indicate other digestive conditions that need to be ruled out.

condition: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis)
source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A group of lifelong diseases causing chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract; the two main types are Crohn's disease, which can affect any part of the GI tract, and ulcerative colitis, which affects the inner lining of the colon and rectum.
symptoms: Persistent diarrhea (often bloody in ulcerative colitis)
Urgent need to have a bowel movement
clinical_signs: Blood or mucus in stool
Abdominal tenderness on examination
Mouth sores (more common in Crohn's disease)
Signs of malnutrition in longstanding disease
warning_signs: Severe, unrelenting abdominal pain
High fever with worsening symptoms (possible fulminant colitis or complication)
Signs of bowel obstruction or perforation
Significant rectal bleeding with dizziness or rapid heartbeat
risk_factors: Younger age (often diagnosed in early adulthood, though it can occur at any age)
Smoking (increases Crohn's disease risk, though associated differently with ulcerative colitis)
Certain environmental and immune factors, not fully understood
causes: Not an infectious disease; thought to result from an abnormal immune response in the GI tract, involving genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers, with the exact cause unknown; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent IBD
Not smoking may reduce the risk or severity of Crohn's disease
Ongoing treatment adherence can help maintain remission and prevent flares and complications
diagnosis: Diagnosed using a combination of blood tests, stool tests, endoscopy (colonoscopy) with biopsies, and imaging studies to assess the location and extent of inflammation.
treatment: Managed with medications that reduce inflammation and modulate the immune system (aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, biologics), along with dietary strategies; surgery may be needed for complications or disease not controlled by medication.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, or blood in the stool lasting more than a few days; seek urgent care for severe abdominal pain, high fever, or signs of significant bleeding.
related_conditions: Psoriasis and other autoimmune conditions (associated comorbidities)

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A condition in which open sores develop in the lining of the stomach or the upper part of the small intestine (duodenum), most often caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or long-term use of NSAIDs.
symptoms: Burning or gnawing pain in the upper abdomen, often between the navel and breastbone
Pain that may improve or worsen with eating
clinical_signs: Epigastric tenderness on abdominal examination
Positive H. pylori testing (breath, stool, or biopsy test)
Ulcer visible on upper endoscopy
warning_signs: Black or tarry stool, or blood mixed with stool
Vomiting blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
Sudden, sharp, or severe abdominal pain that doesn't go away (possible perforation)
Dizziness, fainting, or rapid pulse (possible bleeding or shock)
risk_factors: Regular use of NSAIDs (such as aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen)
Use of corticosteroids or certain other medications alongside NSAIDs
causes: Most commonly caused by Helicobacter pylori infection (believed to spread through close contact and contaminated food or water) or by damage from NSAID medications that impair the stomach's protective lining; not directly transmitted through casual contact.
prevention: Testing for and treating H. pylori infection when present
Using NSAIDs at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, or avoiding them when possible
Avoiding smoking and heavy alcohol use
Using protective medications when long-term NSAID use is necessary
diagnosis: Diagnosed through upper endoscopy to directly visualize the ulcer, along with testing for H. pylori infection (breath, stool antigen, or biopsy-based tests).
treatment: Treatment includes antibiotics to eradicate H. pylori when present, acid-suppressing medications (such as proton pump inhibitors) to allow healing, and stopping NSAID use when possible.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent upper abdominal pain or indigestion, and seek emergency care immediately for black or bloody stool, vomiting blood, or sudden severe abdominal pain.

description: A chronic disease characterized by elevated blood glucose levels, occurring when the pancreas does not produce enough insulin (type 1) or when the body cannot effectively use the insulin it produces (type 2); a major and growing global health problem.
clinical_signs: Elevated blood glucose on testing
Slow-healing cuts, sores, or wounds
Frequent urinary tract or yeast infections
Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet (long-standing disease)
warning_signs: Diabetic ketoacidosis: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, confusion (type 1, medical emergency)
Severe hyperglycemia with confusion or drowsiness
Signs of severe hypoglycemia (shakiness, confusion, loss of consciousness) in treated patients
causes: Not an infectious disease; type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic cells; type 2 diabetes results from insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency, strongly linked to excess weight and inactivity; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Maintaining a healthy body weight
Regular physical activity
Healthy diet with reduced sugar and refined carbohydrate intake
Avoiding tobacco use
No established prevention exists for type 1 diabetes
diagnosis: Diagnosed through blood tests including fasting plasma glucose, oral glucose tolerance test, or glycated hemoglobin (A1C); random blood glucose testing can also support diagnosis in symptomatic individuals.
treatment: Type 1 diabetes requires lifelong insulin therapy; type 2 diabetes is managed with lifestyle changes (diet, physical activity) and oral medications such as metformin, with insulin added if needed; regular blood glucose monitoring and management of cardiovascular risk factors are essential for both types.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, or fatigue; seek emergency care for symptoms of diabetic ketoacidosis (nausea, vomiting, rapid breathing, confusion) or severe low blood sugar.

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
specialty: Endocrinology, Family Medicine, Ophthalmology (for Graves' eye disease)
description: A condition in which the thyroid gland produces too much thyroid hormone, speeding up the body's metabolism; Graves' disease is the most common underlying cause.
symptoms: Unexplained weight loss despite normal or increased appetite
clinical_signs: Goiter (enlarged thyroid)
Bulging eyes (in Graves' disease)
Warm, moist skin
Suppressed TSH with elevated thyroid hormone levels on blood testing
warning_signs: Thyroid storm: high fever, very rapid heart rate, confusion, and agitation (a rare, life-threatening emergency)
Severe chest pain or palpitations
Signs of significant eye involvement (severe pain, vision changes) in Graves' disease
risk_factors: Family history of thyroid disease, particularly Graves' disease
Excess iodine intake (from diet, supplements, or certain medicines)
causes: Not an infectious disease; most commonly caused by Graves' disease (an autoimmune condition), but can also result from thyroid nodules, thyroiditis, or excess iodine intake; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent most causes of hyperthyroidism
Avoiding excessive iodine intake (from supplements or iodine-rich foods) in those at risk
Regular thyroid monitoring in people with a personal or family history of thyroid disease
diagnosis: Diagnosed with blood tests measuring TSH and thyroid hormone levels; imaging tests (such as a thyroid scan) may help identify the specific cause.
treatment: Treatment options include antithyroid medications to reduce hormone production, radioactive iodine therapy to shrink the thyroid, and surgery to remove part or all of the thyroid gland; the best option depends on the cause, severity, and patient preferences.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for symptoms such as rapid heartbeat, unexplained weight loss, or heat intolerance, and seek emergency care for very high fever, severe agitation, or a racing heart with confusion.
related_conditions: Hypothyroidism (differential, opposite condition; can also follow treatment for hyperthyroidism)

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A common condition in which the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone, slowing the body's metabolism; symptoms develop gradually and can be mistaken for other conditions.
clinical_signs: Goiter (enlarged thyroid, causing neck swelling)
Slowed heart rate
Puffy face
Elevated TSH with low thyroid hormone levels on blood testing
warning_signs: Severe lethargy, confusion, or loss of consciousness (possible myxedema coma, a medical emergency, most
often in older adults with untreated severe hypothyroidism)
Significant swelling combined with breathing difficulty
Very slow heart rate with fainting
risk_factors: Previous thyroid surgery or radioactive iodine treatment
causes: Not an infectious disease; most commonly caused by Hashimoto's disease (an autoimmune condition), but can also result from thyroid surgery, radiation treatment, certain medications, or iodine imbalance; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent most causes of hypothyroidism
Adequate dietary iodine intake supports normal thyroid function
Regular monitoring for those at higher risk (family history, autoimmune conditions, prior thyroid treatment)
diagnosis: Diagnosed with blood tests measuring thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and thyroid hormone (T4) levels, since symptoms alone are not specific enough for diagnosis; further testing can help identify the underlying cause.
treatment: Treated with daily thyroid hormone replacement medication (levothyroxine), with the dose adjusted based on regular blood test monitoring; treatment is typically lifelong.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for persistent fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, or other symptoms suggestive of low thyroid function, so blood testing can confirm the diagnosis.

also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A chronic disease involving abnormal or excessive fat accumulation that presents a risk to health; a major and growing global health problem linked to numerous serious diseases, though preventable in many cases.
symptoms: Excess body fat, typically assessed using body mass index (BMI)
Joint pain, particularly in weight-bearing joints
clinical_signs: BMI of 30 or higher in adults
Increased waist circumference
Signs of related conditions such as high blood pressure or insulin resistance
warning_signs: Sudden weight gain with swelling (possible sign of an underlying medical condition)
Signs of severe sleep apnea (loud snoring with pauses in breathing, excessive daytime sleepiness)
Chest pain or severe shortness of breath (possible cardiovascular complication)
risk_factors: Diet high in energy-dense foods, fats, and sugars
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from an energy imbalance between calories consumed and calories expended, influenced by dietary patterns, physical activity levels, genetics, and environmental factors; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Limiting energy intake from fats and sugars
Increasing consumption of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains
Regular physical activity
Reducing sedentary behavior, especially in children
diagnosis: Diagnosed using body mass index (BMI) as a screening tool, calculated from weight and height, along with clinical assessment; BMI is a screening measure and does not directly diagnose body fatness or individual health status.
treatment: Managed through sustainable lifestyle changes (diet and physical activity), behavioral support, and, when appropriate, medications or metabolic and bariatric surgery for more severe obesity, tailored to individual health needs and goals.
when_to_seek_care: Talk with a healthcare provider about weight management if BMI falls in the overweight or obese range or if obesity is affecting health or daily functioning, so an individualized plan can be developed.

source: National Eye Institute (NEI), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A progressive disease that damages the macula, the part of the retina responsible for sharp central vision; a leading cause of irreversible vision loss in people over 60 if left untreated.
symptoms: Straight lines appearing wavy or distorted
Need for brighter light when reading
Dark or empty area in the center of vision (in later stages)
clinical_signs: Drusen (yellow deposits) beneath the retina visible on eye exam
Pigment changes in the retina
Abnormal blood vessel growth beneath the macula in wet AMD
warning_signs: Sudden onset or rapid worsening of distorted or blurred central vision (possible wet AMD requiring prompt
treatment)
A new dark spot or blind area appearing suddenly in central vision
risk_factors: Age 50 and older, with risk increasing further after 60
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from aging-related damage and, in some cases, abnormal blood vessel growth in the macula, influenced by genetic and environmental risk factors; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Not smoking
Eating a diet rich in leafy greens and fish
Managing cardiovascular risk factors
Specific antioxidant and zinc supplements (AREDS formulation) for those with intermediate AMD, as
recommended by an eye care provider
Regular comprehensive eye exams after age 50
diagnosis: Diagnosed through a comprehensive dilated eye exam, often supplemented with imaging tests such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) to examine the retina in detail.
treatment: There is no cure for dry AMD, though nutritional supplements may slow progression in some cases; wet AMD is treated with injectable medications (anti-VEGF therapy) that can slow vision loss and, in some cases, improve vision.
when_to_seek_care: Get regular comprehensive eye exams starting at age 50, and seek prompt evaluation for any sudden change in central vision, such as new distortion or a blind spot, since early treatment of wet AMD works best.
related_conditions: Diabetic retinopathy (differential for central vision changes)

source: National Eye Institute (NEI), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A clouding of the normally clear lens of the eye that affects vision, most often related to aging; a leading cause of vision loss and blindness worldwide, but very treatable with surgery.
symptoms: Colors that seem faded or less vivid
Glare or halos around lights, especially at night
Frequent changes in eyeglass or contact lens prescription
clinical_signs: Visible clouding of the lens on eye examination
Double vision or multiple images in one eye (may improve as the cataract enlarges)
Difficulty reading or performing close-up tasks
warning_signs: Sudden vision loss or eye pain (suggests a different, more urgent eye problem rather than typical cataract
progression)
Rapidly worsening vision affecting daily safety, such as driving
risk_factors: Prolonged exposure to sunlight without eye protection
causes: Not an infectious disease; most commonly caused by age-related changes in the proteins of the eye's lens that cause it to become cloudy over time; cannot spread from one eye to the other or between people.
prevention: Wearing sunglasses that block UV rays
Not smoking
Managing diabetes and other chronic health conditions
Regular comprehensive eye exams, especially after age 60
diagnosis: Diagnosed through a comprehensive dilated eye exam, during which an eye care professional examines the lens for clouding.
treatment: In early stages, updated eyeglass prescriptions and brighter lighting may help; when a cataract significantly affects daily activities, surgery to remove the clouded lens and replace it with an artificial lens is a common and highly effective treatment.
when_to_seek_care: Get a comprehensive dilated eye exam at least every two years starting at age 60, and see an eye care provider sooner for worsening blurry vision, glare, or difficulty with night vision.
related_conditions: Diabetic retinopathy (a differential and associated condition in people with diabetes)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: Inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin layer covering the white of the eye and inner eyelid, causing the eye to appear pink or red; commonly caused by viruses, bacteria, or allergens.
symptoms: Redness or swelling of the white of the eye or inner eyelid
Itching or a gritty feeling in the eye
Crusting of the eyelid or lashes, especially after sleep
clinical_signs: Visible dilated blood vessels on the conjunctiva
Watery discharge (typical of viral or allergic conjunctivitis) or thicker, colored discharge (typical of bacterial
conjunctivitis)
Swollen eyelids
warning_signs: Eye pain, sensitivity to light, or blurred vision affecting the ability to see clearly
Symptoms in a newborn, which need prompt medical evaluation
Intense redness with severe swelling or vision changes (possible more serious eye infection)
risk_factors: Close contact with someone who has viral or bacterial conjunctivitis
Contact lens wear, especially if worn longer than recommended
Seasonal allergies or other allergic conditions
Exposure to chemicals, smoke, or other eye irritants
causes: Caused by viruses, bacteria, allergens, or irritants; viral and bacterial conjunctivitis are very contagious and spread through contact with eye secretions, contaminated hands, or shared objects, while allergic conjunctivitis is not contagious.
prevention: Frequent handwashing
Avoiding touching or rubbing the eyes
Not sharing towels, pillows, or eye makeup
Proper contact lens hygiene
Avoiding known allergens for allergic conjunctivitis
diagnosis: Usually diagnosed based on symptoms and examination of the eye; laboratory testing of eye discharge may be used in certain cases, especially in newborns or when infection is severe.
treatment: Viral conjunctivitis usually resolves on its own with supportive care; bacterial conjunctivitis may be treated with antibiotic eye drops; allergic conjunctivitis is managed with antihistamines and allergen avoidance.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for eye pain, light sensitivity, or vision changes, and seek immediate care for any pink eye symptoms in a newborn.
related_conditions: Neonatal conjunctivitis (a serious form in newborns, often linked to maternal STIs)
Corneal ulcer (a more serious differential requiring urgent care)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve, often associated with elevated eye pressure, and a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide; frequently has no early symptoms.
symptoms: Usually none in early stages (open-angle glaucoma)
Eye pain, blurred vision, and headaches (in acute angle-closure glaucoma)
clinical_signs: Elevated intraocular pressure on eye exam
Optic nerve cupping visible on examination
Visual field loss detectable on formal testing
warning_signs: Sudden severe eye pain with blurred vision, halos around lights, nausea, and vomiting (acute angle-closure
glaucoma, a medical emergency)
Sudden vision loss
risk_factors: Black or Afro-Caribbean descent (higher risk of open-angle glaucoma)
Asian or Inuit descent (higher risk of angle-closure glaucoma)
causes: Not an infectious disease; typically caused by impaired drainage of fluid from the eye leading to increased intraocular pressure, which damages the optic nerve over time; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Regular comprehensive eye exams, especially for those at higher risk
Early detection and treatment to slow progression and preserve vision
Managing underlying conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure
diagnosis: Diagnosed through a comprehensive eye exam including measurement of intraocular pressure, examination of the optic nerve, and visual field testing.
treatment: There is no cure, but treatment can slow or stop progression and preserve remaining vision; options include prescription eye drops to lower eye pressure, laser therapy, and surgery.
when_to_seek_care: Get a baseline eye exam by age 40, and seek regular eye exams thereafter, especially with risk factors such as diabetes or family history; seek emergency care immediately for sudden severe eye pain, vision loss, or halos around lights with nausea.
related_conditions: Age-related macular degeneration (differential for vision loss)

source: National Institutes of Health (NIH), National Library of Medicine (MedlinePlus)
description: A disorder in which the eyes do not align properly and do not look at the same object at the same time, most often appearing in infancy or early childhood; if untreated, it can lead to permanent vision loss in the affected eye.
symptoms: Eyes that appear crossed, turned outward, or misaligned
Tilting or turning the head to see better
clinical_signs: Inward (esotropia), outward (exotropia), or vertical misalignment of the eyes on examination
Abnormal results on corneal light reflex or cover/uncover testing
Reduced vision or depth perception
warning_signs: Sudden onset of crossed eyes or double vision in an older child or adult (may indicate a neurologic problem and
needs prompt evaluation)
Persistent misalignment beyond 3-4 months of age in an infant
Signs of vision loss in one eye (amblyopia) developing without treatment
risk_factors: Certain conditions such as cerebral palsy or Down syndrome
Other eye conditions causing vision loss in one eye
causes: Not an infectious disease; most often results from poor coordination of the eye muscles by the brain, sometimes related to uncorrected refractive error or an underlying neurological or eye condition; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Regular childhood eye exams for early detection
Prompt treatment of significant refractive errors
Early referral to an eye specialist if misalignment persists beyond early infancy
diagnosis: Diagnosed through a comprehensive eye examination, including corneal light reflex testing, cover/uncover testing, and assessment of visual acuity and eye movement.
treatment: Treatment may include corrective glasses, patching or other treatment of amblyopia (lazy eye) in the stronger eye, and, when needed, surgery on the eye muscles to improve alignment; the earlier treatment starts, the better the outcome.
when_to_seek_care: See an eye care provider if a child's eyes appear misaligned beyond 3-4 months of age, or for any sudden onset of crossed eyes or double vision at any age.
related_conditions: Amblyopia (lazy eye, a common complication of untreated strabismus)
Cranial nerve palsy (a differential, especially in sudden-onset cases)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A group of diseases caused by the common environmental mold Aspergillus, ranging from allergic reactions in people with asthma or cystic fibrosis to severe, invasive infection in people with significantly weakened immune systems.
symptoms: Wheezing and shortness of breath (allergic form)
clinical_signs: Abnormal breath sounds on lung exam
Cavitary lesion or "fungus ball" (aspergilloma) on chest imaging
Weight loss and fatigue in chronic pulmonary disease
warning_signs: Severe or worsening shortness of breath
Significant hemoptysis (coughing up blood)
Signs of infection spreading beyond the lungs (to brain, skin, or bone) in invasive disease
risk_factors: Severely weakened immune system (stem cell or organ transplant recipients, prolonged neutropenia)
High-dose corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive therapy
Asthma or cystic fibrosis (for allergic aspergillosis)
causes: Caused by Aspergillus mold species (most commonly Aspergillus fumigatus), found widely in soil, decomposing plant matter, household dust, and building materials; acquired by inhaling airborne spores, not spread person to person.
prevention: Avoiding dusty environments such as construction or excavation sites
Wearing an N95 respirator when dusty exposure cannot be avoided
Antifungal prophylaxis for high-risk transplant or immunosuppressed patients
Environmental infection control during hospital construction/renovation
diagnosis: Diagnosis varies by form and may include chest imaging (CT scan), culture or galactomannan antigen testing, and biopsy; a presumptive diagnosis often combines risk factors, symptoms, and radiographic findings given the difficulty of definitive confirmation.
treatment: Treatment depends on the type of aspergillosis: antifungal medications (such as azole antifungals) for invasive and chronic pulmonary disease; corticosteroids (sometimes with antifungals) for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis; surgery may be considered for localized aspergillomas.
when_to_seek_care: Contact a healthcare provider for symptoms such as fever, cough, or chest pain if you are at high risk (weakened immune system, chronic lung disease, or recent transplant); seek urgent care for coughing up blood or severe breathing difficulty.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
specialty: Infectious Disease, Dermatology, Gynecology, Critical Care (for invasive disease)
description: A fungal infection caused by an overgrowth of Candida yeast, ranging from common, mild infections of the mouth, throat, esophagus, or vagina to rare, life-threatening bloodstream infections (candidemia) in hospitalized or immunocompromised patients.
symptoms: White patches on the tongue, inner cheeks, or throat (oral thrush)
clinical_signs: Whitish plaques on oral or vaginal mucosa
Redness and cracking at affected skin folds
Fever and chills that do not respond to antibacterial treatment (invasive disease)
warning_signs: Persistent fever and chills unresponsive to antibiotics in a hospitalized or immunocompromised patient
Signs of bloodstream infection (candidemia)
Spread to internal organs (endocarditis, meningitis, endophthalmitis)
risk_factors: Central venous catheters, recent surgery, or prolonged ICU stay
Pregnancy and hormonal changes (for vaginal candidiasis)
causes: Caused by an overgrowth of Candida species (most commonly Candida albicans) that normally live harmlessly on skin and mucous membranes; not typically contagious, though invasive infection can rarely spread via healthcare workers' hands or contaminated medical devices.
prevention: Judicious use of antibiotics and corticosteroids
Good hygiene and moisture control for skin-fold and vaginal candidiasis
Infection control measures (catheter care, hand hygiene) to prevent healthcare-associated invasive candidiasis
Blood glucose control in people with diabetes
diagnosis: Diagnosis depends on infection site: clinical examination for oral/vaginal candidiasis; blood cultures for invasive candidiasis/candidemia; endoscopy for esophageal disease.
treatment: Treated with antifungal medications in topical (creams, lozenges, oral rinses), oral, or intravenous form depending on infection type and severity; echinocandin antifungals are typically first-line for invasive candidiasis.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for persistent white oral patches, painful swallowing, recurrent or severe vaginal symptoms, or any fever/chills in a person with a weakened immune system or recent hospitalization.

source: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: An inherited genetic disease that causes the body to produce abnormally thick, sticky mucus that builds up in the lungs and digestive tract, leading to repeated infections and organ damage; a person must inherit two mutated CFTR genes, one from each parent, to have the disease.
symptoms: Persistent cough that produces thick mucus
Poor growth or weight gain despite a good appetite
clinical_signs: Clubbing of fingers and toes (in advanced disease)
Nasal polyps
Greasy, bulky stools from poor fat absorption
Abnormally high salt content in sweat on testing
warning_signs: Inability to breathe or talk easily
Coughing up blood
Confusion or blue lips or skin
Signs of a pulmonary exacerbation: worsening cough, increased mucus, weight loss, or fever
risk_factors: Inheriting a mutated CFTR gene from both biological parents
Family history of cystic fibrosis or being a known carrier couple
causes: An inherited genetic disease caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which controls the movement of salt and water in and out of cells; results in thick, sticky mucus that clogs the lungs and other organs; not contagious and not transmitted between people through contact.
prevention: Genetic carrier screening and counseling for at-risk couples
Newborn screening allows early diagnosis and treatment, improving outcomes
No way to prevent the inherited condition itself in a person who has two mutated genes
diagnosis: Diagnosed through newborn screening, a sweat chloride test to measure salt levels in sweat, and genetic testing to identify CFTR gene mutations.
treatment: Treatment has advanced significantly and includes CFTR modulator therapies that target the underlying protein defect in eligible patients, airway clearance techniques, inhaled medications to thin mucus, pancreatic enzyme supplements, and treatment of lung infections; many people with cystic fibrosis now live well into adulthood.
when_to_seek_care: Contact a healthcare provider promptly for worsening cough, increased mucus, weight loss, or fever, and seek emergency care immediately for severe breathing difficulty or coughing up blood.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: The most common chromosomal condition, occurring when a person has a full or partial extra copy of chromosome 21, causing distinct physical features and varying degrees of intellectual and developmental disability.
symptoms: Characteristic facial features (flattened face, upward-slanting eyes, small ears)
Developmental delays (slower to walk, talk, and reach milestones)
clinical_signs: Single crease across the palm of the hand
Small hands and feet with a wide gap between the first and second toes
Loose joints and ligaments
Small white spots on the iris (Brushfield spots)
warning_signs: Signs of a congenital heart defect (poor feeding, rapid breathing, bluish skin) requiring prompt evaluation in
infancy
Symptoms of intestinal blockage in a newborn
Signs of hearing or vision problems affecting development
risk_factors: Increasing maternal age at conception, especially 35 years or older
Having a previous child with Down syndrome (increases the chance in future pregnancies regardless of age)
causes: Caused by the presence of a full or partial extra copy of chromosome 21 in the body's cells (nondisjunction), usually occurring randomly during the formation of the egg or sperm; not caused by anything the parents did, and not transmitted through contact between people.
prevention: There is no known way to prevent Down syndrome
Genetic counseling can help inform reproductive decisions for at-risk families
Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing are available during pregnancy
diagnosis: Can be diagnosed prenatally through screening tests (which estimate the chance of Down syndrome) or diagnostic tests such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis; after birth, diagnosis is confirmed with a chromosomal blood test (karyotype).
treatment: There is no cure, but early intervention services (physical, occupational, and speech therapy), regular monitoring for associated health conditions (heart defects, thyroid problems, hearing and vision issues), and educational support can help people with Down syndrome reach their full potential.
when_to_seek_care: Ongoing regular medical care and developmental monitoring are recommended throughout life; seek prompt evaluation for feeding difficulties, breathing problems, or any sudden change in a child's condition.

source: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
also_known_as: Bleeding disorder (factor VIII or factor IX deficiency)
description: An inherited bleeding disorder in which the blood does not clot properly due to missing or low levels of a clotting factor, causing prolonged bleeding after injury or surgery, and sometimes bleeding without an obvious cause.
symptoms: Bleeding for longer than expected after cuts, dental work, or surgery
Bleeding into joints, causing swelling, pain, and tightness
clinical_signs: Swollen, warm, painful joints from joint bleeding (most often knees, elbows, and ankles)
Blood in the urine or stool
Bleeding of the mouth and gums
Prolonged bleeding after vaccinations or minor procedures
warning_signs: Severe headache, neck pain, vomiting, or extreme sleepiness (possible bleeding in the brain, a medical
emergency)
Severe pain and swelling in a joint or muscle
Bleeding that does not stop with prolonged direct pressure
Difficulty breathing or swallowing (possible bleeding in the throat or neck)
risk_factors: Being male (hemophilia A and B are X-linked and mostly affect males)
Having a mother who is a known carrier of the gene
causes: Caused by an inherited genetic mutation affecting a blood clotting factor (most often factor VIII in hemophilia A or factor IX in hemophilia B); inherited from a parent in an X-linked pattern; not contagious and not transmitted through contact between people.
prevention: Genetic counseling and carrier testing for at-risk families
Prenatal or early newborn testing when there is a known family history
Avoiding medications that increase bleeding risk, such as aspirin and certain NSAIDs, in people with known
hemophilia
Regular preventive (prophylactic) clotting factor treatment to reduce bleeding episodes
diagnosis: Diagnosed through blood tests that measure the activity level of specific clotting factors, often prompted by a family history of bleeding disorders or unexplained bleeding symptoms.
treatment: Treated with replacement of the missing clotting factor through regular preventive infusions or as needed for bleeding episodes; newer non-factor therapies are also available for some patients; treatment plans are tailored to disease severity.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt medical care for joint swelling and pain, unusual or heavy bruising, or bleeding that doesn't stop with pressure, and seek emergency care immediately for a head injury or symptoms suggesting bleeding in the brain.
related_conditions: Von Willebrand disease (a related but distinct bleeding disorder)
Acquired hemophilia (a rare autoimmune form, unrelated to inherited disease)
Hemophilic arthropathy (joint damage from repeated bleeding, a long-term complication)

source: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: An inherited condition affecting the body's connective tissue, causing tall stature with long limbs and flexible joints; the most serious complications involve the heart and blood vessels, particularly the aorta.
symptoms: Tall, thin body build with long arms, legs, fingers, and toes
A chest that sinks in or sticks out
clinical_signs: Dislocation of the lens of the eye (ectopia lentis)
A high-arched palate and crowded teeth
Flat feet
Enlargement of the aorta detected on imaging
warning_signs: Sudden, severe chest, back, or abdominal pain (possible aortic dissection, a medical emergency)
Sudden vision changes
Fainting or shortness of breath, which may signal heart valve or aortic problems
risk_factors: Family history of Marfan syndrome (inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern in most cases)
A new (spontaneous) genetic mutation, in about 25% of cases with no family history
causes: Caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene, which affects a protein that helps build healthy connective tissue supporting the bones, muscles, and organs; inherited from a parent or occurring as a new mutation; not contagious and not transmitted through contact between people.
prevention: Genetic counseling for affected individuals or families planning pregnancy
Regular cardiovascular monitoring to detect aortic enlargement early
Activity modifications to reduce cardiovascular strain, guided by a specialist
diagnosis: Diagnosed using established clinical criteria that combine family history, physical features, eye examination, and imaging of the heart and aorta (echocardiogram); genetic testing can confirm an FBN1 mutation.
treatment: Managed with medications (such as beta blockers) to reduce stress on the aorta, regular monitoring of the heart and aorta, and preventive surgery to repair the aorta before a dissection occurs when it becomes significantly enlarged.
when_to_seek_care: People with Marfan syndrome should have regular cardiovascular monitoring, and anyone with the condition should seek emergency care immediately for sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain.
related_conditions: Aortic aneurysm and dissection (the most serious complication)
Mitral valve prolapse (a common associated finding)
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (differential, another connective tissue disorder)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
specialty: Neurology, Genetics, Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
description: A group of genetic diseases that cause progressive weakness and loss of muscle mass, caused by changes in over 40 different genes; symptoms, age of onset, and severity vary widely by type.
symptoms: Difficulty rising from the floor or a seated position
Waddling gait or walking on the toes
clinical_signs: Enlarged calf muscles (pseudohypertrophy) in some types
Reduced muscle tone or reflexes
Elevated creatine kinase levels on blood testing
Progressive loss of mobility over months to years
warning_signs: Sudden, rapid loss of muscle strength
Difficulty breathing or swallowing (possible respiratory or bulbar muscle involvement)
Signs of heart involvement (irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath), which occurs in some types
Choking episodes
risk_factors: Being male, for the most common types (Duchenne and Becker), which are inherited in an X-linked pattern
Inheriting a mutated gene associated with a specific type of muscular dystrophy
causes: An inherited genetic disorder caused by mutations affecting proteins that support muscle fiber structure; inheritance patterns vary by type (X-linked, autosomal dominant, or autosomal recessive); not contagious and not transmitted through contact between people.
prevention: Genetic counseling and carrier testing for at-risk families
Prenatal or early diagnostic testing when there is a known family history
No way to prevent the underlying genetic condition itself
diagnosis: Diagnosed through blood tests measuring muscle enzymes (creatine kinase), genetic testing to identify the specific gene mutation, and sometimes muscle biopsy or electromyography.
treatment: There is no cure, but treatment can manage symptoms and slow progression, including corticosteroids, physical and occupational therapy, orthotic devices, and monitoring and treatment of heart and lung complications; some types now have targeted gene-based therapies.
when_to_seek_care: See a doctor for a child with delayed walking, frequent falls, or progressive difficulty with motor skills, or for anyone with new, unexplained muscle weakness.
related_conditions: Respiratory failure (a complication in advanced disease)

source: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: An inherited metabolic disorder in which the body cannot properly break down the amino acid phenylalanine, causing it to build up and become toxic to the brain; detected through routine newborn screening and preventable with early dietary treatment.
symptoms: Infants appear normal at birth and for the first few months of life
Without treatment: poor feeding and weakness in newborns
A musty or "mousy" odor to the breath, skin, or urine
clinical_signs: Lighter skin, hair, and eye color than family members (due to reduced melanin production)
A red skin rash with small pimples
Microcephaly (smaller than normal head size) in untreated cases
Elevated phenylalanine level on newborn blood-spot screening
warning_signs: Progressive developmental delay in the first year of life if untreated
Seizures
Abnormal gait or movement problems
Signs of maternal PKU syndrome effects in babies born to mothers with untreated PKU during pregnancy (heart
defects, low birth weight)
risk_factors: Family history of PKU or being a known carrier couple
Inheriting two copies of a mutated PAH gene, one from each parent
causes: An inherited, autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which is needed to break down phenylalanine; not contagious and not transmitted through contact between people.
prevention: Routine newborn screening allows early diagnosis before symptoms develop
Genetic carrier testing and counseling for at-risk couples
Prenatal testing is available for families with a known genetic risk
Strict dietary management during pregnancy for women with PKU to prevent harm to the fetus
diagnosis: Diagnosed through routine newborn blood-spot screening shortly after birth, which measures phenylalanine levels; elevated results are confirmed with additional testing.
treatment: There is no cure, but a lifelong low-phenylalanine diet, along with special medical formula, prevents intellectual and developmental disabilities; some patients may also benefit from medication that helps the body process phenylalanine.
when_to_seek_care: Ensure newborn screening is completed shortly after birth, and follow up promptly with a metabolic specialist if screening results are abnormal, since early treatment prevents most complications.
related_conditions: Other inborn errors of amino acid metabolism
Maternal PKU syndrome (a complication affecting babies of untreated pregnant women with PKU)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A group of inherited red blood cell disorders in which abnormal hemoglobin causes red blood cells to become hard, sticky, and sickle-shaped, leading to blocked blood flow, chronic anemia, and serious complications throughout the body.
clinical_signs: Pallor and jaundice
Delayed growth in children
Signs of anemia on blood testing
Sickle-shaped cells visible on blood smear
warning_signs: Acute chest syndrome (fever, chest pain, difficulty breathing)
Signs of stroke (sudden weakness, confusion, vision changes)
Severe, unrelieved pain crisis
High fever, which can indicate life-threatening infection
risk_factors: Inheriting the sickle cell gene from both parents (autosomal recessive inheritance)
Family history of sickle cell disease or trait
Ancestry from regions where malaria is/was common, where the sickle cell trait is more prevalent
causes: Not an infectious disease; caused by inherited mutations in the gene for hemoglobin, leading to production of abnormal hemoglobin (hemoglobin S); passed from parents to children through genetic inheritance, not transmitted between people.
prevention: Genetic counseling and carrier screening for at-risk couples
Newborn screening for early diagnosis and preventive care
Vaccination and infection prevention measures for those with SCD
Hydroxyurea and other preventive therapies to reduce complications
diagnosis: Diagnosed through newborn screening or blood tests (hemoglobin electrophoresis or genetic testing) that identify abnormal hemoglobin.
treatment: Managed with pain control during crises, hydroxyurea to reduce the frequency of complications, blood transfusions when needed, and in select cases, hematopoietic stem cell transplant, which can be curative; comprehensive care includes vaccination and infection prevention.
when_to_seek_care: Seek emergency care immediately for signs of acute chest syndrome, stroke symptoms, severe unrelieved pain, or high fever, as infection can be life-threatening for people with SCD.
related_conditions: Aplastic anemia (differential for severe anemia crisis)

source: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), NIH
description: A group of inherited blood disorders in which the body produces reduced or abnormal hemoglobin, leading to varying degrees of chronic anemia, from mild and asymptomatic to severe and transfusion-dependent.
clinical_signs: Small, pale red blood cells on blood smear
Bone changes/facial bone deformities in severe forms
Jaundice
Enlarged spleen or liver
warning_signs: Severe anemia requiring urgent transfusion
Signs of iron overload from repeated transfusions (organ damage)
Signs of heart strain (shortness of breath, palpitations) from chronic severe anemia
risk_factors: Family history of thalassaemia (autosomal recessive inheritance)
Ancestry from the Mediterranean, Middle East, South and Southeast Asia, or Africa, where carrier rates are higher
Both parents being genetic carriers (25% chance of an affected child)
causes: Not an infectious disease; caused by inherited genetic mutations affecting alpha- or beta-globin genes that reduce the body's ability to produce functioning hemoglobin; passed from parents to children through genetic inheritance, not transmitted between people.
prevention: Genetic carrier testing and counseling before pregnancy, especially in high-prevalence populations
Prenatal testing for couples where both partners are carriers
No means of preventing thalassaemia in someone who has inherited the genetic mutations
diagnosis: Diagnosed through blood tests, including full blood count and hemoglobin electrophoresis, with genetic testing to confirm carrier or affected status.
treatment: Mild forms (thalassaemia minor) usually require no treatment; thalassaemia major requires regular blood transfusions and iron chelation therapy to prevent iron overload; hematopoietic stem cell transplant can be curative in some cases.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for unexplained chronic fatigue, pale skin, or slow growth in a child, particularly with a family history of thalassaemia or ancestry from a high-prevalence region; couples planning a family in high-risk populations should consider carrier testing.

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
description: A condition in which the kidneys are damaged or cannot filter blood as well as they should, often progressing silently over years; commonly caused by diabetes and high blood pressure and, if it advances, can lead to kidney failure.
symptoms: Often no symptoms in early stages
Swelling in the legs, ankles, or feet
Changes in urination frequency or appearance
clinical_signs: Elevated blood pressure
Protein or blood in urine (on urinalysis)
Reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) on blood testing
Electrolyte abnormalities
warning_signs: Severe swelling
Shortness of breath from fluid overload
Confusion or difficulty concentrating (advanced kidney failure)
Very low urine output
causes: Not an infectious disease; most commonly caused by diabetes and high blood pressure, which damage the small blood vessels and filtering units (nephrons) in the kidneys over time; other causes include glomerular diseases and structural kidney abnormalities. Not transmitted between people.
prevention: Managing blood pressure and blood glucose levels
Maintaining a healthy weight and being physically active
Avoiding excessive use of medications that can harm the kidneys (e.g., long-term NSAID use)
Regular kidney function testing for those at risk
diagnosis: Diagnosed through blood tests (estimated glomerular filtration rate, eGFR) and urine tests (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) to detect kidney damage or reduced function, typically confirmed with abnormal results persisting for more than 3 months.
treatment: Treatment focuses on managing underlying causes (blood pressure and blood glucose control), dietary changes, and medications to slow progression; advanced kidney failure (end-stage renal disease) requires dialysis or kidney transplant.
when_to_seek_care: People with risk factors such as diabetes, high blood pressure, or a family history of kidney failure should get tested regularly, since early-stage CKD usually causes no symptoms; seek prompt care for swelling, marked fatigue, or reduced urination.

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: Hard deposits made of minerals and salts that form inside the kidneys; small stones may pass unnoticed, while larger stones can cause severe pain and require treatment.
symptoms: Severe pain in the back, side, or lower abdomen (renal colic)
Pain that comes in waves and may radiate to the groin
clinical_signs: Costovertebral angle tenderness on examination
Blood or crystals visible on urinalysis
Stone visible on imaging (ultrasound or CT scan)
warning_signs: Fever and chills with flank pain (possible infected obstructing stone, a urologic emergency)
Inability to urinate
Severe, unrelenting pain not controlled by pain medication
Persistent vomiting preventing fluid intake
risk_factors: Family or personal history of kidney stones
Certain diets (high sodium, high animal protein, high oxalate)
Certain medical conditions (gout, hyperparathyroidism, inflammatory bowel disease)
causes: Not an infectious disease; forms when urine contains more crystal-forming substances (calcium, oxalate, uric acid) than the fluid can dilute, or lacks substances that prevent crystals from sticking together; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Drinking enough fluids to produce more than 2 liters of urine per day
Reducing dietary sodium intake
Moderating animal protein intake
Following stone-type-specific dietary recommendations from a healthcare provider
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on symptoms and confirmed with imaging tests such as ultrasound, CT scan, or X-ray; urine and blood tests help identify the underlying cause and stone type.
treatment: Small stones often pass on their own with hydration and pain control; larger stones may require procedures such as shock wave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy, or percutaneous nephrolithotomy to break up or remove the stone.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt medical care for severe flank or abdominal pain, especially with nausea or blood in the urine, and seek emergency care immediately for fever with flank pain or inability to urinate.
related_conditions: Urinary tract infection (can occur with or complicate stones)
Gout (a risk factor for uric acid stones)

icd11: GC08 (Urinary tract infection, site not specified)
source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: An infection of the urinary tract, most often the bladder, caused primarily by bacteria; common and treatable, but can spread to the kidneys if untreated.
symptoms: Pain or discomfort in the lower abdomen
clinical_signs: Suprapubic tenderness on examination
Bacteria and white blood cells on urinalysis
Low-grade fever in some cases
warning_signs: Fever, chills, and pain in the back, side, or groin (possible kidney infection)
Nausea and vomiting with urinary symptoms
Confusion, especially in older adults (can be a sign of a more serious infection)
Symptoms that don't improve or worsen despite treatment
risk_factors: Blockages in the urinary tract, such as kidney stones
causes: Most commonly caused by bacteria, especially E. coli, entering the urinary tract; not typically transmitted between people, though sexual activity can introduce bacteria into the urinary tract.
prevention: Drinking plenty of liquids, especially water
Urinating regularly and after sexual activity
Wearing loose-fitting clothing
Good hygiene practices
diagnosis: Diagnosed through review of symptoms, a physical exam, and laboratory testing of a urine sample (urinalysis and urine culture) to confirm infection and identify the bacteria involved.
treatment: Most bladder infections are treated with a course of antibiotics; drinking more fluids can help speed recovery and ease symptoms; kidney infections may require longer antibiotic courses or hospitalization in severe cases.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for burning urination, urinary frequency, or lower abdominal pain, and seek prompt care for fever, back or side pain, nausea, or vomiting, which may indicate a kidney infection.
related_conditions: Pyelonephritis (kidney infection, a complication of untreated or ascending UTI)
Kidney stones (a risk factor and differential)
Sexually transmitted infections (differential for urinary symptoms)

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
description: The last stage of chronic liver disease, in which scar tissue progressively replaces healthy liver tissue, impairing liver function and potentially leading to serious, life-threatening complications.
symptoms: Often no symptoms in early stages
clinical_signs: Small, red spider-like blood vessels on the skin (spider angiomas)
Jaundice
Enlarged liver or spleen on examination
Abnormal liver blood tests
warning_signs: Ascites (fluid buildup in the abdomen)
Confusion or difficulty thinking (hepatic encephalopathy)
Vomiting blood or black, tarry stools (variceal bleeding)
Signs of infection with fever and abdominal pain (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis)
risk_factors: Chronic hepatitis B or C infection
causes: Not itself an infectious disease, though some of its underlying causes (hepatitis B and C) are; cirrhosis results from long-term liver damage from causes such as chronic viral hepatitis, alcohol use, or fatty liver disease, leading to progressive scarring (fibrosis).
prevention: Vaccination against and treatment of hepatitis B
Treatment of hepatitis C to prevent progression
Limiting or avoiding alcohol use
Maintaining a healthy weight to prevent fatty liver disease
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on medical history, physical examination, and blood tests showing liver damage; imaging tests (ultrasound, elastography) and sometimes liver biopsy are used to assess the degree of scarring.
treatment: No treatment cures cirrhosis itself, but treating the underlying cause (e.g., antiviral therapy for hepatitis, alcohol cessation) can prevent it from worsening; complications are managed individually, and severe cases may require liver transplant evaluation.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent fatigue, unexplained weight loss, or abdominal swelling, especially with risk factors such as chronic hepatitis or heavy alcohol use; seek emergency care for vomiting blood, black stools, or confusion.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: The most frequently reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis; often causes no symptoms but can lead to serious, irreversible reproductive damage if untreated.
symptoms: Often no symptoms, especially early on
clinical_signs: Cervical discharge or inflammation on examination
Bleeding between periods or after sex
Testicular pain or swelling in men
Rectal pain, discharge, or bleeding with rectal infection
warning_signs: Severe pelvic pain with fever (possible pelvic inflammatory disease)
Signs of ectopic pregnancy (severe one-sided abdominal pain, especially with a missed period)
Testicular pain and swelling with fever (possible epididymitis)
risk_factors: Being sexually active, especially with a new or multiple partners
causes: Caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis; spread through vaginal, anal, or oral sexual contact with an infected person, and can be passed from a mother to her baby during childbirth.
prevention: Consistent and correct condom use
Regular STI screening, especially for sexually active women under 25
Reducing number of sexual partners
Prompt treatment of infected partners to prevent reinfection
diagnosis: Diagnosed with a laboratory test (nucleic acid amplification test) on a urine sample or a swab from the affected site (cervix, urethra, throat, or rectum).
treatment: Treated effectively with a course of antibiotics; sexual partners should also be tested and treated, and people should avoid sex until treatment is completed to prevent reinfection or spread.
when_to_seek_care: Get tested regularly if sexually active, especially with a new partner, and seek care promptly for any genital symptoms, pelvic pain, or if a partner has been diagnosed with an STI.
related_conditions: Trachoma (caused by a different route of transmission of the same bacterial species)

also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A chronic disease in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus, causing a chronic inflammatory reaction; affects roughly 190 million women and girls of reproductive age globally and has no cure.
symptoms: Chronic pelvic pain that does not go away when the menstrual cycle ends
clinical_signs: Tenderness or masses felt on pelvic examination
Endometrial-like lesions or adhesions seen on imaging or during surgery
Infertility or difficulty conceiving
warning_signs: Sudden, severe pelvic pain (possible ovarian cyst rupture or torsion, needing urgent evaluation)
Heavy bleeding causing significant fatigue or dizziness (possible anemia)
New or worsening bowel or bladder symptoms with pelvic pain
risk_factors: Short menstrual cycles or heavy periods
causes: Not an infectious disease; the exact cause is not fully understood, though genetic, hormonal, and immune factors are believed to play a role in the abnormal growth of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent endometriosis
Early recognition and treatment of symptoms may help limit disease progression and its impact on fertility and
quality of life
diagnosis: Diagnosis is often delayed for years; it can be suspected from symptoms and pelvic examination, supported by imaging (ultrasound or MRI), though definitive diagnosis usually requires laparoscopic surgery with tissue biopsy.
treatment: There is no cure; treatment focuses on symptom control and may include pain medication, hormonal therapies (contraceptives, progestins, GnRH agonists) to suppress the menstrual cycle, and surgery to remove endometrial lesions in some cases.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for persistent or severe pelvic pain, painful periods that interfere with daily life, or difficulty becoming pregnant, so that endometriosis can be considered and evaluated.
related_conditions: Irritable bowel syndrome (differential, given overlapping GI symptoms)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A common, lifelong sexually transmitted infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 or HSV-2), often with mild or no symptoms, that causes periodic outbreaks of genital sores.
symptoms: Often no symptoms or very mild symptoms
One or more blisters on or around the genitals, rectum, or mouth
Painful sores after blisters break open
Flu-like symptoms (fever, body aches, swollen glands) during a first outbreak
clinical_signs: Painful genital or perianal ulcers
Tender, swollen inguinal lymph nodes
Recurrent outbreaks, typically shorter and milder than the first episode
warning_signs: Symptoms of aseptic meningitis (severe headache, neck stiffness, light sensitivity)
Widespread or severe sores in someone with a weakened immune system
New genital sores during pregnancy, given the risk to the newborn (neonatal herpes)
risk_factors: Being sexually active, especially with a new or multiple partners
Being female (biologically more susceptible to acquiring HSV during sex)
causes: Caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 or type 2; spread through vaginal, anal, or oral sex with someone who has the virus, including through skin-to-skin contact when no visible sores are present.
prevention: Consistent and correct condom use (reduces but does not eliminate risk)
Avoiding sexual contact during an active outbreak
Daily antiviral suppressive therapy can reduce transmission risk to partners
Disclosure of HSV status to partners
diagnosis: Diagnosed through testing of fluid from a sore (viral culture or PCR) during an outbreak, or blood tests for HSV antibodies, which can detect infection even without visible symptoms.
treatment: There is no cure, but antiviral medications (such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir) can shorten and prevent outbreaks and, when taken daily, reduce the risk of transmission to partners.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for any new genital sores or blisters, and pregnant women with genital herpes should inform their provider to help prevent transmission to the baby during delivery.
related_conditions: Neonatal herpes (a complication of transmission during childbirth)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: The most common sexually transmitted infection, caused by human papillomavirus; most infections clear on their own, but certain HPV types can cause genital warts or, over time, cervical and other cancers.
symptoms: Small, flesh-colored or gray genital warts, single or in clusters
Itching or discomfort in the genital area (with warts)
clinical_signs: Visible warts on the vulva, penis, groin, or anus
Abnormal Pap test result (in women, from cervical cell changes)
Warts may be flat, raised, or cauliflower-shaped
warning_signs: Warts that bleed, grow rapidly, or do not respond to treatment
Abnormal vaginal bleeding (possible sign of HPV-related cervical changes needing evaluation)
Persistent hoarseness or throat symptoms if oral HPV is suspected
risk_factors: Being sexually active, especially with a new or multiple partners
Younger age (most new infections in late teens/early 20s)
causes: Caused by human papillomavirus; spread through vaginal, anal, or oral sex, and through close skin-to-skin genital contact with an infected person, even without visible symptoms.
prevention: HPV vaccination, most effective when given before sexual activity begins
Consistent and correct condom use (reduces but does not eliminate risk)
Regular cervical cancer screening (Pap and/or HPV testing) for early detection of cell changes
