diagnosis: Genital warts are usually diagnosed by visual examination; cervical HPV-related changes are detected through Pap tests and HPV testing as part of routine cervical cancer screening.
treatment: There is no treatment for the virus itself; visible genital warts can be treated with prescription topical medications, freezing, or minor procedures, and abnormal cervical cell changes are managed according to screening guidelines.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for any new genital growths or bumps, and keep up with routine cervical cancer screening, since most HPV-related cell changes cause no symptoms.
related_conditions: Cervical cancer (long-term complication of high-risk HPV types)
Anal, vulvar, penile, and oropharyngeal cancers (associated with high-risk HPV types)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A common sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae bacteria, which can infect the genitals, rectum, and throat; often causes no symptoms but can lead to serious complications including infertility if untreated.
symptoms: Often no symptoms, especially in women
Discharge from the penis (white, yellow, or green)
clinical_signs: Thick, cloudy, or bloody penile or vaginal discharge
Painful or swollen testicles in men
Anal itching, soreness, bleeding, or discharge with rectal infection
warning_signs: Fever, chills, and skin sores with joint pain (possible disseminated gonococcal infection, a medical emergency)
Severe pelvic pain with fever (possible pelvic inflammatory disease)
Signs of infection in a newborn's eyes (redness, discharge), which can lead to blindness if untreated
risk_factors: Being sexually active, especially with a new or multiple partners
Previous gonorrhea or other STI diagnosis
causes: Caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae; spread through vaginal, anal, or oral sex with an infected person, and can be passed from a mother to her baby during childbirth.
prevention: Consistent and correct condom use
Regular STI screening for sexually active individuals with risk factors
Reducing number of sexual partners
Prompt treatment of infected partners
Antibiotic eye ointment given to newborns to prevent transmission during birth
diagnosis: Diagnosed using a nucleic acid amplification test on a urine sample or a swab from the affected site (cervix, urethra, throat, or rectum).
treatment: Treated with antibiotics; due to rising antibiotic resistance, treatment recommendations are updated periodically, and follow-up testing may be advised to confirm the infection has cleared.
when_to_seek_care: Seek testing and treatment promptly for any genital or throat symptoms, or if a sexual partner has been diagnosed with gonorrhea, and seek emergency care for fever with joint pain and skin sores.
related_conditions: Disseminated gonococcal infection (a rare, serious complication)
Neonatal conjunctivitis (a complication of transmission at birth)

description: A common hormonal, reproductive, and metabolic disorder affecting people with ovaries, characterized by irregular menstrual cycles and/or signs of excess androgens; a leading cause of infertility, though ovarian cysts are not required for diagnosis.
symptoms: Irregular, infrequent, or absent menstrual periods
Excess facial or body hair growth (hirsutism)
clinical_signs: Elevated blood androgen (testosterone) levels on testing
Polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasound (not required for diagnosis)
Signs of insulin resistance (e.g., skin darkening at the neck or armpits)
Weight gain, particularly around the waist
warning_signs: Very heavy or prolonged uterine bleeding
Severe pelvic pain (warrants evaluation for other causes)
Signs of diabetes (excessive thirst, frequent urination) reflecting metabolic complications
risk_factors: Family history of PCOS or type 2 diabetes
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from a combination of genetic and hormonal factors leading to excess androgen production and irregular ovulation; the precise cause is not fully understood, and it is not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent PCOS
Maintaining a healthy weight and regular physical activity may help reduce symptom severity and metabolic risk
Early diagnosis and management can reduce long-term complications
diagnosis: Diagnosed using a combination of criteria, which may include irregular or absent ovulation, clinical or laboratory signs of high androgen levels, and ovarian appearance on ultrasound; blood tests help rule out other conditions with similar symptoms.
treatment: Management is tailored to symptoms and goals, and may include hormonal birth control to regulate periods and reduce androgen effects, metformin for insulin resistance, fertility treatments for those trying to conceive, and lifestyle changes such as weight management.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for irregular or absent periods, difficulty conceiving, or bothersome excess hair growth or acne, so that PCOS can be diagnosed and managed, including screening for associated metabolic risks.
related_conditions: Endometrial cancer (increased long-term risk from irregular cycles)

description: A multi-system disorder of pregnancy, usually arising after 20 weeks of gestation, characterized by new-onset high blood pressure often with protein in the urine; a leading cause of maternal and infant illness and death if untreated.
symptoms: Often no noticeable symptoms in mild cases
Vision changes (blurred vision, seeing spots, light sensitivity)
Swelling of the face or hands
Upper abdominal pain, usually under the ribs on the right side
clinical_signs: Blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or higher on two occasions
Protein in the urine (proteinuria)
Rapid weight gain over a few days from fluid retention
Abnormal liver enzymes or low platelet count on blood testing
warning_signs: Severe headache unrelieved by usual measures
Visual disturbances or temporary vision loss
Seizures (eclampsia, a medical emergency)
Severe upper abdominal pain with nausea or vomiting
Shortness of breath from fluid in the lungs
risk_factors: Pregnancy at a very young or older maternal age
causes: Not an infectious disease; believed to originate from abnormal development of blood vessels supplying the placenta early in pregnancy, though the exact cause is not fully understood; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Low-dose aspirin during pregnancy for those at high risk
Calcium supplementation in populations with low dietary calcium intake
Regular prenatal care with blood pressure and urine monitoring
Managing chronic hypertension before and during pregnancy
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on new-onset high blood pressure after 20 weeks of pregnancy, typically combined with proteinuria or other signs of organ involvement, confirmed through blood pressure measurement and urine and blood testing.
treatment: The only definitive treatment is delivery of the baby and placenta; management before delivery includes blood pressure control, magnesium sulfate to prevent seizures in severe cases, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if preterm delivery is needed, and close monitoring of mother and baby.
when_to_seek_care: Seek immediate medical care during pregnancy or postpartum for severe headache, vision changes, upper abdominal pain, or swelling, and attend all scheduled prenatal visits, since pre-eclampsia can be present without noticeable symptoms.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum that progresses through distinct stages if untreated, and can cause serious, potentially fatal complications, but is simple to cure with the right treatment when caught early.
symptoms: A firm, round, usually painless sore (chancre) at the site of infection (primary stage)
Skin rash, often on the palms and soles (secondary stage)
clinical_signs: Painless genital, anal, or oral sore in primary syphilis
Non-itchy rash on the trunk, palms, or soles in secondary syphilis
No visible signs during the latent stage despite ongoing infection
warning_signs: Neurological symptoms (severe headache, vision or hearing changes, confusion) suggesting neurosyphilis
Signs of cardiovascular involvement in late-stage disease
Any syphilis symptoms during pregnancy, given the risk to the baby (congenital syphilis)
risk_factors: Being sexually active, especially with a new or multiple partners
Men who have sex with men (higher reported rates in some regions)
Being pregnant while infected (risk of transmission to the baby)
causes: Caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum; spread through direct contact with a syphilis sore during vaginal, anal, or oral sex, and can be transmitted from a pregnant person to their baby (congenital syphilis).
prevention: Consistent and correct condom use (though sores outside the covered area can still transmit infection)
Regular STI screening, especially during pregnancy
Avoiding sexual contact with an infected partner until treatment is complete
Treating pregnant women promptly to prevent congenital syphilis
diagnosis: Diagnosed primarily through blood tests for syphilis antibodies; direct examination of fluid from a sore can also confirm infection in the early stages.
treatment: Penicillin, given by injection, is the preferred treatment for all stages of syphilis and is the only recommended treatment during pregnancy; the specific dosing schedule depends on the stage of infection.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt testing and treatment for any genital sore or unexplained rash, and all pregnant women should be screened for syphilis, since untreated infection can seriously harm the baby.
related_conditions: HIV (increases risk of and interacts with syphilis)
Congenital syphilis (a complication of untreated infection during pregnancy)
Other genital ulcer diseases (differential for the primary sore)

source: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: Benign (non-cancerous) growths made of smooth muscle cells and other tissue that develop in or on the wall of the uterus; very common in women of reproductive age, though many have no symptoms.
clinical_signs: Enlarged, irregularly shaped uterus on pelvic examination
Fibroids visible on ultrasound or MRI
Anemia from heavy bleeding on blood testing
warning_signs: Very heavy bleeding causing significant fatigue, dizziness, or shortness of breath (possible severe anemia)
Sudden, severe pelvic pain (possible fibroid degeneration or torsion)
Reproductive problems such as recurrent miscarriage or preterm labor
risk_factors: Older reproductive age (though fibroids may shrink after menopause)
Black race/ethnicity (higher risk and often more severe disease)
causes: Not an infectious disease; the exact cause is unknown, though fibroid growth is influenced by hormones (estrogen and progesterone) and genetic factors; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent uterine fibroids
Early evaluation of abnormal bleeding or pelvic symptoms can help guide timely management
diagnosis: Diagnosed through pelvic examination and imaging, most often ultrasound, with MRI used for more detailed evaluation when needed.
treatment: Treatment depends on symptoms, fibroid size and location, and fertility goals, and may include watchful waiting, medications to control bleeding or shrink fibroids, minimally invasive procedures (such as uterine fibroid embolization), or surgery (myomectomy); hysterectomy is currently the only cure.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, pelvic pain or pressure, or difficulty conceiving, so that fibroids and other causes can be evaluated.
related_conditions: Iron-deficiency anemia (a common complication of heavy bleeding)
Infertility (a possible complication depending on fibroid location)

source: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A medical condition characterized by an impaired ability to stop or control alcohol use despite adverse social, occupational, or health consequences; a brain disorder that can range from mild to severe.
symptoms: Drinking more or for longer than intended
Unsuccessful attempts to cut down or stop drinking
Strong cravings or urges to drink
Continuing to drink despite it causing problems at home, work, or school
Needing more alcohol to feel its effects (tolerance)
clinical_signs: Giving up important activities in favor of drinking
Drinking in physically hazardous situations, such as before driving
Continuing to drink despite worsening physical or mental health problems
Withdrawal symptoms when alcohol use is stopped or reduced
warning_signs: Withdrawal symptoms such as a racing heart, sweating, severe shakiness, or a seizure when stopping drinking
(can be medically dangerous and requires supervised care)
Signs of severe liver disease (jaundice, abdominal swelling)
Suicidal thoughts, which are more common among people with heavy alcohol use
risk_factors: Family history of alcohol use disorder
Starting to drink at a young age
Mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from a combination of genetic, psychological, social, and environmental factors that affect brain reward and stress pathways with repeated alcohol use; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Limiting alcohol intake and avoiding binge drinking
Screening and early counseling for at-risk drinking patterns
Addressing mental health conditions and stress through healthy coping strategies
Avoiding early exposure to alcohol in adolescence
diagnosis: Diagnosed using standardized clinical criteria assessing the number and severity of alcohol-related symptoms over the past year; severity is classified as mild, moderate, or severe based on how many criteria are met.
treatment: Treatment options include FDA-approved medications (such as naltrexone, acamprosate, or disulfiram) and behavioral therapies such as cognitive behavioral therapy, delivered in outpatient or residential settings; treatment plans are tailored to severity and individual needs.
when_to_seek_care: Talk to a healthcare provider if drinking is causing problems in daily life or if cutting back feels difficult, and seek medical supervision before stopping heavy, regular drinking, since withdrawal can be dangerous.

also_known_as: Generalized anxiety disorder and related conditions
description: A group of mental disorders characterized by excessive fear and worry and related behavioral disturbances, severe enough to cause significant distress or impairment in daily functioning; among the most common mental disorders worldwide.
clinical_signs: Rapid heart rate or palpitations during anxious episodes
Sweating or trembling
Avoidance behavior around feared situations or objects
Panic attacks (sudden intense fear with physical symptoms) in some anxiety disorders
warning_signs: Panic attacks with chest pain or severe shortness of breath (needs evaluation to rule out other causes)
Anxiety severe enough to prevent basic daily functioning
Thoughts of self-harm accompanying severe anxiety or panic
risk_factors: Other mental health conditions, such as depression
Certain personality traits (e.g., high behavioral inhibition)
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from a combination of genetic, environmental, and psychological factors that heighten the body's fear and stress response; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Stress management techniques
Building social support networks
Regular physical activity
Early treatment of symptoms before they become severe or chronic
diagnosis: Diagnosed through clinical evaluation of the pattern, severity, and duration of fear and worry symptoms, using diagnostic criteria and often standardized screening questionnaires, while ruling out medical causes that can mimic anxiety.
treatment: Effective treatments include psychotherapy, particularly cognitive behavioral therapy, and medications such as certain antidepressants; treatment is tailored to the specific anxiety disorder and its severity.
when_to_seek_care: Seek help from a healthcare or mental health professional for excessive worry or fear that interferes with daily life, work, or relationships, or for panic attacks, especially if physical symptoms raise concern about other medical causes.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A neurodevelopmental disorder involving patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interfere with functioning or development; symptoms typically start in childhood and can continue into adulthood.
symptoms: Difficulty paying attention to details or following instructions
Fidgeting, restlessness, or difficulty staying seated
Excessive talking or difficulty waiting one's turn
clinical_signs: Symptoms present in more than one setting (home, school, work)
Symptoms that have persisted for at least 6 months and are inconsistent with developmental level
Three presentations: mostly inattentive, mostly hyperactive-impulsive, or combined
warning_signs: Symptoms severe enough to cause significant safety concerns (impulsive risk-taking)
Signs of a co-occurring condition (severe anxiety, depression, or behavioral problems) requiring separate
evaluation
Sudden new onset of inattention or behavior change (warrants evaluation for other causes)
risk_factors: Premature birth or low birth weight
Prenatal exposure to tobacco, alcohol, or certain substances
causes: Not an infectious disease and not transmitted between people; results from a combination of genetic and environmental factors affecting brain development and function; the exact cause is not fully understood.
prevention: No known way to prevent ADHD
Avoiding tobacco, alcohol, and other substance use during pregnancy may reduce risk
Early identification and intervention can improve functioning and outcomes
diagnosis: Diagnosed through a comprehensive evaluation process involving history from parents, teachers, or the individual, and standardized rating scales; there is no single test for ADHD, and other conditions with similar symptoms must be ruled out.
treatment: Treatment can include behavior therapy and medication (stimulant or non-stimulant); behavior therapy is recommended as the first-line treatment for young children, while a combination approach is often used for older children, adolescents, and adults.
when_to_seek_care: Talk with a healthcare provider if a child or adult shows persistent difficulty with attention, organization, or hyperactivity/impulsivity that affects school, work, or relationships.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A developmental disability characterized by differences in social communication and interaction, along with restricted or repetitive behaviors and interests; a spectrum condition with wide variation in presentation and support needs.
symptoms: Differences in social communication and interaction (limited eye contact, difficulty with back-and-forth
Restricted or repetitive behaviors, interests, or activities
Differences in learning, moving, or paying attention
Strong reactions to sensory input (sounds, textures, lights)
clinical_signs: Delayed or atypical language development in some individuals
Difficulty understanding others' perspectives or nonverbal cues
Insistence on sameness or routines
Intense, focused interests in specific topics
warning_signs: Significant regression or loss of previously acquired skills
Self-injurious behavior
Co-occurring anxiety, depression, or ADHD symptoms significantly affecting functioning
Difficulty communicating basic needs, which can create safety risks
risk_factors: Having a sibling with autism spectrum disorder
Certain genetic conditions (e.g., fragile X syndrome, tuberous sclerosis)
Very low birth weight or premature birth
causes: Not an infectious disease and not transmitted between people; caused by differences in brain development, with genetic factors playing a significant role and possible additional environmental contributions; the precise cause varies and is not fully understood.
prevention: No known way to prevent autism spectrum disorder
Early identification and intervention can improve developmental outcomes and quality of life
diagnosis: Diagnosed through developmental screening and comprehensive evaluation by trained professionals, assessing social communication and behavior patterns against standardized diagnostic criteria; can be reliably diagnosed as early as age 2.
treatment: There is no single treatment; individualized approaches may include behavioral therapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy, educational support, and treatment of co-occurring conditions; early intervention services can significantly improve outcomes.
when_to_seek_care: Talk with a healthcare provider about developmental screening if a child shows differences in social communication, unusual repetitive behaviors, or developmental delays, since early intervention is linked to better outcomes.
related_conditions: Intellectual disability (co-occurs in a subset of cases)

description: A brain disorder that causes unusual and often extreme shifts in mood, energy, activity levels, and the ability to carry out daily tasks, involving distinct periods called mood episodes that differ drastically from a person's usual mood and behavior.
symptoms: Manic episodes: abnormally elevated or irritable mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, racing
Depressive episodes: persistent sadness, loss of interest, fatigue, hopelessness
Mixed episodes with symptoms of both mania and depression
Changes in sleep, activity, and behavior noticeable to others
clinical_signs: Grandiosity or inflated self-esteem during manic episodes
Increased goal-directed activity or risky behavior during mania
Psychomotor slowing during depressive episodes
Mood episodes lasting most of the day for a week or more (mania) or two weeks or more (depression)
warning_signs: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Severe impulsivity leading to dangerous behavior (reckless spending, risky sexual behavior)
Psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) during a mood episode
Inability to function or care for basic needs
risk_factors: Family history of bipolar disorder (strongest known risk factor)
Onset most often in late teens or early adulthood
High levels of stress or major life changes
causes: Not an infectious disease and not transmitted between people; the exact cause is unknown, but genetics play a major role alongside other contributing biological and environmental factors.
prevention: No known way to prevent bipolar disorder
Early diagnosis and consistent treatment can reduce the frequency and severity of mood episodes and improve
long-term outcomes
diagnosis: Diagnosed through a comprehensive psychiatric evaluation of mood episode history, symptoms, and their impact on functioning; there is no blood test or brain scan that can diagnose bipolar disorder.
treatment: Usually requires lifelong treatment, most often a combination of mood-stabilizing medication (and sometimes antipsychotics or antidepressants) and psychotherapy; treatment can lead to better functioning and improved quality of life even though symptoms may come and go.
when_to_seek_care: Seek help from a mental health professional for extreme or unusual shifts in mood, energy, or behavior lasting a week or more, and seek immediate help for any thoughts of suicide or self-harm.

icd11: 8A20-8A2Z (Disorders with neurocognitive impairment as a major feature)
also_known_as: Alzheimer's disease (most common cause), major neurocognitive disorder
description: A syndrome, usually chronic or progressive, involving deterioration in cognitive function beyond what is expected from normal aging; Alzheimer's disease is the most common underlying cause, and dementia is a leading cause of disability among older people globally.
symptoms: Trouble following conversations or finding words
clinical_signs: Difficulty performing familiar tasks
Misjudging distances visually
Personality changes
Withdrawal from work or social activities
Progressive decline documented on cognitive testing
warning_signs: Rapid or sudden decline in cognition (may suggest a different, treatable cause needing urgent evaluation)
Getting lost and being unable to find one's way home
Severe agitation or behavior that poses safety risks
Signs of an acute confusional state (delirium) superimposed on dementia
risk_factors: Increasing age (strongest known risk factor, though not an inevitable part of aging)
Family history and certain genetic factors
causes: Not an infectious disease and not transmitted between people; caused by diseases and injuries that affect the brain, most commonly Alzheimer's disease, as well as vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, and other conditions.
prevention: Regular physical activity
Not smoking and avoiding harmful alcohol use
Managing weight, blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar
Staying socially and cognitively active
Reducing exposure to air pollution where possible
diagnosis: Diagnosed through clinical history, cognitive and neuropsychological testing, and brain imaging to assess the pattern of impairment and rule out other treatable causes.
treatment: There is no cure for most causes of dementia; treatment focuses on managing symptoms and maintaining quality of life, including cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., donepezil) for Alzheimer's disease and NMDA receptor antagonists (e.g., memantine) for more severe disease, alongside supportive care for the person and caregivers.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent memory loss or cognitive changes that interfere with daily life, and seek prompt care for sudden or rapid cognitive decline, which may indicate a reversible underlying cause.
related_conditions: Parkinson disease (dementia can occur in advanced PD)
Depression (can mimic or coexist with dementia)
Vitamin B12 deficiency or hypothyroidism (reversible differentials)

description: A common mental disorder involving a depressed mood or loss of interest and pleasure in activities for long periods of time, different from normal mood changes and capable of affecting all areas of life; a leading cause of disability worldwide.
symptoms: Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day
Loss of interest or pleasure in activities
Sleeping too much or too little
clinical_signs: Psychomotor slowing or agitation observable to others
Feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt
Reduced ability to think or make decisions
warning_signs: Thoughts of self-harm or suicide
Inability to care for basic needs (eating, hygiene)
Sudden severe withdrawal or hopelessness
Psychotic symptoms accompanying severe depression (hallucinations, delusions)
risk_factors: Personal or family history of depression
Social isolation and lack of support
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from a complex interaction of social, psychological, and biological factors; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Building strong social connections and support networks
Regular physical activity
Managing chronic stress and adverse life circumstances where possible
Early identification and treatment of mild symptoms before they worsen
diagnosis: Diagnosed through clinical assessment of symptoms present for at least two weeks that cause significant distress or impairment, using structured interviews or standardized screening tools, and ruling out other medical causes.
treatment: Effective treatments exist for mild, moderate, and severe depression, including psychotherapy (such as cognitive behavioral therapy), antidepressant medications, and, for severe cases, other interventions; treatment is often combined with lifestyle support.
when_to_seek_care: Seek help from a mental health professional for persistent low mood or loss of interest lasting two weeks or more that affects daily functioning, and seek immediate help for any thoughts of self-harm or suicide.

condition: Eating Disorders (Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa)
description: Serious mental health conditions marked by severe disturbances in eating behavior and related thoughts and emotions about food, weight, or body shape; anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa are the two most widely recognized types, and both can have serious physical and psychological consequences.
symptoms: Anorexia nervosa: severe restriction of food intake and intense fear of gaining weight, even at a dangerously low
Bulimia nervosa: recurrent episodes of eating unusually large amounts of food with a sense of loss of control,
followed by behaviors to prevent weight gain
Preoccupation with food, weight, or body shape
A distorted perception of one's own body
clinical_signs: Significant, rapid weight change (loss in anorexia; weight may be normal or elevated in bulimia)
Signs of malnutrition (fatigue, dizziness, feeling cold)
Menstrual irregularities
Dental or throat problems in bulimia from repeated vomiting
warning_signs: Fainting, chest pain, or an irregular heartbeat
Signs of severe dehydration or electrolyte imbalance
Thoughts of self-harm or suicide
Significant, rapid weight loss or medical instability
risk_factors: Family history of eating disorders or other mental health conditions
Personal history of anxiety or perfectionism
Participation in activities that emphasize thinness (certain sports, dance, modeling)
Social or cultural pressures around body image
History of dieting or weight-related teasing
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from a complex interplay of biological, psychological, and social factors that is still not fully understood; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Early identification and treatment of disordered eating patterns before they become entrenched
Building healthy attitudes toward food and body image
Addressing co-occurring anxiety or mood concerns early
diagnosis: Diagnosed through clinical evaluation by a healthcare or mental health professional based on eating patterns, psychological symptoms, and physical health, using standardized diagnostic criteria; medical evaluation assesses for complications.
treatment: Effective treatment often involves a combination of nutritional rehabilitation, medical monitoring, and psychotherapy (such as cognitive behavioral therapy or family-based therapy); medications may help with bulimia nervosa and co-occurring anxiety or depression, and hospitalization may be needed for medical stabilization in severe cases.
when_to_seek_care: Seek help from a healthcare provider or mental health professional for concerning changes in eating behavior, rapid weight change, or preoccupation with food and weight that is affecting daily life, and seek emergency care for fainting, chest pain, or severe medical symptoms.
related_conditions: Binge-eating disorder (a related but distinct eating disorder)
Osteoporosis (a possible long-term complication of anorexia nervosa)

description: A chronic noncommunicable brain disease characterized by recurrent seizures, defined as having two or more unprovoked seizures; one of the most common neurological diseases globally, with about 50 million people affected worldwide.
symptoms: Recurrent seizures (brief episodes of involuntary movement)
Loss of consciousness or awareness during some seizure types
Unusual sensations, tastes, or smells before a seizure (aura)
clinical_signs: Rhythmic jerking or shaking movements during a seizure
Loss of bowel or bladder control during a seizure
Post-seizure confusion or fatigue (postictal state)
Abnormal electrical activity on electroencephalogram (EEG)
warning_signs: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes (status epilepticus, a medical emergency)
Repeated seizures without recovery of consciousness in between
Seizure followed by difficulty breathing or persistent unresponsiveness
Injury sustained during a seizure
risk_factors: Problems before or during birth (prematurity, low birth weight, birth injury)
causes: Not an infectious disease and not transmitted between people; caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain, arising from structural, genetic, infectious, metabolic, or immune causes, though the cause remains unknown in about half of cases globally.
prevention: Adequate perinatal care to reduce birth-related brain injury
Preventing head injury (helmets, seatbelts, safety measures)
Preventing and appropriately treating infections that can affect the brain
Managing cardiovascular risk factors to reduce stroke-related epilepsy
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on a history of two or more unprovoked seizures, supported by electroencephalogram (EEG) to detect abnormal brain electrical activity and brain imaging (MRI or CT) to identify structural causes.
treatment: Antiseizure medications can control seizures in up to 70% of people with epilepsy when properly diagnosed and treated; surgery, dietary therapy, or neurostimulation may be options for seizures not controlled by medication.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation after any first-time seizure, and seek emergency care immediately for a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, repeated seizures without recovery, or injury during a seizure.

also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A primary headache disorder characterized by recurring, often one-sided, throbbing headache attacks lasting 4-72 hours, accompanied by nausea and sensitivity to light or sound; usually begins around puberty and is more common in women.
symptoms: Throbbing or pulsating headache, often on one side of the head
Aura (visual disturbances, tingling) before the headache in some people
clinical_signs: Attacks lasting 4-72 hours if untreated
Worsening of pain with routine physical activity
Normal neurological exam between attacks
warning_signs: Sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache unlike any before
Headache with fever, stiff neck, confusion, or seizures
New neurological symptoms (weakness, vision loss, difficulty speaking) that don't resolve like a typical aura
Headache after a head injury
risk_factors: Female sex, especially during reproductive years
Certain triggers (stress, sleep changes, specific foods, bright lights, strong smells)
causes: Not an infectious disease; involves activation of pain-producing mechanisms deep in the brain and release of inflammatory substances around nerves and blood vessels of the head, with a likely genetic basis; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Identifying and avoiding personal triggers
Regular sleep, meals, and hydration
Stress management techniques
Preventive medications for people with frequent or severe migraine attacks
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on a detailed history of headache characteristics and associated symptoms; a headache diary can help identify patterns; neuroimaging is used only when symptoms suggest a different underlying cause.
treatment: Acute attacks are treated with pain-relief medications and migraine-specific drugs (such as triptans); people with frequent or disabling migraines may benefit from daily preventive medications; lifestyle and trigger management support both approaches.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for headaches that are frequent, severe, or affecting daily life, and seek emergency care for a sudden, severe "worst headache of your life," headache with fever and stiff neck, or new neurological symptoms.
related_conditions: Stroke or transient ischemic attack (differential for aura-like symptoms)
Medication-overuse headache (a complication of frequent acute treatment use)

description: A long-lasting mental health disorder in which a person experiences uncontrollable, recurring thoughts (obsessions) and/or engages in repetitive behaviors (compulsions) that cause significant distress or interfere with daily life.
symptoms: Intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges, or mental images that cause anxiety (obsessions)
Repetitive behaviors performed to reduce anxiety, such as excessive checking, cleaning, or counting
Spending more than an hour a day on obsessions or compulsions
Significant distress or difficulty functioning due to these symptoms
clinical_signs: Recognition (in most cases) that the obsessions or compulsions are excessive, though the person cannot control
them
Only temporary relief of anxiety from performing compulsions
Symptoms often beginning between late childhood and young adulthood
Sometimes accompanied by motor or vocal tics
warning_signs: Compulsions or avoidance behaviors that severely impair daily functioning, safety, or hygiene
Significant co-occurring depression or anxiety
Thoughts of self-harm accompanying severe distress
risk_factors: Family history of OCD or other mental health conditions
Certain childhood experiences or stressful life events
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from a combination of genetic, neurological, and environmental factors affecting brain circuits involved in anxiety and repetitive behavior; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent OCD
Early identification and treatment can reduce the severity and impact of symptoms over time
diagnosis: Diagnosed through clinical evaluation by a mental health professional based on the presence, severity, and duration of obsessions and/or compulsions, and their impact on daily functioning.
treatment: Although there is no cure, effective treatments include cognitive behavioral therapy (particularly a specific approach called exposure and response prevention) and certain medications, most often selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).
when_to_seek_care: Seek help from a mental health professional for intrusive thoughts or repetitive behaviors that are time-consuming or interfere with daily life, work, or relationships.
related_conditions: Tic disorders and Tourette syndrome (associated conditions)
Body dysmorphic disorder (a related obsessive-compulsive spectrum condition)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A chronic, treatable brain disease characterized by a problematic pattern of opioid use leading to significant impairment or distress, including prescription pain relievers, heroin, and synthetic opioids such as fentanyl.
symptoms: Strong cravings or urges to use opioids
Taking more opioids than intended or for longer than intended
Difficulty cutting down or controlling use
Spending a lot of time obtaining, using, or recovering from opioids
clinical_signs: Needing increasing amounts of opioids to achieve the same effect (tolerance)
Continuing use despite worsening physical or psychological problems
Neglecting responsibilities at work, school, or home due to use
Using opioids in physically hazardous situations
warning_signs: Slow, shallow, or stopped breathing
Choking or gurgling sounds, or inability to wake the person
Blue or gray lips, fingertips, or skin
Pinpoint pupils with unresponsiveness (signs of possible overdose, a medical emergency requiring naloxone and
emergency care)
risk_factors: Personal or family history of substance use disorder
History of opioid misuse or a prior overdose
Taking high-dose or long-acting opioid prescriptions
Combining opioids with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives
causes: Not an infectious disease; develops from repeated opioid use that changes brain circuits involved in reward, stress, and self-control, influenced by genetic and environmental risk factors; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Cautious, guideline-based prescribing of opioids for pain
Screening for risk factors before starting opioid therapy
Access to naloxone for anyone at risk of overdose or those around them
Safe storage and disposal of prescription opioids
Early treatment of opioid misuse before it progresses
diagnosis: Diagnosed using standardized clinical criteria based on a pattern of opioid use causing significant impairment or distress over a 12-month period, assessed by a healthcare or mental health professional.
treatment: The most effective treatment combines FDA-approved medications, such as buprenorphine, methadone, or naltrexone, with counseling and behavioral support; these medications help reduce cravings, prevent withdrawal, and lower the risk of overdose death.
when_to_seek_care: Seek help from a healthcare provider for concerns about opioid use, dependence, or difficulty stopping; call emergency services immediately for any signs of overdose, and administer naloxone if available while waiting for help.
related_conditions: Alcohol use disorder and other substance use disorders (frequent co-occurrence)
Hepatitis C and HIV (increased risk with injection drug use)

description: A progressive brain condition that causes problems with movement, mental health, sleep, pain, and other functions; the second most common neurodegenerative disease worldwide, with disability and death from it rising faster than any other neurological disorder.
symptoms: Tremor, often starting in one hand
clinical_signs: Reduced arm swing while walking
Shuffling gait
Soft or monotone speech
Small, cramped handwriting (micrographia)
Masked, less expressive face
warning_signs: Sudden worsening of mobility or new falls
Signs of severe medication side effects (uncontrolled movements, confusion)
Signs of aspiration (choking, coughing while eating) from swallowing difficulty
New or worsening confusion or hallucinations
risk_factors: Exposure to certain environmental toxins (suspected contributing factor)
causes: Not an infectious disease and not transmitted between people; results from progressive loss of dopamine-producing nerve cells in the brain, with genetic and environmental factors both believed to contribute; the exact cause is not fully understood.
prevention: No proven way to prevent Parkinson disease
Regular physical activity may help support brain health and manage symptoms once diagnosed
Early diagnosis and access to treatment can improve functioning and quality of life
diagnosis: Diagnosed clinically based on characteristic motor symptoms (tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability) and neurological examination; there is no single definitive laboratory test.
treatment: There is no cure, but medicines such as levodopa/carbidopa are the most effective treatment for improving symptoms, functioning, and quality of life; rehabilitation, physical therapy, and in some cases surgical treatments (such as deep brain stimulation) can also help manage symptoms.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent tremor, stiffness, slowness of movement, or balance problems; seek prompt care for sudden worsening of symptoms, new falls, or significant medication side effects.
related_conditions: Alzheimer's disease and other dementias (can co-occur in advanced PD)

description: A mental health condition that can develop after exposure to an extremely threatening or horrific event, characterized by persistent re-experiencing, avoidance, and a heightened sense of current threat that interferes with daily life.
symptoms: Intrusive, unwanted memories or flashbacks of the traumatic event
Avoidance of reminders of the event (places, people, activities)
Feeling constantly on guard or easily startled
clinical_signs: Persistent negative beliefs about oneself or the world
Emotional numbness or detachment
Difficulty sleeping or concentrating
Symptoms lasting more than one month and interfering with relationships or work
warning_signs: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Severe dissociation or feeling disconnected from reality
Substance use as a coping mechanism
Inability to function in daily life
risk_factors: Direct exposure to or witnessing a traumatic event (assault, combat, disaster, serious accident)
Lack of social support after the event
Personal or family history of mental illness
causes: Not an infectious disease and not transmitted between people; develops following exposure to trauma, with the brain's fear and stress response systems remaining activated even after the danger has passed.
prevention: Early access to social support and appropriate care after a traumatic event
Early psychological intervention for those at high risk may reduce the likelihood of PTSD developing
Not all people who experience trauma develop PTSD, and most acute stress reactions improve with time and
support
diagnosis: Diagnosed by a mental health professional based on the presence of characteristic symptoms lasting more than one month following trauma exposure, using standardized clinical interviews and criteria.
treatment: Effective treatments include trauma-focused psychotherapies (such as cognitive processing therapy or prolonged exposure) and certain medications; treatment can significantly reduce symptoms and improve daily functioning.
when_to_seek_care: Seek help from a mental health professional if trauma-related symptoms persist for more than a month and interfere with daily life, and seek immediate help for any thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
related_conditions: Acute stress disorder (a shorter-duration precursor condition)

also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A serious mental disorder characterized by significant impairments in perception and changes in behavior, including delusions, hallucinations, and disorganized thinking; associated with a substantially reduced life expectancy but manageable with effective treatment.
symptoms: Hallucinations (hearing or seeing things that aren't there)
clinical_signs: Disorganized or unusual behavior observable to others
Flat or blunted affect
Social withdrawal
Impaired insight into the illness
warning_signs: Command hallucinations or delusions that could lead to harm to self or others
Extreme agitation or inability to care for basic needs
Suicidal thoughts or behavior
Severe paranoia leading to dangerous behavior
risk_factors: Family history of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders
Substance use, particularly heavy cannabis use in adolescence
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from a combination of genetic vulnerability and environmental factors affecting brain development and function; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No proven way to prevent schizophrenia
Early identification and treatment of first psychotic episodes can improve long-term outcomes
Reducing heavy substance use, particularly in adolescence, may help lower risk in vulnerable individuals
diagnosis: Diagnosed through clinical psychiatric assessment based on the presence and duration of characteristic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking or behavior), after ruling out other medical or substance-related causes.
treatment: A range of effective treatment options exists, including antipsychotic medication, psychoeducation, family interventions, and psychosocial rehabilitation, which together can substantially improve functioning and quality of life.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt mental health evaluation for new or worsening symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized behavior, and seek emergency care for any safety concerns, including suicidal thoughts or risk of harm to others.

description: A parasitic disease caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, spread mainly by triatomine ("kissing") bugs in Latin America, which can cause life-threatening heart and digestive complications years or decades after the initial, often unnoticed, infection.
symptoms: Often no symptoms or mild symptoms in the acute phase
Swelling at the site of the bite
clinical_signs: Romana's sign (swelling of the eyelid on one side of the face)
A skin lesion (chagoma) at the site of entry
Enlarged liver, spleen, or lymph nodes in the acute phase
Cardiac abnormalities (enlarged heart, arrhythmias) in chronic disease
warning_signs: Signs of heart failure (shortness of breath, swelling of the legs) in chronic disease
Irregular or very rapid heartbeat
Severe abdominal symptoms suggesting an enlarged esophagus or colon (megaesophagus/megacolon)
risk_factors: Living in rural areas of Latin America with triatomine bug exposure
Poor-quality housing that allows bugs to nest
Receipt of blood or organs from an infected donor (rare with modern screening)
Congenital transmission from an infected mother
causes: Caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi; transmitted mainly when infected triatomine ("kissing") bug feces contaminate a bite wound or mucous membrane; can also spread via blood transfusion, organ transplant, congenitally, or rarely through contaminated food.
prevention: Vector control (insecticide spraying, house improvement to eliminate bug nesting sites)
Screening of blood and organ donors in endemic and non-endemic areas
Screening pregnant women and newborns in endemic areas
Use of bed nets in high-risk housing
diagnosis: Acute infection is diagnosed by finding the parasite in blood via microscopy or PCR; chronic infection is diagnosed using serological (antibody) blood tests.
treatment: Antiparasitic medications (benznidazole or nifurtimox) are most effective in the acute phase and in early chronic infection; chronic disease with organ damage focuses on managing complications such as heart failure or arrhythmias, sometimes requiring pacemakers or surgery.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for fever with swelling at an insect bite site or eyelid swelling in an endemic area, and seek prompt cardiology evaluation for palpitations, shortness of breath, or leg swelling in anyone with known or suspected Chagas disease.
related_conditions: Other causes of cardiomyopathy and heart failure
African trypanosomiasis (a related but distinct parasitic disease)

description: A crippling parasitic disease nearing global eradication, caused by a long thread-like worm transmitted exclusively through drinking stagnant water contaminated with infected water fleas.
symptoms: Often no symptoms for about a year after infection
Localized swelling and pain, usually in the leg or foot, as the worm approaches the skin
A painful blister at the site where the worm will emerge
clinical_signs: A visible, thread-like worm emerging slowly from a skin blister or ulcer, most often on the leg or foot
Secondary bacterial infection of the wound
Very itchy urticarial rash coinciding with blister development
warning_signs: Signs of severe secondary bacterial infection (spreading redness, worsening pain, fever) at the wound site
The worm breaking during extraction, which can cause severe inflammation
Signs of sepsis
risk_factors: Living in rural, underserved communities in endemic areas (parts of sub-Saharan Africa)
Reliance on unsafe, stagnant water sources such as ponds for drinking water
Lack of access to filtered or treated drinking water
causes: Caused by the parasitic worm Dracunculus medinensis; transmitted exclusively when people drink stagnant water contaminated with tiny water fleas (copepods) carrying the parasite's larvae; not spread directly person to person.
prevention: Drinking only water from safe, filtered sources, or filtering water through a cloth filter
Preventing infected individuals from entering water sources to relieve blister pain, which would continue the
transmission cycle
Community-based surveillance and case containment as part of global eradication efforts
Treating contaminated water sources with larvicide
diagnosis: Diagnosed through clinical observation of the characteristic blister or emerging worm and a history of exposure to contaminated water in an endemic area; there is no blood test for the infection.
treatment: There is no medication to treat or prevent the disease; management involves slowly and carefully extracting the worm over days to weeks by winding it around a stick, along with wound care and pain relief to prevent secondary infection.
when_to_seek_care: Seek care from a local health worker for any painful skin blister or emerging worm, particularly in endemic areas, to ensure proper wound care and to prevent the worm from contaminating water sources.
related_conditions: Other soil- or water-transmitted parasitic infections
Tetanus (risk from the open wound, requiring separate prophylaxis)

specialty: Infectious Disease, Tropical Medicine, Dermatology, Ophthalmology
description: A parasitic eye and skin disease caused by the worm Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by repeated bites of infected blackflies near fast-flowing rivers; the world's second leading infectious cause of blindness.
symptoms: Skin rash and bumps under the skin (nodules)
clinical_signs: Subcutaneous nodules containing adult worms
Visible microfilariae on skin snip examination
Punctate keratitis or other eye lesions visible on slit-lamp examination
Atrophic, thinned skin in chronic disease
warning_signs: Progressive vision loss or blindness
Signs of eye inflammation (pain, marked redness, worsening light sensitivity)
Seizures in children in highly endemic areas (associated "nodding syndrome")
risk_factors: Living in or near fast-flowing rivers in endemic areas of sub-Saharan Africa, Yemen, or parts of Latin America
Occupational or agricultural activity near rivers
causes: Caused by the parasitic worm Onchocerca volvulus; transmitted to humans through repeated bites of infected blackflies (genus Simulium) that breed in fast-flowing rivers and streams; not spread directly person to person.
prevention: Mass drug administration with ivermectin in endemic communities
Vector control targeting blackfly breeding sites
Personal protection against blackfly bites in endemic areas
diagnosis: Diagnosed by identifying microfilariae in skin snip samples, visualizing worms in skin nodules, or eye examination for characteristic lesions; PCR testing can also detect parasite DNA.
treatment: Ivermectin is the core treatment, typically given as part of mass drug administration programs, which kills microfilariae and reduces transmission and symptoms; treatment is usually repeated periodically.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent itching with skin nodules or changes, or any eye redness, pain, or vision changes, especially with a history of living in or traveling to an endemic area.
related_conditions: Other causes of chronic itching or dermatitis
Trachoma (another leading infectious cause of blindness)
Epilepsy (associated "nodding syndrome" in children in endemic areas)

also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A disease of the eye caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis and the leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide, spread through contact with eye or nose discharge, primarily affecting young children in affected communities.
symptoms: In early stages, may be asymptomatic or mild
clinical_signs: Follicles (small bumps) visible on the inner upper eyelid
Conjunctival scarring on examination
Inward-turning eyelashes (trichiasis) in advanced disease
Corneal clouding in severe, longstanding disease
warning_signs: Eyelashes rubbing against the eyeball (trichiasis), which risks permanent corneal damage
Progressive vision loss
Signs of corneal ulceration or severe eye pain
risk_factors: Living in crowded, under-resourced communities with limited access to water and sanitation
Young childhood age (children are the main reservoir of infection)
causes: Caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis; spreads through direct or indirect contact with eye or nose discharge of an infected person, including via hands, clothing, bedding, and certain flies that have contacted infected discharge.
prevention: The WHO SAFE strategy: Surgery for advanced disease (trichiasis), Antibiotics for infection, Facial cleanliness,
and Environmental improvement (water and sanitation access)
Mass antibiotic administration in endemic communities
Reducing fly populations and improving hygiene
diagnosis: Diagnosed through clinical eye examination using the WHO simplified grading system to identify follicles, inflammation, scarring, trichiasis, and corneal opacity.
treatment: Active infection is treated with antibiotics (commonly azithromycin); advanced disease with inward-turning eyelashes (trichiasis) is treated with a simple surgical procedure to prevent further corneal damage and blindness.
when_to_seek_care: Seek care for persistent eye redness, discharge, or irritation, especially in children in endemic areas, and seek prompt evaluation for eyelashes rubbing against the eye, since surgery can prevent blindness if done in time.
related_conditions: Onchocerciasis (another leading infectious cause of blindness)
Chlamydial genital infection (caused by related strains of the same bacterium)

specialty: Infectious Disease, Tropical Medicine, Dermatology (cutaneous form)
description: A neglected tropical disease caused by Leishmania protozoan parasites transmitted by sandfly bites, occurring in visceral (affecting internal organs), cutaneous, and mucocutaneous forms; associated with poverty, malnutrition, and displacement.
clinical_signs: Splenomegaly and hepatomegaly (visceral form)
Anemia and pancytopenia (visceral form)
Disfiguring facial ulcers or scars (cutaneous/mucocutaneous form)
warning_signs: High, persistent fever with marked weakness in visceral disease (can be fatal if untreated)
Severe anemia or bleeding tendency
Destruction of mucosal tissue in mucocutaneous disease
risk_factors: Living in or traveling to endemic tropical/subtropical/Mediterranean regions
causes: Caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Leishmania; transmitted through the bite of infected female phlebotomine sandflies.
prevention: Vector control (insecticide spraying, bed nets)
Early diagnosis and treatment to reduce transmission reservoir
Environmental management to reduce sandfly breeding sites
Personal protection against sandfly bites
diagnosis: In visceral leishmaniasis, diagnosis combines clinical signs with parasitological or serological tests (including rapid diagnostic tests); in cutaneous and mucocutaneous disease, clinical presentation with parasitological confirmation is used, as serological tests have limited value.
treatment: Treatment depends on the disease form, infecting species, and geographic location; options include systemic medicines such as amphotericin B, and requires an immunocompetent host since medicines do not always fully clear the parasite.
when_to_seek_care: People with suspected visceral leishmaniasis should seek medical care immediately, as it can be fatal without treatment; seek evaluation for any non-healing skin ulcer after travel to or residence in an endemic area.

specialty: Infectious Disease, Tropical Medicine, Dermatology, Urology
description: A neglected tropical disease caused by filarial worms transmitted by mosquitoes, which silently damages the lymphatic system and can cause severe, disfiguring swelling of limbs and genitals later in life.
symptoms: Painful swelling of lymph nodes and limbs during acute attacks
clinical_signs: Lymphedema of limbs
Hydrocele (scrotal swelling) in men
Thickened, hardened skin in chronic disease
Microfilariae detectable in blood
warning_signs: Rapidly worsening limb swelling with fever (acute adenolymphangitis, often from secondary bacterial infection)
Chyluria (milky urine)
Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (cough and breathing difficulty)
risk_factors: Living in endemic tropical areas with repeated mosquito exposure
Childhood acquisition of infection (though disease appears later in life)
Poor vector control and sanitation infrastructure
causes: Caused by filarial nematode worms (mainly Wuchereria bancrofti, also Brugia malayi and Brugia timori); transmitted to humans through repeated bites of infected mosquitoes over months to years.
prevention: Mass drug administration (preventive chemotherapy) with antifilarial medicine combinations in endemic areas
Mosquito bite prevention (bed nets, repellents)
Vector control programs
Morbidity management and disability prevention for those already affected
diagnosis: Detection of microfilariae in a blood sample (often collected at night due to periodicity), or antigen/antibody testing; chronic disease is often diagnosed clinically based on characteristic lymphedema or hydrocele.
treatment: Antifilarial medicines (diethylcarbamazine, albendazole, and sometimes ivermectin) are used to clear microfilariae and reduce transmission; chronic lymphedema and hydrocele are managed with an essential care package including hygiene, skin care, and in some cases surgery for hydrocele.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for persistent limb or genital swelling, or recurrent fever with painful lymph node swelling, particularly after living in an endemic area.
related_conditions: Deep vein thrombosis (differential for limb swelling)

also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
specialty: Infectious Disease, Tropical Medicine, Emergency Medicine
description: A life-threatening disease caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, remaining a major cause of illness and death in tropical and subtropical regions.
clinical_signs: Cyclical fever pattern ("hot, wet, cold" phases)
Parasites visible inside red blood cells on blood film microscopy
Splenomegaly in some cases
warning_signs: Severe anemia
Respiratory distress (metabolic acidosis)
Cerebral malaria (confusion, seizures, coma)
Multi-organ involvement in adults
risk_factors: Infants and children under 5 years of age
Non-immune travelers or migrants entering high-transmission areas
Living in or traveling to endemic tropical/subtropical regions
causes: Caused by Plasmodium parasites (including P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. knowlesi); transmitted to people through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes; can also rarely spread via blood transfusion or contaminated needles.
prevention: Insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ITNs)
Indoor residual spraying (IRS)
Antimalarial chemoprophylaxis for travelers and pregnant women in endemic areas
Malaria vaccines (RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M) for children in moderate-to-high transmission settings
Eliminating mosquito breeding sites
diagnosis: Parasitological confirmation by blood film microscopy or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), which can give results in 15 minutes or less; treatment based on symptoms alone is discouraged when testing is available.
treatment: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is the best available treatment, particularly for P. falciparum malaria; prompt treatment is essential, as untreated P. falciparum malaria can progress to severe illness and death within 24 hours.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care urgently for fever, chills, and headache after travel to or residence in a malaria-endemic area, especially if symptoms appear 7 days to several weeks after potential exposure; treat any fever in this context as a medical emergency until malaria is ruled out.

specialty: Infectious Disease, Tropical Medicine, Gastroenterology, Urology
description: A neglected tropical disease caused by parasitic blood flukes acquired through contact with freshwater infested with larval forms released by infected snails; a disease closely linked to poverty and poor sanitation.
symptoms: Itching or rash at the site of skin entry
Flu-like symptoms weeks to months after infection
clinical_signs: Blood in urine (urogenital schistosomiasis)
Blood in stool (intestinal schistosomiasis)
Eosinophilia on blood tests
Hepatosplenomegaly in chronic disease
warning_signs: Vomiting blood
Black, tarry stool
Signs of bladder or kidney damage (chronic urogenital disease)
Neurologic symptoms (rare, from ectopic egg deposition)
risk_factors: Living in or contact with freshwater in endemic tropical/subtropical areas
Lack of access to safe water and sanitation
Occupational, household, or recreational freshwater exposure
Children and adolescents in endemic areas
causes: Caused by parasitic blood flukes of the genus Schistosoma; acquired when people come into contact with fresh water infested with the larval forms (cercariae) released by infected freshwater snails, which penetrate the skin.
prevention: Mass administration of antiparasitic drugs (preventive chemotherapy) in high-risk areas
Improved access to safe water and sanitation
Health education on avoiding contact with contaminated water
Snail control measures
diagnosis: Detection of parasite eggs in stool or urine; serological tests can support diagnosis, particularly in low-intensity or chronic infections where eggs may not be readily detected.
treatment: Praziquantel is the medicine of choice for treatment, effective against all major Schistosoma species affecting humans.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for unexplained blood in urine or stool, persistent abdominal symptoms, or flu-like illness after freshwater exposure in an endemic area.
related_conditions: Inflammatory bowel disease (can mimic chronic intestinal schistosomiasis)
Bladder cancer (long-term complication of chronic urogenital disease)

source: National Institutes of Health (NIH), National Library of Medicine (NCBI Bookshelf)
specialty: Allergy and Immunology, Otolaryngology (ENT), Family Medicine
description: An allergic reaction affecting the nose and upper airways, triggered by airborne allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold, or animal dander; despite the name "hay fever," it is not caused by hay and does not cause fever.
clinical_signs: Pale, swollen nasal mucosa on examination
Clear nasal discharge
Dark circles under the eyes ("allergic shiners") in some individuals
Symptoms that are seasonal (pollen-related) or year-round (indoor allergens)
warning_signs: Wheezing or shortness of breath (possible progression to or coexisting asthma)
Signs of sinus infection (facial pain, colored discharge, fever) if symptoms worsen instead of improving
Severe facial swelling or difficulty breathing (possible severe allergic reaction requiring emergency care)
risk_factors: Family history of allergies, asthma, or eczema
Exposure to indoor allergens (dust mites, pet dander, mold)
Exposure to outdoor allergens (tree, grass, or weed pollen)
causes: Not an infectious disease and not contagious; occurs when the immune system overreacts to an otherwise harmless airborne substance, releasing histamine and other chemicals that cause inflammation in the nasal passages; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Avoiding known triggers when possible (keeping windows closed during high pollen periods, using air
conditioning)
Using allergen-proof bedding covers and reducing dust mite exposure
Washing hands after contact with animals
Using a dehumidifier to reduce mold growth
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on characteristic symptoms and history of exposure to triggers; allergy skin testing or blood tests can help identify specific allergens.
treatment: Managed with allergen avoidance, oral or nasal antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroid sprays, and, for persistent or severe cases, allergen immunotherapy (allergy shots or tablets).
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider if symptoms are frequent, severe, or not well controlled with over-the-counter treatments, or if symptoms interfere with sleep, work, or school.

also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
specialty: Pulmonology, Allergy and Immunology, Family Medicine
description: A chronic lung disease affecting people of all ages, caused by inflammation and muscle tightening around the airways, which makes breathing harder; symptoms can be mild or severe and come and go over time, but the condition can be managed with proper treatment.
clinical_signs: Wheeze audible on chest examination
Reduced peak expiratory flow or spirometry values during an attack
Symptoms that worsen at night or with exercise, cold air, or allergen exposure
warning_signs: Severe difficulty breathing or being unable to speak in full sentences
Blue lips or face
No improvement or worsening despite using a reliever inhaler
Rapidly worsening wheeze and chest tightness (severe asthma attack, a medical emergency)
risk_factors: Family history of asthma or allergic disease
Exposure to tobacco smoke, indoor and outdoor air pollution
Occupational exposure to irritants or allergens
causes: Not an infectious disease; results from chronic airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness, triggered by allergens, irritants, exercise, cold air, or respiratory infections in genetically susceptible individuals; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Avoiding known personal triggers (allergens, smoke, air pollution)
Taking prescribed controller medications consistently to reduce inflammation
Getting recommended vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal) to reduce infection-triggered attacks
Developing and following a personal asthma action plan
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on a history of characteristic symptoms and confirmed with lung function tests such as spirometry, which measure airflow limitation and its reversibility.
treatment: Managed with inhaled medications: reliever (bronchodilator) inhalers for quick symptom relief and controller (usually inhaled corticosteroid) medications taken regularly to reduce airway inflammation and prevent attacks; treatment intensity is adjusted based on symptom control.
when_to_seek_care: Speak to a health professional about any asthma symptoms, and seek emergency care immediately for severe breathing difficulty, blue lips, or a reliever inhaler not providing relief.

description: A common lung disease causing restricted airflow and breathing problems, in which the lungs become damaged or clogged with phlegm over time; largely caused by tobacco smoking and household air pollution.
clinical_signs: Reduced airflow on spirometry testing
Barrel-shaped chest in advanced disease
Prolonged expiratory phase on lung exam
Reduced exercise tolerance
warning_signs: Severe shortness of breath at rest
Blue lips or fingertips (cyanosis)
Confusion or extreme drowsiness
Coughing up blood or significantly increased sputum with fever (possible exacerbation with infection)
risk_factors: Tobacco smoking (the leading cause in high-income countries)
Household air pollution from solid fuel cooking or heating (a major cause in low- and middle-income countries)
causes: Not an infectious disease; caused by long-term exposure to harmful particles or gases (most commonly tobacco smoke) that damage and narrow the airways and lung tissue; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Not smoking and avoiding secondhand smoke
Reducing exposure to indoor air pollution (cleaner cooking fuels and ventilation)
Reducing occupational exposure to dust and chemicals
Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcal disease to prevent exacerbations
diagnosis: Diagnosed using spirometry, a breathing test that measures airflow limitation and confirms the diagnosis in someone with characteristic symptoms and risk factor exposure.
treatment: There is no cure, but treatment can relieve symptoms, improve quality of life, and reduce risk of exacerbations, including bronchodilator inhalers, inhaled corticosteroids for some patients, pulmonary rehabilitation, and oxygen therapy for severe disease; smoking cessation is the single most effective intervention.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider for persistent cough, phlegm production, or breathlessness, particularly with a smoking history, and seek urgent care for a sudden worsening of breathing, high fever, or confusion.

specialty: Infectious Disease, Pulmonology, Family Medicine, Critical Care (for severe cases)
description: A respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, ranging from asymptomatic or mild infection to severe pneumonia and death; continues to circulate globally with ongoing hospitalizations and deaths.
clinical_signs: Reduced oxygen saturation in more severe cases
Abnormal lung findings on chest imaging (ground-glass opacities)
Tachypnea in moderate-to-severe disease
warning_signs: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath
Persistent chest pain or pressure
New confusion
Inability to stay awake
Bluish lips or face
risk_factors: Being unvaccinated or not up to date on vaccination
causes: Caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus; spreads through the air in infectious respiratory particles from an infected person, with transmission more likely in close contact or shared indoor spaces; can also spread via contaminated surfaces.
prevention: COVID-19 vaccination, including risk-based revaccination for high-risk groups
Good ventilation of indoor spaces
Hand hygiene
Masking in high-risk or high-transmission settings
Staying home when symptomatic
diagnosis: Laboratory confirmation via RT-PCR or rapid antigen testing; clinical and epidemiological assessment is used when testing is inconclusive or unavailable.
treatment: Most people have mild illness and recover with symptomatic and supportive care (rest, fluids, fever/pain relief); antiviral or other targeted treatments may be used for high-risk or severe cases per current clinical guidance.
when_to_seek_care: Seek immediate medical care for difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, new confusion, or bluish lips or face; seek routine medical advice for high fever or worsening symptoms, especially in older adults or those with underlying conditions.

also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
specialty: Pulmonology, Infectious Disease, Pediatrics, Family Medicine
description: An acute infection of the lungs that can be caused by viruses, bacteria, or fungi; the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide, though presenting features and severity vary by cause and age.
clinical_signs: Fast breathing rate for age
Lower chest wall indrawing (retractions)
Crackles or reduced breath sounds on auscultation
Nasal flaring in young children
warning_signs: Severe difficulty breathing or grunting
Bluish discoloration of lips or skin (cyanosis)
Inability to feed or drink (infants)
Lethargy or unresponsiveness
Chest indrawing with danger signs
risk_factors: Lack of exclusive breastfeeding in infants
Lack of vaccination against pneumonia-causing pathogens
causes: Caused by viruses, bacteria, or fungi commonly found in the nose or throat that infect the lungs when inhaled; spreads via airborne droplets from coughing or sneezing, and occasionally through the bloodstream, especially around birth.
prevention: Vaccination (e.g., against pneumococcus, Hib, measles, pertussis, influenza)
Adequate nutrition, including exclusive breastfeeding in infancy
Reducing indoor air pollution (clean cooking fuels)
Hand hygiene and reducing exposure to respiratory infections
diagnosis: Clinical assessment of cough and/or difficult breathing combined with fast breathing rate or chest wall indrawing (per WHO/Integrated Management of Childhood Illness criteria); chest X-ray and laboratory tests may be used to confirm and characterize the cause.
treatment: Bacterial pneumonia is treated with antibiotics (amoxicillin is a common first-line choice in children); viral pneumonia is managed with supportive care; severe cases may require hospitalization, oxygen therapy, and closer monitoring.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for cough with fast or difficult breathing, especially with fever, and seek emergency care for severe breathing difficulty, bluish skin color, or inability to feed or stay alert.

source: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A common skin condition that occurs when hair follicles become clogged with oil (sebum) and dead skin cells, leading to outbreaks of pimples most often on the face, back, chest, and shoulders.
symptoms: Pimples with pus at the tip (pustules)
Larger, painful lumps under the skin (nodules or cysts) in more severe cases
clinical_signs: Lesions concentrated on the face, back, chest, and shoulders
Post-inflammatory redness or dark marks after lesions heal
Scarring in moderate to severe, longstanding cases
warning_signs: Sudden, severe outbreak with fever and joint pain (a rare, serious form called acne fulminans)
Deep, painful nodules or cysts at risk of permanent scarring
Signs of skin infection (increasing redness, warmth, spreading swelling)
risk_factors: Friction or pressure from helmets, straps, or tight clothing
causes: Not contagious; occurs when oil, dead skin cells, and bacteria that normally live on the skin become trapped in a hair follicle, causing inflammation; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Gentle, regular skin cleansing without harsh scrubbing
Avoiding picking or squeezing lesions, which can worsen scarring
Using non-comedogenic (non-pore-clogging) skin and hair products
Managing known personal triggers such as friction from sports equipment
diagnosis: Diagnosed through visual examination of the skin and the characteristic pattern and types of lesions present.
treatment: Treatment depends on severity and may include topical treatments (retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, topical antibiotics), oral antibiotics for more extensive disease, hormonal therapy in some cases, and oral isotretinoin for severe, treatment-resistant acne.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider or dermatologist for acne that doesn't improve with over-the-counter treatment, causes emotional distress, or risks scarring.
related_conditions: Hidradenitis suppurativa (a related but distinct chronic condition)
Polycystic ovary syndrome (an underlying cause in some cases of hormonal acne)

source: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
description: A chronic, non-contagious inflammatory skin disease causing dry, itchy, and often discolored skin; the most common type of eczema and usually begins in childhood, though it can occur at any age.
clinical_signs: Thickened, leathery skin (lichenification) from chronic scratching
Patches typically in skin folds (elbows, knees) or on the face and hands
Redness in lighter skin tones; brown, purple, or gray hyperpigmentation in darker skin tones
warning_signs: Signs of skin infection (increasing pain, warmth, pus, fever)
Widespread blistering with fever and feeling unwell (possible eczema herpeticum, a medical emergency)
Severe, uncontrolled flare affecting large areas of the body
risk_factors: Family history of eczema, asthma, or hay fever (atopic conditions)
Living in a city or dry climate
Exposure to tobacco smoke and certain air pollutants
Certain fragrances and compounds in skin products and soaps
causes: Not contagious; results from an overactive immune response combined with a weakened skin barrier, allowing more moisture to escape and irritants to enter, influenced by genetics and environmental triggers; not transmitted between people.
prevention: Regular use of moisturizing cream, especially after bathing
Avoiding known triggers such as harsh soaps, certain fabrics, and tobacco smoke
Using a humidifier in dry environments
Daily bathing followed by moisturizer to help control flares
diagnosis: Diagnosed based on characteristic symptoms and appearance of the skin after ruling out other possible causes; there is no single definitive laboratory test.
treatment: Managed with daily moisturizing, avoidance of triggers, topical corticosteroids or other anti-inflammatory creams for flares, and in more severe cases, systemic medications such as biologics; treatment is tailored to severity and location.
when_to_seek_care: See a healthcare provider or dermatologist for persistent itchy, inflamed skin that affects quality of life, and seek prompt care for signs of skin infection or widespread blistering with fever.
