related_conditions: Asthma and allergic rhinitis (commonly co-occurring atopic conditions)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A common bacterial infection of the deeper layers of the skin that can spread quickly and become serious, most often affecting the legs but occurring anywhere on the body.
symptoms: Redness that spreads over a few days
Pain and tenderness in the affected area
clinical_signs: Indistinct, non-sharp borders of redness (except in erysipelas, a related condition with sharp borders)
Skin that may appear slightly pitted, like an orange peel
Fluid-filled blisters in some cases
Red streaking (lymphangitis) extending from the area in some cases
warning_signs: High fever or chills
Rapidly spreading redness or swelling
Increasing pain out of proportion to appearance
Signs of bloodstream infection (confusion, rapid heartbeat, low blood pressure)
risk_factors: A break in the skin (cut, scrape, surgical wound, insect bite)
Skin conditions that crack the skin, such as athlete's foot or eczema
causes: Caused by bacteria, most commonly Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species, entering the skin through a break, cut, or crack; not usually spread from person to person.
prevention: Prompt cleaning and care of any skin wounds, cuts, or scrapes
Treating conditions that break the skin barrier, such as athlete's foot or eczema
Managing chronic conditions like diabetes and leg swelling
Good general skin hygiene
diagnosis: Usually diagnosed based on physical examination of the affected skin; blood tests or wound cultures may be used if the person is very unwell or the infection doesn't respond to initial treatment.
treatment: Treated with antibiotics, given orally for mild cases and intravenously for more severe or systemic infections; elevating the affected area can help reduce swelling.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt medical care for spreading redness, warmth, swelling, or pain in the skin, and seek emergency care for high fever, rapidly worsening symptoms, or signs of confusion or bloodstream infection.
related_conditions: Necrotizing fasciitis (a rare, severe differential requiring emergency care)

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) / World Health Organization (WHO)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A chronic, non-contagious autoimmune skin condition in which the immune system causes skin cells to grow too quickly, resulting in raised, scaly plaques; recognized by WHO as a serious noncommunicable disease.
symptoms: Raised patches of red, inflamed skin covered with silvery-white scales
Dry, cracked skin that may bleed
clinical_signs: Sharply demarcated plaques, typically on elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back
Auspitz sign (tiny bleeding points when scales are removed)
Symmetrical distribution of plaques on both sides of the body
warning_signs: Widespread, rapidly worsening skin redness and shedding (possible erythrodermic psoriasis, a medical
emergency)
New joint pain and swelling (possible psoriatic arthritis)
Signs of skin infection in cracked or broken plaques
risk_factors: Certain infections and skin injuries (Koebner phenomenon)
causes: Not contagious; caused by an overactive immune system that speeds up skin cell growth, with genetic and environmental factors contributing to risk; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent psoriasis
Identifying and avoiding personal flare triggers (stress, skin injury, certain medications) can help reduce flare
frequency
Ongoing treatment can help control symptoms and reduce flare severity
diagnosis: Usually diagnosed by a healthcare provider or dermatologist based on the appearance of the skin; a skin biopsy may be used to confirm the diagnosis or rule out other conditions.
treatment: Treatment depends on severity and may include topical treatments (corticosteroids, vitamin D analogs), phototherapy (ultraviolet light), and systemic medications (methotrexate, biologics) for more extensive disease.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for persistent, unexplained skin patches with scaling, and seek prompt care for widespread skin redness and shedding, signs of infection, or new joint pain and swelling.
related_conditions: Cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome (associated comorbidities)

source: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), National Institutes of Health (NIH)
also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: A chronic autoimmune disorder that causes patches of skin to lose their natural color (pigment) because the pigment-producing cells (melanocytes) are attacked and destroyed by the immune system.
symptoms: Milky-white patches of skin, often on the hands, feet, arms, and face
Premature whitening or graying of scalp or body hair
Loss of color in the tissue lining the mouth or nose
Change in color of the inner layer of the eye
clinical_signs: Symmetrical white patches appearing on both sides of the body in the more common non-segmental form
Patches confined to one area or side of the body in the less common segmental form
Patches that may enlarge or spread over time
warning_signs: Rapid spread of depigmentation over a large body area
Eye pain or vision changes (possible associated eye inflammation)
Signs suggesting another autoimmune condition (unexplained fatigue, weight changes)
causes: Not contagious; an autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys melanocytes, the cells that produce skin pigment; not transmitted between people.
prevention: No known way to prevent vitiligo
Sun protection can help prevent sunburn and reduce contrast between affected and unaffected skin
diagnosis: Often diagnosed through visual examination of the characteristic depigmented patches; a Wood's lamp (UV light) exam or skin biopsy can help confirm the diagnosis in uncertain cases.
treatment: There is no cure, but treatments can help stop progression and restore some skin color, including topical corticosteroids, other topical anti-inflammatory medications, light therapy (phototherapy), and, for extensive disease, depigmentation of remaining pigmented skin.
when_to_seek_care: See a dermatologist for new or spreading patches of lighter skin, especially if accompanied by other symptoms suggesting an autoimmune condition.
related_conditions: Other autoimmune diseases (thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, alopecia areata)

description: A mosquito-borne viral infection found in tropical and subtropical regions, ranging from mild flu-like illness to severe, potentially fatal disease; WHO graded it a Grade 3 emergency in 2023.
symptoms: Severe headache with pain behind the eyes
clinical_signs: Positive tourniquet test
Petechiae or minor bleeding manifestations
Leukopenia and low platelet count on blood tests
warning_signs: Severe abdominal pain or tenderness
Persistent vomiting
Mucosal bleeding (e.g., bleeding gums, blood in vomit)
Rapid breathing
Lethargy or restlessness
Clinical fluid accumulation
risk_factors: Living in or traveling to tropical/subtropical areas with Aedes mosquitoes
Prior dengue infection with a different serotype
causes: Caused by one of four dengue viruses (DENV-1 to DENV-4); transmitted by the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito (mainly Aedes aegypti); not spread directly person to person.
prevention: Avoiding mosquito bites (repellents, protective clothing, screens, bed nets)
Eliminating mosquito breeding sites (standing water)
Dengue vaccination in some eligible populations per national guidance
Community vector control programs
diagnosis: Clinical assessment using WHO case classification (dengue with or without warning signs, severe dengue), confirmed by laboratory tests such as NS1 antigen or antibody (IgM/IgG) testing.
treatment: No specific antiviral treatment exists; management focuses on relieving symptoms, monitoring for warning signs, and supportive care including careful fluid management; severe dengue requires hospitalization.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt medical care for high fever with severe headache and body pain, and seek emergency care immediately if warning signs develop (severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, or difficulty breathing).

description: A preventable viral disease of the central nervous system transmitted through bites or scratches from infected mammals; once symptoms appear, rabies is fatal in essentially 100% of cases.
symptoms: Pain, tingling, or itching at the exposure/bite site
clinical_signs: Hydrophobia (fear of water) and aerophobia (fear of air movement)
Hypersalivation
Autonomic instability
warning_signs: Agitation, confusion, and anxiety ("furious" rabies)
Progressive paralysis ("paralytic" rabies)
Seizures
Coma
risk_factors: Bite or scratch from a potentially rabid animal (especially dogs, bats, raccoons, foxes)
Living in or traveling to areas with endemic dog-mediated rabies
causes: Caused by rabies virus (genus Lyssavirus); transmitted through a bite or scratch from an infected mammal, most commonly dogs, through contact with saliva or infected nervous tissue.
prevention: Immediate, thorough washing of any bite or scratch wound with soap and water for at least 15 minutes
Prompt post-exposure prophylaxis after any potential exposure
Pre-exposure vaccination for high-risk occupations or travelers
Mass dog vaccination programs
Avoiding contact with wild or stray animals
diagnosis: No test can confirm rabies in humans before symptoms appear; diagnosis relies on history of animal exposure and clinical presentation of rapidly progressive encephalitis; laboratory confirmation is possible after symptom onset in specialized settings.
treatment: There is no effective treatment once symptoms appear. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) — thorough wound washing, a course of rabies vaccine, and rabies immunoglobulin when indicated — is highly effective if started promptly after exposure and before symptoms develop.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care immediately after any animal bite or scratch, especially from an unfamiliar or wild animal — post-exposure treatment is effective only before symptoms start, so care should never be delayed.
related_conditions: Psychiatric conditions with fear-related presentations (rare differential)

also_known_as: Not specified in the cited source.
description: An acute viral hemorrhagic disease transmitted by infected mosquitoes, endemic to tropical areas of Africa and Central and South America; named for the jaundice that affects some patients.
clinical_signs: Jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes)
Relative bradycardia despite fever (Faget sign)
Brief remission of symptoms before a more severe second phase in some patients
warning_signs: Bleeding from the mouth, nose, eyes, or gastrointestinal tract
Recurring high fever after a brief improvement (entering the toxic phase)
Abdominal pain with vomiting
Signs of kidney or liver failure (reduced urination, worsening jaundice)
risk_factors: Living in or traveling to endemic tropical areas of Africa or Central/South America without vaccination
Occupational or outdoor exposure to mosquitoes in endemic areas
Being unvaccinated when required by travel regulations
causes: Caused by the yellow fever virus; transmitted to people through the bite of infected Aedes or Haemagogus mosquitoes, which become infected by feeding on infected primates; not spread directly person to person.
prevention: Yellow fever vaccination, the single most important preventive measure, often required for travel to endemic areas
under International Health Regulations
Avoiding mosquito bites (repellents, protective clothing, screened or air-conditioned rooms)
Vector surveillance and control, especially of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes
Rapid outbreak detection and emergency vaccination campaigns
diagnosis: Diagnosed through blood tests to detect the virus or antibodies, combined with clinical presentation and travel or residence history in an endemic area.
treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment; supportive care to manage dehydration, fever, and liver or kidney failure improves survival, and associated bacterial infections can be treated with antibiotics; early hospital-based supportive care is important.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care promptly for fever with headache, muscle pain, and vomiting after travel to an endemic area, and seek emergency care immediately for bleeding, recurring high fever, or jaundice.

description: A mosquito-borne viral infection that is usually mild or asymptomatic in most people but can cause serious birth defects when a pregnant woman is infected, and is linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome in some cases.
clinical_signs: Symptoms typically lasting 2-7 days when present
Only about 1 in 4 infected people develop noticeable symptoms
Symptoms can resemble dengue or chikungunya
warning_signs: Signs of Guillain-Barre syndrome (progressive limb weakness, tingling) developing after infection
Any Zika symptoms or exposure during pregnancy, given the risk to the fetus
Neurological symptoms in infants born to infected mothers
risk_factors: Living in or traveling to areas with active Zika virus transmission
Pregnancy (risk to the fetus rather than increased personal risk of infection)
Unprotected sex with a partner who has traveled to or lives in an affected area (rare sexual transmission)
causes: Caused by the Zika virus; transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, and can also be transmitted from a pregnant woman to her fetus, through sexual contact, or rarely through blood transfusion.
prevention: Avoiding mosquito bites (repellents, protective clothing, screens, bed nets)
Eliminating mosquito breeding sites (standing water)
Pregnant women avoiding travel to areas with active transmission when possible
Safe sex practices or abstinence with partners who may have been exposed
diagnosis: Diagnosed through blood or urine testing to detect the virus (RT-PCR) during acute infection or antibody testing, combined with a history of possible exposure.
treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment or vaccine; management is supportive, including rest, fluids, and medication for fever and pain (avoiding aspirin and other NSAIDs until dengue is ruled out, due to bleeding risk).
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for symptoms after travel to an area with Zika transmission, and pregnant women with possible exposure should seek medical advice promptly regardless of symptoms.
related_conditions: Dengue (differential, overlapping symptoms and mosquito vector)
Chikungunya (differential, overlapping symptoms and mosquito vector)
Congenital Zika syndrome (microcephaly and other birth defects from prenatal infection)

also_known_as: Ebola virus disease, Ebola hemorrhagic fever
specialty: Infectious Disease, Tropical Medicine, Critical Care
description: A severe, often fatal viral illness caused by orthoebolaviruses, transmitted through contact with infected body fluids; occurs in periodic outbreaks, mainly in parts of Africa, and requires intensive supportive care and strict infection control.
clinical_signs: Progression from "dry" symptoms (fever, aches, fatigue) to "wet" symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea)
Abdominal pain
Skin rash
Signs of impaired kidney and liver function
warning_signs: Unexplained bleeding or bruising
Signs of shock (rapid heartbeat, low blood pressure, confusion)
Severe, uncontrolled vomiting or diarrhea leading to dehydration
Difficulty breathing or altered consciousness
risk_factors: Close contact with a person who is sick with or has died from Ebola
Contact with blood or body fluids of infected wildlife (fruit bats, primates)
Healthcare or caregiving work without proper protective equipment
Participation in traditional burial practices involving contact with the body
causes: Caused by orthoebolaviruses; spread through direct contact with the blood, body fluids, or tissues of a person (or animal) who is sick with or has died from Ebola, and through contact with contaminated surfaces or materials.
prevention: Avoiding contact with blood and body fluids of sick or deceased individuals
Safe and dignified burial practices
Use of personal protective equipment by healthcare and care workers
Vaccination, available for Ebola virus disease specifically, used in outbreak response
Community engagement and contact tracing during outbreaks
diagnosis: Diagnosed through laboratory testing of blood or other body fluids (such as RT-PCR) to detect the virus, in the context of clinical symptoms and known exposure or travel history.
treatment: Early supportive care with rehydration and treatment of specific symptoms significantly improves survival; monoclonal antibody treatments approved for Ebola virus disease can improve outcomes when given early.
when_to_seek_care: Seek immediate medical care and isolation for fever and other compatible symptoms after possible exposure to Ebola, such as travel to an outbreak area or contact with a known case.
related_conditions: Marburg virus disease (a related, similarly severe viral hemorrhagic fever)

description: A viral infection that attacks the liver; infection acquired in infancy is much more likely to become chronic than infection acquired in adulthood, which is why infant vaccination is a global priority.
symptoms: Often no symptoms, especially in young children
clinical_signs: Jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes)
Dark urine
Hepatomegaly (enlarged liver) on examination
warning_signs: Marked jaundice
Signs of advanced liver disease (fluid buildup/ascites, confusion, easy bruising)
risk_factors: Being born to a mother with hepatitis B
Injection drug use with shared equipment
Healthcare or occupational exposure to blood
Living in or originating from a high-prevalence region
causes: Caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV); spread through contact with infected blood or body fluids (semen, vaginal fluids), from mother to child at birth, needlestick injuries, tattooing/piercing with contaminated equipment, or sharing needles.
prevention: Hepatitis B vaccination, including a birth dose for infants
Hepatitis B immune globulin plus vaccine for infants born to infected mothers
Safe injection practices and blood screening
Safer sex practices
diagnosis: Blood tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and related markers; WHO recommends testing of blood donors, pregnant women, and people in high-risk groups.
treatment: No specific treatment exists for acute hepatitis B beyond supportive care; chronic hepatitis B can be managed with oral antiviral medications (WHO recommends tenofovir or entecavir) that suppress the virus, though these usually do not cure the infection.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical evaluation for symptoms such as jaundice, persistent fatigue, or abdominal pain, or for testing if you may have been exposed or belong to a higher-risk group.

description: A viral liver infection that can cause both acute and chronic illness; no vaccine exists, but direct-acting antivirals can cure more than 95% of infected people.
symptoms: Often no symptoms in acute infection
clinical_signs: Jaundice (yellowing of skin or eyes)
Dark urine
Hepatomegaly or signs of cirrhosis in chronic disease
warning_signs: Marked abdominal pain
Signs of decompensated cirrhosis (ascites, confusion, gastrointestinal bleeding)
risk_factors: Injection drug use with shared equipment
Sexual practices leading to blood exposure
causes: Caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV); spread through contact with infected blood, including unsafe injections and medical procedures, unscreened blood transfusions, sharing needles/syringes among people who inject drugs, and sexual practices involving blood exposure.
prevention: Safe injection practices and avoiding needle-sharing
Screening of donated blood and organs
Safer sex practices
No vaccine currently exists, so prevention relies on avoiding blood exposure
diagnosis: Blood test for HCV antibodies to determine exposure, followed by a nucleic acid test to confirm chronic infection.
treatment: Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) medicines cure more than 95% of people with hepatitis C, typically with a course of oral therapy.
when_to_seek_care: Seek testing if you have risk factors for exposure to infected blood, and seek medical evaluation for symptoms such as jaundice, dark urine, or persistent fatigue.

also_known_as: Human immunodeficiency virus / Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
description: A viral infection that attacks the body's CD4 immune cells; AIDS is the most advanced stage, defined by opportunistic infections or related cancers. No cure exists, but antiretroviral therapy allows long, healthy lives.
symptoms: Flu-like illness (fever, sore throat, headache, rash) within weeks of initial infection
clinical_signs: Generalized lymphadenopathy
Oral candidiasis or oral hairy leukoplakia
Wasting in advanced disease
Low CD4 cell count on laboratory testing
warning_signs: Persistent fever and night sweats
Significant unexplained weight loss
Chronic diarrhea
Opportunistic infections (e.g., tuberculosis, severe fungal or viral infections)
HIV-related cancers
risk_factors: Sharing needles, syringes, or other injection drug equipment
causes: Caused by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV); transmitted through contact with infected blood, semen, vaginal fluids, rectal fluids, or breast milk, most commonly through unprotected sex, sharing needles/syringes, or from mother to child during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding.
prevention: Consistent and correct condom use
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for people at high risk
Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) within 72 hours of possible exposure
Not sharing needles or syringes
Antiretroviral treatment during pregnancy and breastfeeding to prevent mother-to-child transmission
Regular HIV testing
diagnosis: HIV testing (antibody, antigen/antibody, or nucleic acid tests) using blood or oral fluid; CD4 cell count is used to monitor immune system status.
treatment: Antiretroviral therapy (ART), a combination of HIV medicines taken daily, suppresses the virus, prevents progression to AIDS, and prevents transmission when viral load is undetectable ("Undetectable = Untransmittable").
when_to_seek_care: Seek testing and medical care promptly after a possible exposure (PEP works best within 72 hours) or if experiencing flu-like symptoms after a potential exposure; anyone diagnosed with HIV should begin care and treatment as soon as possible.
related_conditions: Opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcal meningitis, etc.)
Kaposi sarcoma and other HIV-associated cancers

description: A common acute respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses that circulates worldwide each year and can cause severe illness or death in high-risk groups.
clinical_signs: Elevated temperature
Pharyngeal erythema
Rhinorrhea
Crackles or wheeze if lower respiratory tract involved
warning_signs: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath
Signs of pneumonia (persistent high fever, chest pain)
Severe dehydration
Worsening of chronic medical conditions
risk_factors: Chronic medical conditions (cardiac, pulmonary, renal, metabolic, liver, or blood disorders)
causes: Caused by influenza viruses (mainly types A and B); spread through respiratory droplets and small particles produced when infected people cough or sneeze, and via contact with contaminated surfaces.
prevention: Annual influenza vaccination
Hand hygiene and respiratory etiquette
Avoiding close contact with sick individuals
diagnosis: Primarily clinical; laboratory confirmation (such as PCR) can be used, particularly during surveillance or for high-risk patients.
treatment: Supportive care aimed at relieving symptoms, including rest and adequate fluid intake; antiviral medicines and medical care may be needed for severe cases or high-risk patients.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for difficulty breathing, persistent high fever, or worsening symptoms, especially in young children, older adults, pregnant women, or those with chronic conditions.

description: A highly contagious viral disease and leading cause of childhood mortality worldwide, preventable through vaccination.
symptoms: Tiny white spots inside the mouth (Koplik spots)
Rash starting on the face/neck and spreading downward
clinical_signs: Maculopapular rash progressing head-to-toe
Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
Conjunctival injection
warning_signs: High fever spiking above 40C (104F) with rash onset
Signs of pneumonia (difficulty breathing)
Signs of encephalitis (severe headache, confusion, seizures)
risk_factors: Children under 5 years and adults over 20-30 years
causes: Caused by the measles virus; highly contagious, spreading via respiratory droplets when an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes, and can remain airborne or on surfaces for up to 2 hours.
prevention: Two doses of measles-containing vaccine (e.g., MMR)
Maintaining high community vaccination coverage
Isolation of infected individuals to limit spread
diagnosis: Clinical evaluation of characteristic symptoms and rash, confirmed with laboratory testing of blood, nasal/throat swabs, or urine.
treatment: No specific antiviral treatment exists; supportive care includes good nutrition, adequate fluids, oral rehydration solution for diarrhea, vitamin A supplementation, and antibiotics for secondary bacterial infections such as pneumonia or ear infections.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for high fever with rash and cough, especially in unvaccinated individuals, and seek urgent care for breathing difficulty, persistent high fever, or signs of confusion.

source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
description: A contagious viral disease best known for causing painful salivary gland swelling; usually mild and self-limited but can occasionally cause more serious complications, particularly in adults.
symptoms: Puffy cheeks and swollen, tender jaw (parotitis)
clinical_signs: Unilateral or bilateral parotid gland swelling
Obscured angle of the jaw on examination
Tenderness over the parotid gland
warning_signs: Signs of meningitis or encephalitis (severe headache, stiff neck, confusion, seizures)
Testicular swelling and pain (orchitis)
Severe abdominal pain (pancreatitis)
risk_factors: Close contact settings such as college campuses or crowded communities
Close contact with an infected person
causes: Caused by the mumps virus (a paramyxovirus); spread through respiratory droplets and close contact with an infected person (e.g., saliva).
prevention: Two doses of MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine
Isolation of infected individuals during the contagious period
diagnosis: Clinical evaluation of parotitis and associated symptoms; confirmed with laboratory testing (PCR or serology) when needed, especially in vaccinated individuals with atypical presentation.
treatment: No specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive, including rest, fluids, and pain/fever medication; self-isolation is recommended for about 5 days after onset of swelling to limit spread.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical care for jaw or facial swelling with fever, and seek urgent care for severe headache, neck stiffness, confusion, or testicular pain and swelling.

description: A highly infectious viral disease that largely affects children under 5 years of age, which can invade the nervous system and cause irreversible paralysis; global vaccination has cut cases by over 99% since 1988.
clinical_signs: Asymmetric flaccid limb weakness
Absent or diminished deep tendon reflexes in affected limbs
Preserved sensation despite motor weakness
warning_signs: Irreversible paralysis (occurs in about 1 in 200 infections, usually in the legs)
Difficulty breathing if respiratory muscles are affected
risk_factors: Living in or traveling to areas with ongoing poliovirus transmission
Poor sanitation and limited access to clean water
causes: Caused by poliovirus (types 1, 2, and 3); spread person to person, mainly via the fecal-oral route, or less commonly through contaminated water or food.
prevention: Polio vaccination (oral polio vaccine or inactivated polio vaccine)
Maintaining high routine immunization coverage
Improved sanitation and access to clean water
Surveillance for acute flaccid paralysis
diagnosis: Detection of poliovirus in stool samples; clinical suspicion based on acute flaccid paralysis, which triggers mandatory investigation and reporting.
treatment: No specific antiviral treatment exists; management is supportive and symptomatic, including heat therapy and physical therapy to stimulate muscles; treatment can improve mobility but does not reverse permanent paralysis.
when_to_seek_care: Seek prompt medical evaluation for any case of sudden onset limb weakness or paralysis in a child, and ensure vaccination status is up to date, especially before travel to areas with ongoing transmission.
related_conditions: Acute flaccid myelitis (e.g., due to enterovirus D68)

specialty: Infectious Disease, Pediatrics, Obstetrics (for pregnancy-related risk)
description: A contagious viral disease usually mild in children and adults, but capable of causing serious harm to a developing fetus if a woman is infected during early pregnancy (congenital rubella syndrome).
symptoms: Mild rash starting on the face and spreading to the body
clinical_signs: Fine, pink maculopapular rash
Postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy
Transient joint swelling in adults
warning_signs: Arthritis and joint pain (more common in adults)
Signs of congenital rubella syndrome in infants born to infected mothers (heart, eye, ear, or brain defects)
risk_factors: Pregnancy without immunity to rubella (risk to the fetus)
Close contact with an infected person
causes: Caused by the rubella virus; spread through respiratory droplets from an infected person.
prevention: Rubella-containing vaccine (typically given as MMR)
Ensuring immunity before pregnancy
Avoiding contact with infected individuals during pregnancy
diagnosis: Clinical presentation combined with laboratory confirmation (serology or PCR), particularly important to distinguish from measles and to confirm during pregnancy.
treatment: No specific antiviral treatment exists; care is supportive, focused on relieving symptoms such as fever.
when_to_seek_care: Seek medical advice if a pregnant woman is exposed to rubella or develops symptoms, and seek care for fever with rash to confirm diagnosis and prevent further spread.

treatment: Often triggered by physical activity or stress and relieved by rest. Risk factors include high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, family history. Requires ECG and cardiac evaluation. If pain is severe, sudden, or at rest, treat as emergency.
Can range from harmless to life-threatening. An ECG or Holter monitor is typically needed. Fainting episodes warrant urgent evaluation.

symptoms: burning sensation in hands or feet
treatment: Often related to diabetes, vitamin deficiency, or nerve compression. Needs neurological exam and possibly nerve conduction studies.
Functional gut disorder, diagnosis of exclusion. Chronic symptoms warrant evaluation to rule out other conditions.

symptoms: Dull or sharp pain in lower back
pain radiating to leg if nerve involved
treatment: Most cases improve with rest, physiotherapy. Numbness, weakness, or loss of bladder control needs urgent evaluation.

symptoms: inability to bear weight or move the joint normally
treatment: Needs X-ray to confirm. Visible deformity or inability to move the limb requires urgent imaging.

symptoms: Itchy red rash with defined edges
treatment: Common and treatable with antifungal creams. Spreading rapidly or affecting large areas needs evaluation.

condition: Common Cold / Viral Upper Respiratory Infection
treatment: Usually self-limiting, resolves in 7-10 days. Supportive care recommended.
Can be viral or bacterial. Persistent symptoms beyond 10 days may need antibiotics.
Common mental health condition, very treatable with therapy and/or medication. Persistent symptoms affecting daily life warrant evaluation.
Common in older men. Complete inability to urinate (urinary retention) is an emergency requiring immediate care.

symptoms: Cramping lower abdominal pain during periods
treatment: Very common. Usually manageable with pain relief and heat. Severe pain that disrupts daily life, or pain with heavy/irregular bleeding, warrants gynecological evaluation.
Confirm with a pregnancy test and obstetric evaluation. Heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, or fainting during pregnancy is an emergency.
Common in children, usually viral. Fever above 40°C, a child who is difficult to wake, a rash that doesn't fade under pressure, or signs of dehydration needs urgent pediatric evaluation.
Common, contagious viral illness in children, usually mild and self-limiting. Refusal to drink fluids or signs of dehydration needs evaluation.

symptoms: Itchy raised red welts on skin that can move/change location
treatment: Often allergic in origin. Usually resolves with antihistamines. If accompanied by facial/throat swelling or breathing difficulty, treat as anaphylaxis emergency.
Contagious skin infestation requiring topical treatment and household-level precautions. Close contacts should be evaluated too.
Usually viral, sometimes bacterial (strep). Severe difficulty swallowing or breathing, or drooling in a child, needs urgent evaluation.

symptoms: swollen tonsils sometimes with white patches
treatment: Can be viral or bacterial. Recurrent episodes may need ENT evaluation. Difficulty breathing or swallowing saliva needs urgent care.

symptoms: Brief spinning sensation triggered by head movement
treatment: Common inner-ear condition, often resolves with repositioning maneuvers. Vertigo with slurred speech, weakness, or persistent severe symptoms needs urgent neurological evaluation to rule out stroke.

symptoms: blurred vision that improves with blinking
treatment: Common, often related to screen use or environment. Managed with lubricating drops. Persistent symptoms warrant an eye exam.

symptoms: Painful red bump on eyelid margin
treatment: Usually resolves with warm compresses. Spreading redness, vision changes, or significant swelling needs evaluation.
Sudden vision changes or eye trauma are time-sensitive emergencies — same-day or immediate ophthalmology evaluation is needed to prevent permanent vision loss.
Common and treatable, though symptoms can closely mimic a heart attack. First episode with chest pain should be medically evaluated to rule out cardiac causes before assuming panic attack.
Common, often linked to stress, anxiety, or habits. Persistent insomnia affecting daily function warrants evaluation.
Develops over weeks to months. Managed with physiotherapy; sometimes requires injections. More common with diabetes.

Needs dental evaluation; may indicate cavity, abscess, or cracked tooth. Facial swelling spreading toward the eye or throat, fever, or difficulty swallowing/breathing needs emergency care (risk of spreading infection).
